28.document_title: Kate Sheppard: Pioneer of Women's Suffrage in New Zealand - Life and Legacy
28.document_summary: Katherine Wilson Sheppard (1847-1934) was a pioneering feminist and political leader who championed women's suffrage in New Zealand. Born in Liverpool, she immigrated to New Zealand in 1869 and settled in Christchurch. After joining the Women's Christian Temperance Union in 1885, she recognized that voting rights were essential for social reforms. As national superintendent of the franchise department from 1887, Sheppard coordinated campaigns resulting in three major petitions to Parliament, with the largest containing nearly 32,000 signatures. Her efforts culminated in the Electoral Act 1893, making New Zealand the first country where all women could vote. She founded and led the National Council of Women (1896-1899) and edited the White Ribbon newspaper, advocating for women's economic independence and constitutional reforms. Following her departure to England in 1903, she remained active in the suffrage movement through writing and correspondence. After returning to New Zealand in 1904, she helped revive the National Council of Women in 1916 and was elected honorary vice president of the International Council of Women in 1909. She experienced significant personal events including her son Douglas's death in 1910, her husband's death in 1915, and her own remarriage in 1925. Kate Sheppard died on 13 July 1934 at age 78, leaving a lasting legacy as a pioneering figure in New Zealand's women's franchise movement.

29.document_title: Kate Milligan Edger: Pioneer of Women's Education in New Zealand
29.document_summary: Kate Milligan Edger (1857-1935) was the first woman in the British Empire to earn a bachelor of arts degree, awarded on 11 July 1877. Born in England to Reverend Samuel Edger, she immigrated to New Zealand as a child. Despite barriers to girls' education, she studied with boys at Auckland College and obtained a scholarship to the University of New Zealand. After graduating, she taught at Christchurch Girls' High School and earned an MA in 1882. She became the first principal of Nelson College for Girls in 1883, establishing it as a premier institution for girls' education. After marrying William Albert Evans in 1890, she continued her career as an educator and community activist in Wellington, teaching, coaching students, and examining for university entrance until 1929. She was active in suffrage, temperance, and child protection movements. Her pioneering achievement demonstrated women's intellectual capacity and established her as a leading advocate for women's education in New Zealand.

30.text:
[Page 7] In 1916 Kate Sheppard, Christina Henderson and Jessie Mackay met with the intention of reconvening the National Council of Women. Personal letters were sent to women in the various centres; local branch councils were formed in the main centres. Kate Sheppard was unable to attend the first conference of the revived council in Wellington in 1919, but her address, written in her capacity as founding president, was read for her. She was made a national life member in 1923.

1.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of voting rights in New Zealand from 1853 through the 20th century. Initially restricted to male British subjects aged 21+ with property qualifications, the franchise gradually expanded: miners gained rights in 1860, Māori men in 1867 through four dedicated electorates, and all adult European men in 1879. Most significantly, New Zealand became the first self-governing nation to grant women full voting rights on 19 September 1893, following campaigns by the Women's Christian Temperance Union that collected nearly 32,000 signatures, with approximately 80% of eligible women registering to vote subsequently. The document details property qualifications, plural voting practices, and exclusions affecting various groups. Key 20th-century reforms include lowering the voting age from 21 to 18 (1969-1974), removing the "British subject" requirement in 1975 to allow permanent residents to vote, and allowing Māori electors to choose between the Māori roll or general roll. These reforms demonstrate New Zealand's progressive journey toward universal democratic participation.

chunkHighlights.text: Votes for women

On 19 September 1893, when the governor, Lord Glasgow, signed a new Electoral Act into law, New Zealand became the first self-governing country in the world to grant the right to vote to all adult women. At the time this was a truly radical change: many other democracies did not allow women to vote until decades later.

2.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of women's movements in Aotearoa New Zealand from the late 19th century through the early 2000s. It begins with the Canterbury Women's Institute (1892) and the Women's Christian Temperance Union (WCTU) led by Kate Sheppard, which spearheaded the suffrage campaign resulting in New Zealand becoming the first country to grant women the right to vote in 1893. The document details working-class women's activism through tailoresses' unions and the suffrage movement that collected over 30,000 petition signatures. Following the 1893 victory, numerous women's organizations emerged addressing marriage equality, divorce laws, employment rights, and civil disabilities. The mid-20th century witnessed incremental progress with women gaining the right to stand for Parliament (1919) and the election of the first female MP Elizabeth McCombs (1933). The late 1960s-1970s marked a dramatic shift with the emergence of the women's liberation movement, which adopted radical approaches including consciousness-raising and challenged traditional gender roles. This period saw the development of socialist and Marxist feminist groups like the Working Women's Alliance, alongside major campaigns for economic equality, equal pay legislation (1960, 1972), and pay equity initiatives (1980s). The document extensively covers feminist activism across multiple sectors: healthcare reform through the Homebirth Association and Save the Midwives Association; education initiatives addressing sex-role stereotyping; arts and spirituality movements; and violence prevention efforts including women's refuges (established 1974) and rape crisis centers (from 1978). It documents Māori-specific services like Te Kākano o te Whānau (1985) and Women Against Pornography (1983), whose activism contributed to the Films, Videos and Publications Classification Act (1993). Throughout, the document highlights internal divisions within movements regarding class, race, and sexuality, while demonstrating broad-based women's political engagement.

chunkHighlights.text: ‘We used to hear only of women’s rights,’ wrote the editor of the New Zealand Herald in 1878, ‘now we hear about their liberty and even what seems like their licence’. 1 Some women wanted not only an equal partnership in marriage, but also sexual fulfilment and the right to control their fertility.
By the end of the 1880s the right to vote in national elections was the focus of a mass movement, spearheaded by the Women’s Christian Temperance Union (WCTU).

In 1893 New Zealand became the first country in the world to give women (both Pākehā and Māori) the right to vote in general elections. After this, activists turned their attention to other issues. Debate and lobbying focused on women’s rights within marriage, employment rights, and the repeal, reform or passing of legislation concerning prostitution, the age of consent, incest and other matters.
Māori women sought the right to vote for, and stand for, Te Kotahitanga, the Māori parliament. They also joined with other women in the temperance movement.

In the early 1900s the radicalism of the 1880s and 1890s died down. Differences between some groups and the ageing of many of those involved led to less activism around women’s issues. Although some groups continued to campaign, others faded away.

5.fileDescription: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth examination of New Zealand's Parliament, covering its legislative system, historical evolution, and contemporary governance structures. It explains Parliament's fundamental structure and functions, including the House of Representatives and governor-general, detailing how elected representatives pass laws, oversee government, and approve funding. The document covers the complete legislative process, including the three-reading system for bills, select committees, and parliamentary procedures. Historically, it traces Parliament's development from 1854 through 2023, highlighting major milestones including women's suffrage in 1893 (making New Zealand the first country to grant women's voting rights), Māori representation beginning in 1867, and the introduction of the Mixed-Member Proportional (MMP) representation system in 1996. It explains responsible government and parliamentary accountability, detailing how the opposition holds government accountable through debates, question time, and scrutiny. The document describes the physical parliamentary complex in Wellington and outlines mechanisms for public engagement, including petitions, submissions, and select committee participation. It addresses significant institutional changes including the abolition of the Legislative Council in 1951, parliamentary modernization in the 1980s, and the formation of the Māori Party in 2004. Notable developments include improved ethnic representation (Māori MPs rising from 13% to 27%, Pacific Islander representation from 3% to 6%, and Asian MPs from 1% to 7%), and the transformation from a bicameral system with 37 MPs in 1854 to a 120-member unicameral legislature under MMP.

response.response_text:
## A World First for Women's Suffrage

New Zealand made history on **19 September 1893**, when Governor Lord Glasgow signed the Electoral Act into law, making New Zealand the first self-governing country in the world to grant all adult women the right to vote. [[1]](cite://1/1)

![embed-1](embed://1)

This was a genuinely radical achievement — many other democracies wouldn't extend the same right to women until decades later. [[1]](cite://1/2) Crucially, the right applied to both Pākehā and Māori women. [[2]](cite://2/1)[[3]](cite://3/1)

## The Road to the Vote

The campaign was hard-won. The Women's Christian Temperance Union (WCTU), established in 1885, led the charge, with Kate Sheppard as a key organiser. [[4]](cite://4/1) Suffragists knocked on doors and visited factories across the country, gathering signatures on three major petitions in 1891, 1892, and 1893. [[5]](cite://5/1) The final petition — signed by nearly one-quarter of all adult women in the colony — was so long it ran to 300 yards of names when unrolled in Parliament. [[5]](cite://5/2)

![embed-2](embed://2)

In Parliament, a franchise bill passed in 1893 after two Legislative Council members unexpectedly gave it their support, despite significant opposition from many MPs. [[6]](cite://6/1)

## Women Rush to the Polls

The response from women was immediate and enthusiastic. Within just six weeks of the Electoral Bill passing, 78 percent of adult women had enrolled to vote. On polling day, 28 November, 85 percent of those enrolled cast their ballots. [[7]](cite://7/1) New Zealand had become the first country in which all women exercised the right to vote. [[8]](cite://8/1)

Would you like to know more about Kate Sheppard and the key figures behind the suffrage campaign?

[6] [New Zealand Parliament: Comprehensive Guide to Legislative System, Evolution, and Democratic Governance](https://teara.govt.nz/en/parliament)
[7] [Polling Day, New Plymouth, 1893](https://www.nzgeo.com/stories/a-leap-into-the-light/)

1.document_title: New Zealand Electoral History: The Evolution of Voting Rights from 1853 to the 20th Century
1.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of voting rights in New Zealand from 1853 through the 20th century. Initially restricted to male British subjects aged 21+ with property qualifications, the franchise gradually expanded: miners gained rights in 1860, Māori men in 1867 through four dedicated electorates, and all adult European men in 1879. Most significantly, New Zealand became the first self-governing nation to grant women full voting rights on 19 September 1893, following campaigns by the Women's Christian Temperance Union that collected nearly 32,000 signatures, with approximately 80% of eligible women registering to vote subsequently. The document details property qualifications, plural voting practices, and exclusions affecting various groups. Key 20th-century reforms include lowering the voting age from 21 to 18 (1969-1974), removing the "British subject" requirement in 1975 to allow permanent residents to vote, and allowing Māori electors to choose between the Māori roll or general roll. These reforms demonstrate New Zealand's progressive journey toward universal democratic participation.

2.text:
[Page 4] ‘We used to hear only of women’s rights,’ wrote the editor of the New Zealand Herald in 1878, ‘now we hear about their liberty and even what seems like their licence’. 1 Some women wanted not only an equal partnership in marriage, but also sexual fulfilment and the right to control their fertility. By the end of the 1880s the right to vote in national elections was the focus of a mass movement, spearheaded by the Women’s Christian Temperance Union (WCTU). 1890s In 1893 New Zealand became the first country in the world to give women (both Pākehā and Māori) the right to vote in general elections. After this, activists turned their attention to other issues. Debate and lobbying focused on women’s rights within marriage, employment rights, and the repeal, reform or passing of legislation concerning prostitution, the age of consent, incest and other matters. Māori women sought the right to vote for, and stand for, Te Kotahitanga, the Māori parliament. They also joined with other women in the temperance movement. 1900s In the early 1900s the radicalism of the 1880s and 1890s died down. Differences between some groups and the ageing of many of those involved led to less activism around women’s issues. Although some groups continued to campaign, others faded away.
{}

2.document_title: Women's Movements in Aotearoa New Zealand: From 19th Century Suffrage to Contemporary Activism (1892-2000s)
2.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of women's movements in Aotearoa New Zealand from the late 19th century through the early 2000s. It begins with the Canterbury Women's Institute (1892) and the Women's Christian Temperance Union (WCTU) led by Kate Sheppard, which spearheaded the suffrage campaign resulting in New Zealand becoming the first country to grant women the right to vote in 1893. The document details working-class women's activism through tailoresses' unions and the suffrage movement that collected over 30,000 petition signatures. Following the 1893 victory, numerous women's organizations emerged addressing marriage equality, divorce laws, employment rights, and civil disabilities. The mid-20th century witnessed incremental progress with women gaining the right to stand for Parliament (1919) and the election of the first female MP Elizabeth McCombs (1933). The late 1960s-1970s marked a dramatic shift with the emergence of the women's liberation movement, which adopted radical approaches including consciousness-raising and challenged traditional gender roles. This period saw the development of socialist and Marxist feminist groups like the Working Women's Alliance, alongside major campaigns for economic equality, equal pay legislation (1960, 1972), and pay equity initiatives (1980s). The document extensively covers feminist activism across multiple sectors: healthcare reform through the Homebirth Association and Save the Midwives Association; education initiatives addressing sex-role stereotyping; arts and spirituality movements; and violence prevention efforts including women's refuges (established 1974) and rape crisis centers (from 1978). It documents Māori-specific services like Te Kākano o te Whānau (1985) and Women Against Pornography (1983), whose activism contributed to the Films, Videos and Publications Classification Act (1993). Throughout, the document highlights internal divisions within movements regarding class, race, and sexuality, while demonstrating broad-based women's political engagement.

3.text:
[Page 5] Responses to discrimination For women, change between the mid 19th century and the early 21st century has been profound. There have been two periods of intense activism. In the 1880s and 1890s women and their male supporters fought for women to be able to vote, for women’s rights within marriage, and against the double standard that prevailed in relation to sexual behaviour. In 1893, as a result of efforts by the Women’s Christian Temperance Union and other suffragist groups, New Zealand became the first country in the world to give women (Pākehā and Māori) the right to vote in national elections. Many women also worked to repeal the Contagious Diseases Act 1869, which legalised the inspection of women for venereal disease and their confinement for compulsory treatment. This legislation was repealed in 1910. Women also highlighted the need for women’s rights within marriage and as a result the Married Women’s Property Act was passed in 1884. Married women got the right to hold property in their own name and enter into contracts independently of their husbands.

3.document_title: Women's Rights and Equality in New Zealand: A Comprehensive Historical Analysis from the 19th to 21st Century
3.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of women's rights and equality in New Zealand from the 19th century to the early 21st century across multiple domains. It examines how colonisation undermined Māori women's traditional power and how European settlers' gender ideologies shaped laws, property rights, education, and employment. Key legal milestones include the Married Women's Property Act (1884), women's suffrage in 1893 (first country globally), equal pay legislation (1960-1972), marital rape criminalization (1985), and the Human Rights Commission Act (1977). The document documents two major waves of feminist activism: the 1880s-1890s suffrage movement and the 1970s-1980s women's liberation movement. Progress is evident in women's increased parliamentary representation (60 of 120 MPs by 2022), three female prime ministers, and expanded access to education and employment. Women now comprise 61% of tertiary students and achieved academic parity with boys. However, persistent inequalities remain, including wage gaps (12% in 2016), underrepresentation in STEM fields and leadership roles, occupational segregation, and high rates of intimate partner violence. The document also examines women's roles in the arts, sports, religion, and cultural participation, highlighting both barriers overcome and ongoing disparities.

4.text:
[Page 15] New Zealand was the first country to introduce votes for women. The possibility was discussed in Parliament from the 1870s but was not taken seriously until the Women’s Christian Temperance Union organised in the late 1880s and petitioned Parliament. In the early 1890s many MPs opposed legislation allowing women to vote, including Richard John Seddon, who became premier in 1893. In that year a franchise bill went through Parliament after two Legislative Council members unexpectedly gave it their support. Women flocked to the polls in late 1893 and at subsequent elections.

4.document_title: New Zealand Parliament: Comprehensive Guide to Legislative System, Evolution, and Democratic Governance
4.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth examination of New Zealand's Parliament, covering its legislative system, historical evolution, and contemporary governance structures. It explains Parliament's fundamental structure and functions, including the House of Representatives and governor-general, detailing how elected representatives pass laws, oversee government, and approve funding. The document covers the complete legislative process, including the three-reading system for bills, select committees, and parliamentary procedures. Historically, it traces Parliament's development from 1854 through 2023, highlighting major milestones including women's suffrage in 1893 (making New Zealand the first country to grant women's voting rights), Māori representation beginning in 1867, and the introduction of the Mixed-Member Proportional (MMP) representation system in 1996. It explains responsible government and parliamentary accountability, detailing how the opposition holds government accountable through debates, question time, and scrutiny. The document describes the physical parliamentary complex in Wellington and outlines mechanisms for public engagement, including petitions, submissions, and select committee participation. It addresses significant institutional changes including the abolition of the Legislative Council in 1951, parliamentary modernization in the 1980s, and the formation of the Māori Party in 2004. Notable developments include improved ethnic representation (Māori MPs rising from 13% to 27%, Pacific Islander representation from 3% to 6%, and Asian MPs from 1% to 7%), and the transformation from a bicameral system with 37 MPs in 1854 to a 120-member unicameral legislature under MMP.

5.text:
[Page 11] In 150 years, women in New Zealand moved from political insignificance to a position of legal equality with men. In the mid 19th century, women could not vote, stand for election, serve on a jury, sit as a judge, or keep their New Zealand nationality if married to a foreign national. In the late 19th century women won the vote; in the 20th century they won the right to stand for Parliament, to retain their own nationality after marriage, to serve on a jury, and to sit as justices of the peace and judges. The Ministry of Women’s Affairs was established in 1986. In the 21st century women still lagged behind in practice, but the possibility of equality was real.

6.document_title: Scottish Immigration and Cultural Heritage in New Zealand (1840-1945 and Beyond)
6.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces Scottish immigration to New Zealand from the late 18th century through the mid-20th century. Early Scottish presence included sailors, whalers, and sealers, with organized settlement beginning in 1840s when Scots comprised about 20% of British migrants. The Otago settlement, founded in 1847-1848 by Free Church Scots, became a Scottish heartland in southern New Zealand. Between 1853-1870, Scots comprised over 30% of UK-born immigrants, peaking at nearly 18% of the total non-Māori population in 1864. The Scottish-born population peaked at 54,810 in 1886 and 54,188 by 1936. Scottish immigrants were primarily farmers, artisans, and skilled workers who significantly shaped New Zealand's development. In education, Scottish values influenced New Zealand's 1877 education system modeled after Scotland's 1872 system, with Scottish educators establishing the country's first university in Otago (1869). Notable figures include Ernest Rutherford and Prime Minister Peter Fraser. Scottish cultural heritage remains visible through surnames, Caledonian societies, pipe bands, Highland games, and Burns Night celebrations. Despite most settlers being Lowlanders, Highland symbols and Scottish identity persisted through community organizations that remain active today.

7.document_title: New Zealand's Constitution: Comprehensive Overview of Sources, Conventions, and Democratic Framework
7.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines New Zealand's unique constitutional structure comprising multiple laws, court judgments, government documents, and conventions rather than a single written document. It covers foundational concepts including the landmark case Fitzgerald v Muldoon (1976), which established that the Prime Minister cannot suspend laws. Key sources include UK statutes (Magna Carta, Bill of Rights Act 1689), NZ Parliament statutes (Constitution Act 1986, Electoral Act 1993), and constitutional conventions governing ministerial responsibility and caretaker protocols. The document details the executive, legislative, and independent judiciary structures with separation of powers. It examines New Zealand's constitutional evolution around two pillars: the Treaty of Waitangi (1840)—an agreement between the British Crown and Māori chiefs—and representative democracy, with voting rights extended to all adult males (1879) and women (1893). The Waitangi Tribunal (established 1975) reinterpreted the Treaty's meaning in the late 20th century. Mixed-member proportional representation (1996) fundamentally altered constitutional dynamics. The document traces executive power evolution from the 1930s-1990s, describing how reforms including the Official Information Act 1982 and Bill of Rights Act 1990 limited executive authority. New Zealand's constitution is notably flexible, changing through statute amendments and convention shifts, with citizens protected through complaint mechanisms including ombudsmen and human rights commissions. Parliament maintains supremacy stronger than other Westminster democracies.

8.document_title: New Zealand History: From Māori Settlement to Modern Bicultural Society
8.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces New Zealand's historical trajectory from Māori settlement around 1250-1300 CE through the early 21st century. It covers Polynesian settlement and tribal societies, European discovery by Abel Tasman (1642) and James Cook (1769-70), and early European interaction through sealers, whalers, and traders. From 1814, missionaries introduced Christianity and European farming techniques. The Treaty of Waitangi (1840) established British sovereignty while guaranteeing Māori rights, though interpretation differences complicated implementation. European settlement escalated through the New Zealand Company, the 1852 Constitution Act, and land conflicts resulting in the Taranaki Wars and Waikato campaign with large-scale land confiscation. Economic development progressed through wool production, gold discoveries, Julius Vogel's public works program, and the frozen-meat industry. Politically, the Liberal Party's 1890 victory established a "family farm" economy, women's suffrage followed in 1893, and the First World War established the Anzac tradition. Labour's 1935 victory under Michael Joseph Savage introduced welfare reforms, while Labour's 1984 economic liberalization transformed the nation. From the 1970s onwards, New Zealand underwent bicultural and multicultural transformation, highlighted by the 1981 Springbok rugby tour, the Waitangi Tribunal's establishment (1975), Māori cultural renaissance and language revitalization, and the emergence of significant Pasifika and Asian populations.

[Page 1] 19th century women’s movement In the 19th century New Zealand women were part of an international movement fighting for women’s rights. They objected to inequalities in marriage, education, employment and politics and to not being allowed to vote. Temperance and the vote Many women campaigned for temperance limiting the sale and drinking of alcohol. They were worried about alcohol abuse and its effects on women and children. The New Zealand Women’s Christian Temperance Union (WCTU) was set up in 1885. It was the first national women’s organisation, and was concerned with all issues affecting women. The WCTU led the campaign for the vote for women (women’s suffrage), with Kate Sheppard a key organiser. A petition was signed by more than 30,000 women. Many other groups worked on the campaign, including tailoresses’ unions around the country. In 1893 New Zealand women became the first in the world to win the vote in national elections. Women’s groups, 1890s Many women’s groups were set up in the 1890s. They focused on the status of women in marriage, divorce laws, the repeal of the Contagious Diseases Act (a law under which women suspected of prostitution could be held and forcibly treated) and employment issues. The National Council of Women, set up in 1896, is still active in the 21st century. The mid 20th century Things improved gradually for women over the 20th century. Women could stand for Parliament from 1919, and the first woman member of Parliament, Elizabeth McCombs, was elected in 1933. Women’s liberation movement In the 1970s the women’s liberation movement became active in New Zealand. Groups formed around the country, arguing that ‘the personal is political’. Women began to see aspects of their personal lives as political. Who did the housework or childcare, and how women were expected to dress, were no longer trivial issues. 9.document_title: Women's Movements in Aotearoa New Zealand: From 19th Century Suffrage to Contemporary Activism (1892-2000s)
9.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of women's movements in Aotearoa New Zealand from the late 19th century through the early 2000s. It begins with the Canterbury Women's Institute (1892) and the Women's Christian Temperance Union (WCTU) led by Kate Sheppard, which spearheaded the suffrage campaign resulting in New Zealand becoming the first country to grant women the right to vote in 1893. The document details working-class women's activism through tailoresses' unions and the suffrage movement that collected over 30,000 petition signatures. Following the 1893 victory, numerous women's organizations emerged addressing marriage equality, divorce laws, employment rights, and civil disabilities. The mid-20th century witnessed incremental progress with women gaining the right to stand for Parliament (1919) and the election of the first female MP Elizabeth McCombs (1933). The late 1960s-1970s marked a dramatic shift with the emergence of the women's liberation movement, which adopted radical approaches including consciousness-raising and challenged traditional gender roles. This period saw the development of socialist and Marxist feminist groups like the Working Women's Alliance, alongside major campaigns for economic equality, equal pay legislation (1960, 1972), and pay equity initiatives (1980s). The document extensively covers feminist activism across multiple sectors: healthcare reform through the Homebirth Association and Save the Midwives Association; education initiatives addressing sex-role stereotyping; arts and spirituality movements; and violence prevention efforts including women's refuges (established 1974) and rape crisis centers (from 1978). It documents Māori-specific services like Te Kākano o te Whānau (1985) and Women Against Pornography (1983), whose activism contributed to the Films, Videos and Publications Classification Act (1993). Throughout, the document highlights internal divisions within movements regarding class, race, and sexuality, while demonstrating broad-based women's political engagement.

11.text: "Polling day, New Plymouth, 1893probably the earliest photograph anywhere in the world of women voting. Although women had only six weeks after the passage of the Electoral Bill to get their names on the roll, 78 per cent of adult women did so, and, on November 28, 85 per cent of these voted. When Maori women voted three weeks later, about 4000 cast their votes. These turn-outs gave the lie to the claim that New Zealand women didn\u2019t want the vote. One of the arguments in favour of women voting was that they would clean up politics. 11 was widely believed that women would vote for men of high principle and upright character. In the event, it is difficult to claim that the women\u2019s vote made a significant difference to the election outcome. The Liberals were elected in 1893, but there was a swing towards that party across the electorate, among both men and women."

21.document_title: Kate Sheppard: Pioneer of Women's Suffrage in New Zealand - Life and Legacy
21.document_summary: Katherine Wilson Sheppard (1847-1934) was a pioneering feminist and political leader who championed women's suffrage in New Zealand. Born in Liverpool, she immigrated to New Zealand in 1869 and settled in Christchurch. After joining the Women's Christian Temperance Union in 1885, she recognized that voting rights were essential for social reforms. As national superintendent of the franchise department from 1887, Sheppard coordinated campaigns resulting in three major petitions to Parliament, with the largest containing nearly 32,000 signatures. Her efforts culminated in the Electoral Act 1893, making New Zealand the first country where all women could vote. She founded and led the National Council of Women (1896-1899) and edited the White Ribbon newspaper, advocating for women's economic independence and constitutional reforms. Following her departure to England in 1903, she remained active in the suffrage movement through writing and correspondence. After returning to New Zealand in 1904, she helped revive the National Council of Women in 1916 and was elected honorary vice president of the International Council of Women in 1909. She experienced significant personal events including her son Douglas's death in 1910, her husband's death in 1915, and her own remarriage in 1925. Kate Sheppard died on 13 July 1934 at age 78, leaving a lasting legacy as a pioneering figure in New Zealand's women's franchise movement.

22.text:
[Page 3] While in London Kate Sheppard was requested by the International Council of Women to form a national council of women in New Zealand. On her return to Christchurch she found that the Canterbury Women's Institute had already called a meeting of the franchise leagues and other women's societies, in order to form a federation of women's organisations. It was decided to make this April 1896 meeting the inaugural session of the National Council of Women of New Zealand, and Kate Sheppard was elected president, a position she held for the next three years. Sheppard's absence had resulted in some disarray among her supporters in the House. A bill to include women's representation in Parliament was thwarted by her two previous stalwarts, Alfred Saunders and Sir John Hall, who wanted a separate chamber for women. Kate Sheppard had never advocated a separationist policy, and the loss of her influence meant, perhaps, that the crucial moment for women's complete political equality was also lost. The annual conferences of the NCW, often called the 'Women's Parliament', were frequently reported with full coverage by the local daily papers, and the resolutions passed were covered by the national press. These meetings also became an arena for public debate on social issues and affairs of state. In her presidential address at the second session in Christchurch in 1897 Kate Sheppard stated: 'In Wellington is every year assembled a National Council of men, which holds a session lasting several months.…From that Council women excluded.…Under these circumstances a National Council which largely represents the thinking and working women of the colony (and which, it may be remarked, costs the country nothing) becomes a necessity. I trust the day is not far distant…when the necessity for men's councils and women's councils, as such, will be swept away.' are In 1895 the WCTU began publishing its own newspaper, the White Ribbon, which was then the only paper in New Zealand to be started, owned, edited, managed and published by women. Under the editorship of Kate Sheppard this became the 'Hansard' of both the WCTU and the NCW. Its 16 pages were used to keep the branch unions informed of activities, to co ordinate and report on organisations affiliated with the NCW and to conduct the ongoing campaign for the creation of a just society within the ideals of Christian socialism. Articles were included on health and rational dress, education, education against alcohol, women's political and legal disabilities, and equal wages for women. [Page 2] The WCTU was at the forefront of the agitation for women's suffrage in New Zealand, and it was during Schnackenberg's time as national president that women in this country were granted the vote. Schnackenberg thought that this achievement was just as important as the temperance aspect of the WCTU's work. In 1893 she publicly thanked God for the enfranchisement of women and suggested that members should try to influence other women to make the best use of the rights they had gained. 23.document_title: Annie Jane Schnackenberg: Pioneer Missionary and Women's Temperance Leader
23.document_summary: Annie Jane Allen (1835-1905) was a pioneering missionary and social reformer in New Zealand. Born in England, she emigrated to New Zealand in 1861 and worked as a teacher at Wesleyan mission schools in Kāwhia and Raglan, where she married minister Cort Schnackenberg. After his death in 1880, she became a founding member and national president (1891-1901) of the New Zealand Women's Christian Temperance Union (WCTU). During her leadership, women gained voting rights in 1893. She championed temperance education in schools, women's suffrage, raising the age of consent, and repeal of the Contagious Diseases Act. Fluent in Māori, she advocated temperance among Māori communities. She also served on the YWCA board and was remembered for her sincerity and common sense.

24.document_title: Kate Sheppard: Pioneer of Women's Suffrage in New Zealand - Life and Legacy
24.document_summary: Katherine Wilson Sheppard (1847-1934) was a pioneering feminist and political leader who championed women's suffrage in New Zealand. Born in Liverpool, she immigrated to New Zealand in 1869 and settled in Christchurch. After joining the Women's Christian Temperance Union in 1885, she recognized that voting rights were essential for social reforms. As national superintendent of the franchise department from 1887, Sheppard coordinated campaigns resulting in three major petitions to Parliament, with the largest containing nearly 32,000 signatures. Her efforts culminated in the Electoral Act 1893, making New Zealand the first country where all women could vote. She founded and led the National Council of Women (1896-1899) and edited the White Ribbon newspaper, advocating for women's economic independence and constitutional reforms. Following her departure to England in 1903, she remained active in the suffrage movement through writing and correspondence. After returning to New Zealand in 1904, she helped revive the National Council of Women in 1916 and was elected honorary vice president of the International Council of Women in 1909. She experienced significant personal events including her son Douglas's death in 1910, her husband's death in 1915, and her own remarriage in 1925. Kate Sheppard died on 13 July 1934 at age 78, leaving a lasting legacy as a pioneering figure in New Zealand's women's franchise movement.

[Page 6] After an unsuccessful attempt at a rest cure, Kate Sheppard was advised by her doctors that she would need to spend the winters in the south of France. Although an attempt was made to continue the council's work by electing new officers with Kate Sheppard as president, the council went into recess in 1906. That same year Sheppard declined the office of franchise superintendent of the World's WCTU. She lived quietly, retiring from public speaking, but continued to influence the women's movement through her writing and work with the franchise and legislation department of the New Zealand WCTU, and by acting in an advisory capacity to the White Ribbon. In 1909, at the Toronto quinquennial meeting of the International Council of Women, Kate Sheppard was elected honorary vice president, even though she was unable to attend.

27.document_title: Anna Paterson Stout: A Life of Women's Advocacy and Social Reform
27.document_summary: Anna Paterson Stout (1858-1931) was a New Zealand women's rights advocate and social reformer. Born in Dunedin to Scottish parents involved in temperance and freethought movements, she married barrister Robert Stout in 1876 and supported his political career, including his tenure as premier (1884-1887). Initially constrained by family duties and her husband's prominent positions, Anna gradually developed an independent public role from the 1890s onward. She championed women's equality, political participation, and social purity reform through organizations like the Women's Franchise League and Southern Cross Society. During her time in England (1909-1912), she became actively involved with the militant Women's Social and Political Union, leveraging New Zealand's pioneering women's suffrage as evidence for the British suffrage movement. Returning to Wellington, she continued advocating for sexual equality through various campaigns, including opposition to double standards in legal proceedings and compulsory medical examinations. Her life exemplified strategic negotiation for women's advancement at a pivotal moment in women's public roles.

29.document_title: Kate Milligan Edger: Pioneer of Women's Education in New Zealand
29.document_summary: Kate Milligan Edger (1857-1935) was the first woman in the British Empire to earn a bachelor of arts degree, awarded on 11 July 1877. Born in England to Reverend Samuel Edger, she immigrated to New Zealand as a child. Despite barriers to girls' education, she studied with boys at Auckland College and obtained a scholarship to the University of New Zealand. After graduating, she taught at Christchurch Girls' High School and earned an MA in 1882. She became the first principal of Nelson College for Girls in 1883, establishing it as a premier institution for girls' education. After marrying William Albert Evans in 1890, she continued her career as an educator and community activist in Wellington, teaching, coaching students, and examining for university entrance until 1929. She was active in suffrage, temperance, and child protection movements. Her pioneering achievement demonstrated women's intellectual capacity and established her as a leading advocate for women's education in New Zealand.

1.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of voting rights in New Zealand from 1853 through the 20th century. Initially restricted to male British subjects aged 21+ with property qualifications, the franchise gradually expanded: miners gained rights in 1860, Māori men in 1867 through four dedicated electorates, and all adult European men in 1879. Most significantly, New Zealand became the first self-governing nation to grant women full voting rights on 19 September 1893, following campaigns by the Women's Christian Temperance Union that collected nearly 32,000 signatures, with approximately 80% of eligible women registering to vote subsequently. The document details property qualifications, plural voting practices, and exclusions affecting various groups. Key 20th-century reforms include lowering the voting age from 21 to 18 (1969-1974), removing the "British subject" requirement in 1975 to allow permanent residents to vote, and allowing Māori electors to choose between the Māori roll or general roll. These reforms demonstrate New Zealand's progressive journey toward universal democratic participation.

chunkHighlights.text: Votes for women

On 19 September 1893, when the governor, Lord Glasgow, signed a new Electoral Act into law, New Zealand became the first self-governing country in the world to grant the right to vote to all adult women. At the time this was a truly radical change: many other democracies did not allow women to vote until decades later.

2.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of women's movements in Aotearoa New Zealand from the late 19th century through the early 2000s. It begins with the Canterbury Women's Institute (1892) and the Women's Christian Temperance Union (WCTU) led by Kate Sheppard, which spearheaded the suffrage campaign resulting in New Zealand becoming the first country to grant women the right to vote in 1893. The document details working-class women's activism through tailoresses' unions and the suffrage movement that collected over 30,000 petition signatures. Following the 1893 victory, numerous women's organizations emerged addressing marriage equality, divorce laws, employment rights, and civil disabilities. The mid-20th century witnessed incremental progress with women gaining the right to stand for Parliament (1919) and the election of the first female MP Elizabeth McCombs (1933). The late 1960s-1970s marked a dramatic shift with the emergence of the women's liberation movement, which adopted radical approaches including consciousness-raising and challenged traditional gender roles. This period saw the development of socialist and Marxist feminist groups like the Working Women's Alliance, alongside major campaigns for economic equality, equal pay legislation (1960, 1972), and pay equity initiatives (1980s). The document extensively covers feminist activism across multiple sectors: healthcare reform through the Homebirth Association and Save the Midwives Association; education initiatives addressing sex-role stereotyping; arts and spirituality movements; and violence prevention efforts including women's refuges (established 1974) and rape crisis centers (from 1978). It documents Māori-specific services like Te Kākano o te Whānau (1985) and Women Against Pornography (1983), whose activism contributed to the Films, Videos and Publications Classification Act (1993). Throughout, the document highlights internal divisions within movements regarding class, race, and sexuality, while demonstrating broad-based women's political engagement.

chunkHighlights.text: ‘We used to hear only of women’s rights,’ wrote the editor of the New Zealand Herald in 1878, ‘now we hear about their liberty and even what seems like their licence’. 1 Some women wanted not only an equal partnership in marriage, but also sexual fulfilment and the right to control their fertility.
By the end of the 1880s the right to vote in national elections was the focus of a mass movement, spearheaded by the Women’s Christian Temperance Union (WCTU).

In 1893 New Zealand became the first country in the world to give women (both Pākehā and Māori) the right to vote in general elections. After this, activists turned their attention to other issues. Debate and lobbying focused on women’s rights within marriage, employment rights, and the repeal, reform or passing of legislation concerning prostitution, the age of consent, incest and other matters.
Māori women sought the right to vote for, and stand for, Te Kotahitanga, the Māori parliament. They also joined with other women in the temperance movement.

In the early 1900s the radicalism of the 1880s and 1890s died down. Differences between some groups and the ageing of many of those involved led to less activism around women’s issues. Although some groups continued to campaign, others faded away.

3.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of women's rights and equality in New Zealand from the 19th century to the early 21st century across multiple domains. It examines how colonisation undermined Māori women's traditional power and how European settlers' gender ideologies shaped laws, property rights, education, and employment. Key legal milestones include the Married Women's Property Act (1884), women's suffrage in 1893 (first country globally), equal pay legislation (1960-1972), marital rape criminalization (1985), and the Human Rights Commission Act (1977). The document documents two major waves of feminist activism: the 1880s-1890s suffrage movement and the 1970s-1980s women's liberation movement. Progress is evident in women's increased parliamentary representation (60 of 120 MPs by 2022), three female prime ministers, and expanded access to education and employment. Women now comprise 61% of tertiary students and achieved academic parity with boys. However, persistent inequalities remain, including wage gaps (12% in 2016), underrepresentation in STEM fields and leadership roles, occupational segregation, and high rates of intimate partner violence. The document also examines women's roles in the arts, sports, religion, and cultural participation, highlighting both barriers overcome and ongoing disparities.

chunkHighlights.text: Responses to discrimination

For women, change between the mid-19th century and the early 21st century has been profound. There have been two periods of intense activism. In the 1880s and 1890s women and their male supporters fought for women to be able to vote, for women’s rights within marriage, and against the double standard that prevailed in relation to sexual behaviour. In 1893, as a result of efforts by the Women’s Christian Temperance Union and other suffragist groups, New Zealand became the first country in the world to give women (Pākehā and Māori) the right to vote in national elections. Many women also worked to repeal the Contagious Diseases Act 1869, which legalised the inspection of women for venereal disease and their confinement for compulsory treatment. This legislation was repealed in 1910. Women also highlighted the need for women’s rights within marriage and as a result the Married Women’s Property Act was passed in 1884. Married women got the right to hold
property in their own name and enter into contracts independently of their husbands.

6.fileDescription: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth examination of New Zealand's Parliament, covering its legislative system, historical evolution, and contemporary governance structures. It explains Parliament's fundamental structure and functions, including the House of Representatives and governor-general, detailing how elected representatives pass laws, oversee government, and approve funding. The document covers the complete legislative process, including the three-reading system for bills, select committees, and parliamentary procedures. Historically, it traces Parliament's development from 1854 through 2023, highlighting major milestones including women's suffrage in 1893 (making New Zealand the first country to grant women's voting rights), Māori representation beginning in 1867, and the introduction of the Mixed-Member Proportional (MMP) representation system in 1996. It explains responsible government and parliamentary accountability, detailing how the opposition holds government accountable through debates, question time, and scrutiny. The document describes the physical parliamentary complex in Wellington and outlines mechanisms for public engagement, including petitions, submissions, and select committee participation. It addresses significant institutional changes including the abolition of the Legislative Council in 1951, parliamentary modernization in the 1980s, and the formation of the Māori Party in 2004. Notable developments include improved ethnic representation (Māori MPs rising from 13% to 27%, Pacific Islander representation from 3% to 6%, and Asian MPs from 1% to 7%), and the transformation from a bicameral system with 37 MPs in 1854 to a 120-member unicameral legislature under MMP.

chunkHighlights.text: New Zealand was the first country to introduce votes for women. In the early 1890s many MPs opposed legislation allowing women to vote, including Richard John Seddon, who became premier in 1893. In that year a franchise bill went through Parliament after two Legislative Council members unexpectedly gave it their support. Women flocked to the polls in late 1893 and at subsequent elections.

8.fileDescription: Katherine Wilson Sheppard (1847-1934) was a pioneering feminist and political leader who championed women's suffrage in New Zealand. Born in Liverpool, she immigrated to New Zealand in 1869 and settled in Christchurch. After joining the Women's Christian Temperance Union in 1885, she recognized that voting rights were essential for social reforms. As national superintendent of the franchise department from 1887, Sheppard coordinated campaigns resulting in three major petitions to Parliament, with the largest containing nearly 32,000 signatures. Her efforts culminated in the Electoral Act 1893, making New Zealand the first country where all women could vote. She founded and led the National Council of Women (1896-1899) and edited the White Ribbon newspaper, advocating for women's economic independence and constitutional reforms. Following her departure to England in 1903, she remained active in the suffrage movement through writing and correspondence. After returning to New Zealand in 1904, she helped revive the National Council of Women in 1916 and was elected honorary vice president of the International Council of Women in 1909. She experienced significant personal events including her son Douglas's death in 1910, her husband's death in 1915, and her own remarriage in 1925. Kate Sheppard died on 13 July 1934 at age 78, leaving a lasting legacy as a pioneering figure in New Zealand's women's franchise movement.

## A World First: Wāhine and the Vote

New Zealand made history on **19 September 1893**, when Governor Lord Glasgow signed the Electoral Act into law, making New Zealand the first self-governing country in the world to grant all adult women the right to vote. [[1]](cite://1/1)

![embed-1](embed://1)

The achievement was the result of years of tireless campaigning, led largely by the Women's Christian Temperance Union (WCTU), with Kate Sheppard as a key organiser. [[2]](cite://2/1) Suffragists gathered signatures across the country — knocking on doors and visiting factories — resulting in three major petitions to Parliament in 1891, 1892 and 1893. The final petition was signed by just under one-quarter of all adult women in the colony. [[3]](cite://3/1)

Both Pākehā and Māori women were granted the right to vote, making the achievement all the more significant for its time. [[4]](cite://4/1)

![embed-2](embed://2)

## Turning Out in Force

New Zealand women wasted no time exercising their new right. Within six weeks of the Electoral Act being passed, 78 percent of adult women had enrolled to vote. On election day, 85 percent of those enrolled cast their ballots — and about 4,000 Māori women voted three weeks later. [[5]](cite://5/1) In total, 65 percent of all New Zealand women over 21 voted in that first election. [[6]](cite://6/1)

The Electoral Act was passed by Parliament after two Legislative Council members unexpectedly gave it their support — despite significant opposition from many MPs, including Richard John Seddon, who had become premier that same year. [[7]](cite://7/1) Following the signing, Governor Glasgow symbolically presented Sheppard with the pen used to sign the bill. [[8]](cite://8/1)

It was a truly radical moment — many other democracies did not allow women to vote until decades later. [[1]](cite://1/2)

Would you like to know more about Kate Sheppard and the key figures who led the suffrage campaign?

## Sources

[2] [Women's Movements in Aotearoa New Zealand: From 19th Century Suffrage to Contemporary Activism (1892-2000s)](https://teara.govt.nz/en/womens-movement)

1.text:
[Page 8] Votes for women On 19 September 1893, when the governor, Lord Glasgow, signed a new Electoral Act into law, New Zealand became the first self governing country in the world to grant the right to vote to all adult women. At the time this was a truly radical change: many other democracies did not allow women to vote until decades later.

1.document_title: New Zealand Electoral History: The Evolution of Voting Rights from 1853 to the 20th Century
1.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of voting rights in New Zealand from 1853 through the 20th century. Initially restricted to male British subjects aged 21+ with property qualifications, the franchise gradually expanded: miners gained rights in 1860, Māori men in 1867 through four dedicated electorates, and all adult European men in 1879. Most significantly, New Zealand became the first self-governing nation to grant women full voting rights on 19 September 1893, following campaigns by the Women's Christian Temperance Union that collected nearly 32,000 signatures, with approximately 80% of eligible women registering to vote subsequently. The document details property qualifications, plural voting practices, and exclusions affecting various groups. Key 20th-century reforms include lowering the voting age from 21 to 18 (1969-1974), removing the "British subject" requirement in 1975 to allow permanent residents to vote, and allowing Māori electors to choose between the Māori roll or general roll. These reforms demonstrate New Zealand's progressive journey toward universal democratic participation.

2.text:
[Page 4] ‘We used to hear only of women’s rights,’ wrote the editor of the New Zealand Herald in 1878, ‘now we hear about their liberty and even what seems like their licence’. 1 Some women wanted not only an equal partnership in marriage, but also sexual fulfilment and the right to control their fertility. By the end of the 1880s the right to vote in national elections was the focus of a mass movement, spearheaded by the Women’s Christian Temperance Union (WCTU). 1890s In 1893 New Zealand became the first country in the world to give women (both Pākehā and Māori) the right to vote in general elections. After this, activists turned their attention to other issues. Debate and lobbying focused on women’s rights within marriage, employment rights, and the repeal, reform or passing of legislation concerning prostitution, the age of consent, incest and other matters. Māori women sought the right to vote for, and stand for, Te Kotahitanga, the Māori parliament. They also joined with other women in the temperance movement. 1900s In the early 1900s the radicalism of the 1880s and 1890s died down. Differences between some groups and the ageing of many of those involved led to less activism around women’s issues. Although some groups continued to campaign, others faded away.

2.document_title: Women's Movements in Aotearoa New Zealand: From 19th Century Suffrage to Contemporary Activism (1892-2000s)
2.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of women's movements in Aotearoa New Zealand from the late 19th century through the early 2000s. It begins with the Canterbury Women's Institute (1892) and the Women's Christian Temperance Union (WCTU) led by Kate Sheppard, which spearheaded the suffrage campaign resulting in New Zealand becoming the first country to grant women the right to vote in 1893. The document details working-class women's activism through tailoresses' unions and the suffrage movement that collected over 30,000 petition signatures. Following the 1893 victory, numerous women's organizations emerged addressing marriage equality, divorce laws, employment rights, and civil disabilities. The mid-20th century witnessed incremental progress with women gaining the right to stand for Parliament (1919) and the election of the first female MP Elizabeth McCombs (1933). The late 1960s-1970s marked a dramatic shift with the emergence of the women's liberation movement, which adopted radical approaches including consciousness-raising and challenged traditional gender roles. This period saw the development of socialist and Marxist feminist groups like the Working Women's Alliance, alongside major campaigns for economic equality, equal pay legislation (1960, 1972), and pay equity initiatives (1980s). The document extensively covers feminist activism across multiple sectors: healthcare reform through the Homebirth Association and Save the Midwives Association; education initiatives addressing sex-role stereotyping; arts and spirituality movements; and violence prevention efforts including women's refuges (established 1974) and rape crisis centers (from 1978). It documents Māori-specific services like Te Kākano o te Whānau (1985) and Women Against Pornography (1983), whose activism contributed to the Films, Videos and Publications Classification Act (1993). Throughout, the document highlights internal divisions within movements regarding class, race, and sexuality, while demonstrating broad-based women's political engagement.

3.text:
[Page 5] Responses to discrimination For women, change between the mid 19th century and the early 21st century has been profound. There have been two periods of intense activism. In the 1880s and 1890s women and their male supporters fought for women to be able to vote, for women’s rights within marriage, and against the double standard that prevailed in relation to sexual behaviour. In 1893, as a result of efforts by the Women’s Christian Temperance Union and other suffragist groups, New Zealand became the first country in the world to give women (Pākehā and Māori) the right to vote in national elections. Many women also worked to repeal the Contagious Diseases Act 1869, which legalised the inspection of women for venereal disease and their confinement for compulsory treatment. This legislation was repealed in 1910. Women also highlighted the need for women’s rights within marriage and as a result the Married Women’s Property Act was passed in 1884. Married women got the right to hold property in their own name and enter into contracts independently of their husbands.

3.document_title: Women's Rights and Equality in New Zealand: A Comprehensive Historical Analysis from the 19th to 21st Century
3.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of women's rights and equality in New Zealand from the 19th century to the early 21st century across multiple domains. It examines how colonisation undermined Māori women's traditional power and how European settlers' gender ideologies shaped laws, property rights, education, and employment. Key legal milestones include the Married Women's Property Act (1884), women's suffrage in 1893 (first country globally), equal pay legislation (1960-1972), marital rape criminalization (1985), and the Human Rights Commission Act (1977). The document documents two major waves of feminist activism: the 1880s-1890s suffrage movement and the 1970s-1980s women's liberation movement. Progress is evident in women's increased parliamentary representation (60 of 120 MPs by 2022), three female prime ministers, and expanded access to education and employment. Women now comprise 61% of tertiary students and achieved academic parity with boys. However, persistent inequalities remain, including wage gaps (12% in 2016), underrepresentation in STEM fields and leadership roles, occupational segregation, and high rates of intimate partner violence. The document also examines women's roles in the arts, sports, religion, and cultural participation, highlighting both barriers overcome and ongoing disparities.

4.text:
[Page 15] New Zealand was the first country to introduce votes for women. The possibility was discussed in Parliament from the 1870s but was not taken seriously until the Women’s Christian Temperance Union organised in the late 1880s and petitioned Parliament. In the early 1890s many MPs opposed legislation allowing women to vote, including Richard John Seddon, who became premier in 1893. In that year a franchise bill went through Parliament after two Legislative Council members unexpectedly gave it their support. Women flocked to the polls in late 1893 and at subsequent elections.
{}

metadata.author: John E. Martin, New Zealand Parliament

4.document_title: New Zealand Parliament: Comprehensive Guide to Legislative System, Evolution, and Democratic Governance
4.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth examination of New Zealand's Parliament, covering its legislative system, historical evolution, and contemporary governance structures. It explains Parliament's fundamental structure and functions, including the House of Representatives and governor-general, detailing how elected representatives pass laws, oversee government, and approve funding. The document covers the complete legislative process, including the three-reading system for bills, select committees, and parliamentary procedures. Historically, it traces Parliament's development from 1854 through 2023, highlighting major milestones including women's suffrage in 1893 (making New Zealand the first country to grant women's voting rights), Māori representation beginning in 1867, and the introduction of the Mixed-Member Proportional (MMP) representation system in 1996. It explains responsible government and parliamentary accountability, detailing how the opposition holds government accountable through debates, question time, and scrutiny. The document describes the physical parliamentary complex in Wellington and outlines mechanisms for public engagement, including petitions, submissions, and select committee participation. It addresses significant institutional changes including the abolition of the Legislative Council in 1951, parliamentary modernization in the 1980s, and the formation of the Māori Party in 2004. Notable developments include improved ethnic representation (Māori MPs rising from 13% to 27%, Pacific Islander representation from 3% to 6%, and Asian MPs from 1% to 7%), and the transformation from a bicameral system with 37 MPs in 1854 to a 120-member unicameral legislature under MMP.

5.text:
[Page 11] In 150 years, women in New Zealand moved from political insignificance to a position of legal equality with men. In the mid 19th century, women could not vote, stand for election, serve on a jury, sit as a judge, or keep their New Zealand nationality if married to a foreign national. In the late 19th century women won the vote; in the 20th century they won the right to stand for Parliament, to retain their own nationality after marriage, to serve on a jury, and to sit as justices of the peace and judges. The Ministry of Women’s Affairs was established in 1986. In the 21st century women still lagged behind in practice, but the possibility of equality was real.

Women whose outlooks were shaped by the Scottish readiness to educate girls played a significant role in the struggle for the franchise. They included Kate Sheppard, Learmonth Dalrymple, Margaret Sievwright and Jessie Mackay. Many of these were also leading lights in the temperance or prohibition movements. 6.document_title: Scottish Immigration and Cultural Heritage in New Zealand (1840-1945 and Beyond)
6.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces Scottish immigration to New Zealand from the late 18th century through the mid-20th century. Early Scottish presence included sailors, whalers, and sealers, with organized settlement beginning in 1840s when Scots comprised about 20% of British migrants. The Otago settlement, founded in 1847-1848 by Free Church Scots, became a Scottish heartland in southern New Zealand. Between 1853-1870, Scots comprised over 30% of UK-born immigrants, peaking at nearly 18% of the total non-Māori population in 1864. The Scottish-born population peaked at 54,810 in 1886 and 54,188 by 1936. Scottish immigrants were primarily farmers, artisans, and skilled workers who significantly shaped New Zealand's development. In education, Scottish values influenced New Zealand's 1877 education system modeled after Scotland's 1872 system, with Scottish educators establishing the country's first university in Otago (1869). Notable figures include Ernest Rutherford and Prime Minister Peter Fraser. Scottish cultural heritage remains visible through surnames, Caledonian societies, pipe bands, Highland games, and Burns Night celebrations. Despite most settlers being Lowlanders, Highland symbols and Scottish identity persisted through community organizations that remain active today.

7.document_title: New Zealand's Constitution: Comprehensive Overview of Sources, Conventions, and Democratic Framework
7.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines New Zealand's unique constitutional structure comprising multiple laws, court judgments, government documents, and conventions rather than a single written document. It covers foundational concepts including the landmark case Fitzgerald v Muldoon (1976), which established that the Prime Minister cannot suspend laws. Key sources include UK statutes (Magna Carta, Bill of Rights Act 1689), NZ Parliament statutes (Constitution Act 1986, Electoral Act 1993), and constitutional conventions governing ministerial responsibility and caretaker protocols. The document details the executive, legislative, and independent judiciary structures with separation of powers. It examines New Zealand's constitutional evolution around two pillars: the Treaty of Waitangi (1840)—an agreement between the British Crown and Māori chiefs—and representative democracy, with voting rights extended to all adult males (1879) and women (1893). The Waitangi Tribunal (established 1975) reinterpreted the Treaty's meaning in the late 20th century. Mixed-member proportional representation (1996) fundamentally altered constitutional dynamics. The document traces executive power evolution from the 1930s-1990s, describing how reforms including the Official Information Act 1982 and Bill of Rights Act 1990 limited executive authority. New Zealand's constitution is notably flexible, changing through statute amendments and convention shifts, with citizens protected through complaint mechanisms including ombudsmen and human rights commissions. Parliament maintains supremacy stronger than other Westminster democracies.

[Page 11] The Liberal government reinforced an established pattern of state involvement in the economy and regulation of society. Its old age pensions and workers’ dwellings anticipated the welfare state. In 1893, after campaigns led by women like Kate Sheppard , New Zealand became the first country in the world to give women the vote .

8.document_title: New Zealand History: From Māori Settlement to Modern Bicultural Society
8.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces New Zealand's historical trajectory from Māori settlement around 1250-1300 CE through the early 21st century. It covers Polynesian settlement and tribal societies, European discovery by Abel Tasman (1642) and James Cook (1769-70), and early European interaction through sealers, whalers, and traders. From 1814, missionaries introduced Christianity and European farming techniques. The Treaty of Waitangi (1840) established British sovereignty while guaranteeing Māori rights, though interpretation differences complicated implementation. European settlement escalated through the New Zealand Company, the 1852 Constitution Act, and land conflicts resulting in the Taranaki Wars and Waikato campaign with large-scale land confiscation. Economic development progressed through wool production, gold discoveries, Julius Vogel's public works program, and the frozen-meat industry. Politically, the Liberal Party's 1890 victory established a "family farm" economy, women's suffrage followed in 1893, and the First World War established the Anzac tradition. Labour's 1935 victory under Michael Joseph Savage introduced welfare reforms, while Labour's 1984 economic liberalization transformed the nation. From the 1970s onwards, New Zealand underwent bicultural and multicultural transformation, highlighted by the 1981 Springbok rugby tour, the Waitangi Tribunal's establishment (1975), Māori cultural renaissance and language revitalization, and the emergence of significant Pasifika and Asian populations.

9.text:
[Page 1] 19th century women’s movement In the 19th century New Zealand women were part of an international movement fighting for women’s rights. They objected to inequalities in marriage, education, employment and politics and to not being allowed to vote. Temperance and the vote Many women campaigned for temperance limiting the sale and drinking of alcohol. They were worried about alcohol abuse and its effects on women and children. The New Zealand Women’s Christian Temperance Union (WCTU) was set up in 1885. It was the first national women’s organisation, and was concerned with all issues affecting women. The WCTU led the campaign for the vote for women (women’s suffrage), with Kate Sheppard a key organiser. A petition was signed by more than 30,000 women. Many other groups worked on the campaign, including tailoresses’ unions around the country. In 1893 New Zealand women became the first in the world to win the vote in national elections. Women’s groups, 1890s Many women’s groups were set up in the 1890s. They focused on the status of women in marriage, divorce laws, the repeal of the Contagious Diseases Act (a law under which women suspected of prostitution could be held and forcibly treated) and employment issues. The National Council of Women, set up in 1896, is still active in the 21st century. The mid 20th century Things improved gradually for women over the 20th century. Women could stand for Parliament from 1919, and the first woman member of Parliament, Elizabeth McCombs, was elected in 1933. Women’s liberation movement In the 1970s the women’s liberation movement became active in New Zealand. Groups formed around the country, arguing that ‘the personal is political’. Women began to see aspects of their personal lives as political. Who did the housework or childcare, and how women were expected to dress, were no longer trivial issues. The movement boomed, with thousands of women attending United Women’s Conventions. Activists fought for women’s rights in: economics, including equal pay, financial independence for married women, and support of single mothers through the domestic purposes benefit (DPB) politics the Women’s Electoral Lobby worked to educate male politicians and get women into Parliament health, including safe, easily available

[Page 12] Milestones Between the mass movement of the late 19th century and that of the 1970s and 1980s, women inched closer to full citizenship. A trickle of ‘firsts’ marked their progress. Women won the right to stand for Parliament in 1919, and in 1933 Elizabeth McCombs became the first woman MP. In 1927 Dr Nina Muir, New Zealand’s first woman house surgeon, became the first woman president of the Medical Association of New Zealand. In 1941 Edna Pearce walked the beat as the first woman police officer. Mary Anderson became the country’s first woman judge in 1945.

11.text: "Polling day, New Plymouth, 1893probably the earliest photograph anywhere in the world of women voting. Although women had only six weeks after the passage of the Electoral Bill to get their names on the roll, 78 per cent of adult women did so, and, on November 28, 85 per cent of these voted. When Maori women voted three weeks later, about 4000 cast their votes. These turn-outs gave the lie to the claim that New Zealand women didn\u2019t want the vote. One of the arguments in favour of women voting was that they would clean up politics. 11 was widely believed that women would vote for men of high principle and upright character. In the event, it is difficult to claim that the women\u2019s vote made a significant difference to the election outcome. The Liberals were elected in 1893, but there was a swing towards that party across the electorate, among both men and women."

21.document_title: Kate Sheppard: Pioneer of Women's Suffrage in New Zealand - Life and Legacy
21.document_summary: Katherine Wilson Sheppard (1847-1934) was a pioneering feminist and political leader who championed women's suffrage in New Zealand. Born in Liverpool, she immigrated to New Zealand in 1869 and settled in Christchurch. After joining the Women's Christian Temperance Union in 1885, she recognized that voting rights were essential for social reforms. As national superintendent of the franchise department from 1887, Sheppard coordinated campaigns resulting in three major petitions to Parliament, with the largest containing nearly 32,000 signatures. Her efforts culminated in the Electoral Act 1893, making New Zealand the first country where all women could vote. She founded and led the National Council of Women (1896-1899) and edited the White Ribbon newspaper, advocating for women's economic independence and constitutional reforms. Following her departure to England in 1903, she remained active in the suffrage movement through writing and correspondence. After returning to New Zealand in 1904, she helped revive the National Council of Women in 1916 and was elected honorary vice president of the International Council of Women in 1909. She experienced significant personal events including her son Douglas's death in 1910, her husband's death in 1915, and her own remarriage in 1925. Kate Sheppard died on 13 July 1934 at age 78, leaving a lasting legacy as a pioneering figure in New Zealand's women's franchise movement.

22.text:
[Page 3] While in London Kate Sheppard was requested by the International Council of Women to form a national council of women in New Zealand. On her return to Christchurch she found that the Canterbury Women's Institute had already called a meeting of the franchise leagues and other women's societies, in order to form a federation of women's organisations. It was decided to make this April 1896 meeting the inaugural session of the National Council of Women of New Zealand, and Kate Sheppard was elected president, a position she held for the next three years. Sheppard's absence had resulted in some disarray among her supporters in the House. A bill to include women's representation in Parliament was thwarted by her two previous stalwarts, Alfred Saunders and Sir John Hall, who wanted a separate chamber for women. Kate Sheppard had never advocated a separationist policy, and the loss of her influence meant, perhaps, that the crucial moment for women's complete political equality was also lost. The annual conferences of the NCW, often called the 'Women's Parliament', were frequently reported with full coverage by the local daily papers, and the resolutions passed were covered by the national press. These meetings also became an arena for public debate on social issues and affairs of state. In her presidential address at the second session in Christchurch in 1897 Kate Sheppard stated: 'In Wellington is every year assembled a National Council of men, which holds a session lasting several months.…From that Council women excluded.…Under these circumstances a National Council which largely represents the thinking and working women of the colony (and which, it may be remarked, costs the country nothing) becomes a necessity. I trust the day is not far distant…when the necessity for men's councils and women's councils, as such, will be swept away.' are In 1895 the WCTU began publishing its own newspaper, the White Ribbon, which was then the only paper in New Zealand to be started, owned, edited, managed and published by women. Under the editorship of Kate Sheppard this became the 'Hansard' of both the WCTU and the NCW. Its 16 pages were used to keep the branch unions informed of activities, to co ordinate and report on organisations affiliated with the NCW and to conduct the ongoing campaign for the creation of a just society within the ideals of Christian socialism. Articles were included on health and rational dress, education, education against alcohol, women's political and legal disabilities, and equal wages for women.
