10.filePath: pdf/Government's freshwater bill will result in more polluted waterways, critics say.pdf
fileAuthor: Kate Green - Health Correspondent, Niva Chittock - WorldWatch Presenter/Producer
10.fileDescription: New Zealand's Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment Bill is facing significant criticism for prioritizing agricultural profit over environmental protection. The bill would relax rules for keeping farm animals out of waterways, suspend biodiversity protection requirements, and remove the "hierarchy of obligations" that currently prioritizes environmental considerations in resource consents. Critics, including environmental organizations like Greenpeace and indigenous groups such as Ngāi Tahu, warn this will increase water pollution, nitrogen contamination, and health risks including nitrate-related illnesses. Research shows 60% of freshwater sources already exceed safe nitrate levels. While some farmers argue incentives are preferable to regulation, environmental experts contend the changes represent an alarming trajectory that undermines drinking water protection and ecosystem health. The bill will be reviewed by the primary production select committee.

chunkHighlights.text: Government's freshwater bill will result in more polluted waterways, critics say

ByKate Green - Health Correspondent, Niva Chittock - WorldWatch Presenter/Producer
2024-06-01 12:06:32+12:00

The Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment
Bill will relax rules for keeping farm animals out of waterways. File photo. A bill changing freshwater protection rules is prompting more accusations of the coalition government prioritising profit over protection. The Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment Bill will make a series of "targeted changes that can take effect quickly ... while the government develops new legislation to replace the Resource Management Act 1991", according to RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop. "The bill will also speed up the process for preparing or amending national direction. The current process for making or amending national direction is unnecessarily onerous, costly, and it takes too long." Agriculture Minister Todd McClay said the government was "backing" New Zealand farmers. "Improving primary sector profitability is key to remaining competitive internationally and getting value back into farmers' back pockets." If passed, the bill would mean councils no longer need to abide by the "hierarchy of obligations" (that is, the order of priorities) laid out in the existing legislation when issuing resource consents. It would mean a relaxation of rules for keeping farm animals out of waterways - a move the government said would reduce costs for farmers - and more permissive rules for intensive winter grazing. It would also suspend requirements for councils to identify areas of precious biodiversity as new Significant Natural Areas (SNAs) and include them in district plans for the next three years, a piece of advice over which Hoggard previously faced criticism. The bill follows the repeal of the Natural and Built Environment Act and the Spatial Planning Act in December, and the introduction of the Fast-track Approvals Bill in March, with organisations like Greenpeace dubbing the changes "a war on nature". no caption Could the rule changes affect our drinking water and our health? Greenpeace spokesperson Amanda
Larsson said the rule changes would result in more polluted lakes and

rivers, and more water species' extinction. It would also likely increase
the amount of nitrogen - a main component in fertiliser and stock urine - entering waterways, which could directly impact the quality of drinking water. "Nitrate contamination of drinking water has been connected to increased risk of health issues such as bowel cancer and pre-term birth," she said. GNS Science research found almost 60 percent of freshwater sources analysed had nitrate-N concentrations of more than 0.9 milligrams per litre. The current national standard allows for a maximum of 11.3 milligrams per litre, but some overseas studies have suggested it should be as low as 1 milligrams per litre, finding a correlation with colo-rectal cancers for anything higher. "We have been finding that even public drinking water supplies in rural Canterbury in particular are approaching levels that are increasing the risk of pre-term birth - 5 milligrams per litre," Larsson said. "Ecological studies have also shown that above 1.0 mg/L, that the environmental quality of stream habitats are affected and biodiversity begins to decline." Hoggard said it was important to remember that many farmers had already excluded livestock from a "substantial portion" of waterways throughout the country. "I don't believe they get enough recognition for that." He said it would be up to regional councils to determine how winter grazing was managed. "Where there are no local rules, the onus would be on farmers to voluntarily follow good practice." Otago University Wellington research fellow Marnie Prickett said removing priority environmental implications when issuing resource consents was an "alarming trajectory". "It says to regional councils, you don't have to consider - will this protect people's drinking water? Will this be consistent with protecting a healthy waterway? "We can read between the lines there and see that it's actually just going to put commercial actions back up the chain and take away that really necessary weight that we've now got to protect people's drinking water sources and the health of their rivers." Ngāi Tahu rūnanga chair Justin Tipa. Removing protection 'unacceptable', iwi says Removing Te Mana o te Wai - the from
fundamental concept of the Essential Freshwater regulations introduced
by the previous government in 2020 - was absolutely unacceptable for
Ngāi Tahu, rūnanga chair Justin Tipa said. The High Court at Christchurch
recently ruled Canterbury Regional Council unlawfully granted an
irrigation consent in Ashburton, in part because it failed to properly take
into consideration how it would affect the nearby freshwater and coastal

waterways. "The [current] hierarchy places the health and well being of
the wai, of freshwater first. And that's a critical protection, particularly where freshwater ecosystems are under serious threat," Tipa said. Ngāi Tahu was absolutely supportive of economic development and wanted to see the regions thrive, but not at the expense of the environment, he said. "If we continue to blindly over-allocate our freshwater resources and use it in a way that's not sustainable, it's not going to benefit anyone. We can strike a better balance." Freshwater, and the wider natural environment, had been mismanaged for decades, if not centuries, he said. It was time to change that and take a more intergenerational approach, instead of working to three-year political cycles. Incentives more helpful than regulation, farmer says A farm owner says farmers are sick of rules being "forced upon us" and want to inspire change. John Burke and his brother Rick own Pukekauri Farm in Katikati in the Western Bay of Plenty. The sheep and beef farm covers 300 hectares. The brothers' environmental restoration journey began 25 years ago. The water quality was poor, running clear through protected land at the top of the catchment, but dirtied by sedimentation as it passed through the farm. "We're farming pastoral land on really steep, erosion-prone sites," John Burke said. In the early days, there was "no riparian planting, no wetlands, it was a bit of a mess", he said. Farmers want to inspire change, John Burke says. File photo. "So progressively, over that time, with the assistance of the regional council and specialist advisory services, including ecological input, we've retired what we call the red zone areas of our farm." They planted the edges of waterways and retired some steep areas, instated large setbacks along waterways and restored eight wetlands. These days, the water runs clearer, and deposits far less sediment at the bottom - and the brothers are not losing money. "By taking those red zone areas out of our farm, we have not reduced our total pastoral farming profit, we've actually maintained our total profit - not profit per hectare, but total profit - which tells us that the land we took out was contributing nothing to the bottom line,
and in many instances was running at a loss." But farmers needed
support to put up that initial cost, and access to knowledge, Burke said.

11.fileDescription:
This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's extensive river systems across both the North and South Islands, covering over 180,000 kilometres of mapped rivers including the Waikato (425 km) and Clutha (largest by volume). It details river formation through high rainfall, glacial activity, and geological processes, describing distinct river types: deep, fast-flowing rivers in the North Island hills and wide, braided rivers in the South Island's east.

The document emphasizes the profound cultural significance of rivers to Māori people, including their roles in exploration, transportation, food sources, and spiritual traditions involving taniwha (river spirits). It documents European settlement impacts including military conquest, transport use, 19th-century gold rushes, and industrial/agricultural pollution.

The content examines ecological transformations over two centuries, detailing how introduced species like rainbow trout, brown trout, and salmon impacted native fish populations. It describes the creation of eight artificial lakes along the Waikato River through hydroelectric dams (1945-1970s) and habitat loss through forest clearance. Conservation efforts are discussed, from late 19th-century catchment protection through the 1941 Soil Conservation Act to the 1981 Wild and Scenic Rivers Amendment protecting 12 rivers.

Modern challenges including invasive species like didymo, dairy farming impacts on water quality, and off-road vehicle use are addressed. The document highlights Māori guardianship cases involving the Waikato and Whanganui rivers, explores rivers' cultural significance through 19th and 20th-century art, literature, and film, and examines contemporary management practices including jet boat tourism, riparian protection through native tree planting, and regional council monitoring.

chunkHighlights.text: Since the 1980s, Māori have declared their traditional interests in rivers, water and water quality to the Waitangi Tribunal. Cases have been taken to the Environment Court since the passing of the Resource Management Act in 1991. Two of the most significant rivers in New Zealand, the Waikato and Whanganui, both await resolution between the government and the respective tribes over management and protection.

12.fileDescription: Environment Canterbury (ECan) has declared a nitrate emergency following a 9-7 council vote, amid growing water pollution concerns and public protests. Recent groundwater surveys of 349 wells revealed E. coli in 14% of wells and nitrate-nitrogen levels above safe drinking water standards in 10% of wells, with 62% showing rising nitrate trends over the past decade. The emergency declaration recognizes intensive dairy farming as a key driver of groundwater pollution. Government ministers criticized the motion as political grandstanding, while Greenpeace and residents demanded stronger action. ECan chairperson Craig Pauling outlined non-statutory interventions including working with farmers, reducing fertilizer inputs, and establishing wetlands, while acknowledging government policy changes have complicated regulatory efforts.

14.fileDescription: This comprehensive collection examines New Zealand's freshwater crisis through multiple perspectives, exploring the tension between agricultural productivity and environmental protection. The documents analyze how agricultural intensification, particularly dairy farming, has contaminated waterways like the Selwyn River, Tomahawk Lagoon, and Lake Ellesmere through nitrate, phosphate, sediment, and microbial pollution. Key themes include: environmental tipping points causing regime shifts from clear-water to algae-dominated states; regulatory challenges in controlling cumulative agricultural contamination; innovative mitigation strategies including virtual fencing (eShepherd), satellite monitoring, precision irrigation (reducing emissions up to 85%), riparian fencing, and treatment wetlands; the importance of farming's "social licence to operate" and community engagement; climate change exacerbating water quality issues through reduced flows and increased algal blooms; legacy nutrient contamination persisting 60-100 years in groundwater; and the need for transformative change from commodity exports to premium products. Solutions require integrated approaches addressing both emissions and water quality, with environmental costs reflected in land values and public funding supporting sustainable practices.

chunkHighlights.text: one place to another.

Scott Larned, a NIWA ecologist with a strong interest in how ecosystems interact with water, told me it can take 60 to 100 years for rainwater falling on the upper Canterbury Plains to percolate to the ocean, picking up and transporting contaminants from farmland as it moves through the ground.

We were standing next to the Halswell River, which runs through Lincoln, at the time. He said that if you took a beaker of water from the Halswell and aged every molecule, the average age would be 60 years, which means the water bears the signature of 60-year-old farm activities.
“Since that was prior to a lot of intensification,” he said, “it means we haven’t seen the most contaminated groundwater yet.”
Davies-Colley agreed the full impact of agricultural intensification on river-water quality will not be felt for several decades: there is still a half-century of nutrients to leak into rivers.

When it comes to water quality, “we all live downstream,” says Canadian environmentalist David Suzuki. It is relatively easy to prevent pollution of waterways from concentrated sources such as a milking shed, but much harder to contain contamination from leaky soils. New Zealand looks to innovative science, strong regulatory frameworks and an energised public to protect this precious commodity: fresh water.
Meanwhile, the government has set a goal of doubling exports by 2025, which could mean more hooves on paddocks, more fertiliser and supplemental feed, and more risk of eutrophication to rivers.
How can New Zealand avoid a hard landing on freshwater, I asked Davies-Colley.

“Across-the-board recognition that land use affects both water quality and our greenhouse gas footprint, and that we have to control what happens on land. In some catchments, meeting freshwater targets will involve combinations of mitigations such as riparian fencing and planting, treatment wetlands and denitrification filters. In other catchments, it may be necessary to de-stock or change to lower footprint enterprises.”
“But it’s no good just shutting down half of New Zealand’s export income,” added Chris Tanner, NIWA’s principal scientist for aquatic pollution. “You’ve got to find a positive way to solve this.”

Tanner, who co-leads the challenge’s innovative and resilient land use theme, says part of the problem is the fact that land values have not reflected the cost of environmental impacts. “Two properties, one very leaky and the other which retains contaminants, are likely to be valued the same if they produce the same milk solids per hectare,” he said.
Perhaps all land in New Zealand is overpriced relative to what can be produced from it, he added, because the costs of mitigating environmental damage haven’t been taken into account.

“The whole system has been allowed to drift,” he said, “because it’s hard, and it takes political will, and it’s against the tide of growth incentives. But the further out you get on a limb, the harder it is to come back.”

But come back we must. For Tanner, that means learning to look at land in a different way—“not just at how many kilograms of milkfat per hectare it might yield, but asking, ‘How susceptible is it to contaminant loss? Where are the water and contaminants moving, where are the critical leakage points, where can I achieve the best contaminant reductions?’”
Asking, too, if it’s time to rethink what the land is being used for.

15.filePath: pdf/Court decision sets up a big year for freshwater.pdf
15.fileDescription: A High Court decision in December 2025 found that Canterbury's regional council (ECan) erred in including rule 5.63 in its regional plan, which permitted farm pollution under certain circumstances. Justice Cameron Mander ruled that ECan failed to provide adequate evidence and clear reasoning for the decision, though the judicial review was ultimately barred by section 83 of the Resource Management Act due to delay. The case highlights Canterbury's critical importance to New Zealand's freshwater management, as the region contains 63% of the country's irrigated agricultural land. The judgment underscores ongoing tensions between agricultural intensification and environmental protection, with poor water quality in lowland and urban waterways. The decision sets the stage for freshwater to become a major election issue in 2026, requiring political consensus and clear vision for sustainable water management.

chunkHighlights.text: Court decision sets up a big year for freshwater

[repub:newsroom] David Williams Canterbury has almost two thirds of
the country's irrigated agricultural land area. Analysis: Canterbury is, once again, putting freshwater issues front and centre - not just for the province itself but arguably for the country, in an election year. Three days before Christmas, the High Court found Canterbury's regional council, ECan, errantly included a rule in its regional plan permitting farm pollution, under certain circumstances. But the Environmental Law Initiative, which took the judicial review, didn't get everything it wanted. The legal challenge was found to be barred by a section of the Resource Management Act, and Justice Cameron Mander said he wouldn't have quashed the rule anyway. Before delving into the judgment let's consider the context in which it landed. Over the past two years, the coalition government has prevented councils from bringing in greater protections under Labour's national policy statement to manage freshwater, ordered a review of that statement, changed the law to thwart court judgments, and foreshadowed a more permissive resource management regime, including for farmers. There's also the axe hovering over regional councils, and the government's pre-Christmas announcement of a mega-ministry, merging environment, transport, housing and urban development, and Internal Affairs' local government functions. It's reasonable to assume freshwater will be a hot topic in this year's election - partly, perhaps, because cow herds are expanding, including in areas already experiencing poor water quality. Politically, there's room within the coalition for National, New Zealand First and Act to differentiate themselves on freshwater - especially when much of the policy moves have tended in one direction. Given Act's firm, pro-farming role via Associate Environment Minister Andrew Hoggard, the National Party, in particular, has a golden opportunity to set a more centrist agenda. The bigger risk, perhaps, is staying silent on freshwater. The opposition's job may seem easier but isn't necessarily so. Articulating a vision is important - but it needs to be realistic, and easily understood. Labour had a go when it was in power by saying it wanted to see
material changes to waterways within five years. Those five years were

up in August last year, with little progress. Obviously, progress was
hindered - or reversed, in some cases - by the government quashing Te Mana o Te Wai, a policy requiring councils to put environmental health first, and halting the rollout of farm environment plans. Two big problems are getting in the way: the lack of consensus, leading to dramatic policy swings, and the time it takes for central government direction to flow through councils and their plans. (Add to that opposition from well-organised and well-funded vested interests.) If the two big political parties believe there should be a consensus for infrastructure, they should be working on similar plans for freshwater. We know what the problems are, and the fixes, while difficult, are clear. The public has already waited years while experts debated the finer points, and the Land and Water Forum honed its recommendations. What's needed now is a clear vision and funding, paired with concrete improvements over realistic timeframes, and trigger points for action if bottom lines aren't met. If politicians are unwilling or unable to protect freshwater, others are willing to intervene by taking court action, including Ngāi Tahu, and the Environmental Law Initiative. Which brings us back to the December 22 High Court judgment. A section of the Rakaia River in Canterbury. Jurisdictional precondition The Law Initiative's argument was that ECan was required, under section 70 of the Resource Management Act (RMA), to be "satisfied" rule 5.63 in the Canterbury land and water regional plan wasn't likely to cause adverse environment effects on aquatic life. (The proposed regional plan was first notified in 2012 - after John Key's government sacked elected councillors and appointed commissioners - with the council receiving the amended plan the following year, and partially approving it in August 2015.) The rule said discharging nutrients onto or into land, which may contaminate water, is permitted if the farming activity was allowed under other plan rules. Barrister David Bullock, for the initiative, said at the hearing, this was, like a controversial Court of Appeal decision, a jurisdictional precondition for which the council had produced no evidence - so the rule had to go.
Among the arguments put by ECan's lawyer Philip Maw were the case
was an attempt to re-litigate matters considered years ago, and there
was a fatal legal blow to the judicial review under section 83 of the RMA.
Farmers couldn't just immediately cease discharging nutrients, ECan
said, and farm companies argued they'd be at risk of widespread and
significant non-compliance. Quashing the rule would require thousands

of new consents to be processed, ECan said, creating a years-long
backlog. Justice Mander In his decision, Justice Mander said there was no written record to show an assessment of the likelihood of environmental effects from rule 5.63, and it wasn't explicitly addressed in an independent hearing panel's report. The issue should have been grappled with by the panel, and "squarely decided on the basis of expressed reasons". "Taken as a whole, the state of the evidence regarding the potential impact of the discharge of contaminants as a result of farming activities on the health of the region's waterways was, at best, equivocal." There was a "clear controversy", and expert witnesses expressed "competing professional views". "In large measure, the uncertainty of the expert opinion regarding the efficacy of the proposed nutrient management rules, in terms of their potential effects on water quality and consequent impact on aquatic life, and the uncertainty of the science relating to nutrient loss, contributed, at least in part, to the nutrient management rules being 'completely rewritten'." (However, rule 5.63 was largely unchanged.) The controversy centred on the connection between zones with poor water quality and the significant adverse effects from nutrient levels. But the hearing panel didn't explain how the revised rules "resolved this ambiguity". In a practical sense, Justice Mander had "considerable reservations" about whether the RMA test, of assessing the likely environmental effects of a permissive regime, could realistically be applied in such a proposed region-wide rule, or assessed with "any degree of confidence". But that didn't mean, as a matter of law, the council could shirk its statutory obligations. The council had argued its decision to include the rule was valid. But Mander said the lack of evidence, and clear reasons for its decision, "severely undermines that stance". Mander found the council did err "because the decision-making record does not allow me to conclusively determine that it properly addressed itself to that issue, or had an adequate evidential basis upon which to make that decision". (The Law Initiative's attempt to admit further evidence - a 2024 email
exchange between an ECan staffer with a Ministry for the Environment
official - was declined by the judge.) However, ECan's lawyer, Maw,
argued - and Mander agreed - the judicial review was barred by section
83 of the RMA, which limits challenges to a regional plan once it's made
operative. Last month's judgment said the court would not have been
obligated to set aside or quash the decision to include rule 5.63 in the

regional plan, because of the delay in the challenge being made, the
"significant prejudice" to farmers, and extensive changes made subsequently to the plan. "The subject of the proceeding is an administrative decision made some 10 years ago about a rule that formed part of a highly detailed and complex regulatory scheme which largely no longer applies, at least … to the 'at-risk' catchments which have since been made subject to specific, sub-regional rules." Mander declined to grant the judicial review and awarded costs to the council. Water ecosystem health is still moderate to high in the Canterbury mountains, high and hill country, but is extremely poor in lowland and urban water bodies. Canterbury: A freshwater powerhouse In a statement on December 23, the Law Institute's director of research and legal, Matt Hall, said rule 5.63 "effectively green-lit further intensive farming" in catchments "already under stress". That meant higher pollution loads were "locked in", he said, making freshwater restoration harder. "There is a clear public interest in ensuring Canterbury's freshwater is protected by evidence-based, precautionary decisions that put people and ecosystems first." Newsroom asked ECan for comment on December 23 but its offices were closed. Why is Canterbury so important to freshwater? In 2022, it had 480,000 hectares of irrigated agricultural land area, about 63 percent of the country's total. (Irrigation enables more intensive farming.) Even before a recent spike in agricultural intensification, there were serious concerns about water quality, with many degraded river catchments. At hearings in 2013, freshwater ecologist Russell Death, who gave evidence for Fish & Game, said ecosystem health in many of Canterbury's lowland and urban waterbodies was extremely poor. (Death worried increased agricultural intensification could result in significant adverse effects, if not managed properly. However, environmental scientist Shirley Hayward, for Fonterra, DairyNZ and Horticulture NZ, said data in Death's evidence "illustrates a lack of correlation between nitrate concentrations and indicators of aquatic health".) Given the decline in Canterbury
waterways, as stated, repeatedly, during
last year's Ngāi Tahu
freshwater case, there is arguably a stronger case for environment
improvements now. This article was first published by Newsroom.

retrieved_chunks.text: [Page 11] A 2010 report from MfE assessed water quality trends in 112 New Zealand lakes between 2005 and 2009. Over the study period, 12 per cent of the lakes assessed had improved, while 28 per cent had worsened. The report then extrapolated those findings across 4000 lakes smaller than a hectare, and found that 32 per cent were likely to have poor or very poor (nutrient enriched) water quality. Those surrounded by farmland fared worst: 44 per cent were eutrophic (meaning they carried excessive nutrient loads) or worse. When extrapolated, the study concluded that out of 3820 New Zealand lakes, more than a third would be eutrophic or worse. For 35 years, Levin poured its treated sewage into Lake Horowhenua. The abuses stopped in 1987, but still the lake looks jaundiced. The town now spreads its sewage over land, but some of it has been found to leach into the lake anyway. When it reflects a blue sky, it might pass a postcard test. Catch it on the wrong day, however, and it morphs into something green and glowering. In waters opaque with slime, suspended sediment and algae—“probably the result of faecal contamination from farmland runoff,” according to MfE—you wouldn’t see your hand at arm’s length. In fact, such a test would be unwise: last summer, NIWA freshwater scientist Max Gibbs warned Horizons Regional Council, which covers ManawatuWanganui, that after heavy rain, Lake Horowhenua’s waters, deemed among the 10 most polluted in the country, might well kill a small child. The problem is not just in lakes. In 2010, NIWA reported that water quality in our major rivers had declined between 1989 and 2007. Over that period, nitrogen and phosphorus loadings (see sidebar) had increased greatly at many sites. Nitrogen had increased by about 1.4 per cent each year over most of the country, and no sites recorded a drop. ## Aotearoa's Freshwater Policy: A Decade of Change and Contention

New Zealand's approach to freshwater management has shifted dramatically over the past decade — swinging between stronger environmental protections and a more deregulatory stance — and it remains one of the country's most contested policy arenas.

---

## The Legislative Foundation

The bedrock of freshwater management has long been the Resource Management Act (RMA) 1991, which provides the legal framework for using water, managing its quality, and balancing competing interests — from farmers and industry through to swimmers and iwi [[1]](cite://1/1). Regional councils have traditionally been responsible for monitoring and enforcement, with considerable variation in how they have applied national direction [[1]](cite://1/2).

The National Policy Statement (NPS) for Freshwater Management was first introduced in 2011, and it was, as Fish & Game's Neil Deans noted at the time, "30 years late" — meaning tens of thousands of water permits had been allocated in many regions without any compulsory management plan in place [[2]](cite://2/1).

---

## The Push for Stronger Protections (2013–2020)

A significant reform attempt began with the Land and Water Forum, which spent four years bringing together water users from across the spectrum to find common ground. It delivered 158 recommendations to government, which were incorporated into a *Freshwater Reform 2013 and Beyond* discussion document [[3]](cite://3/1). Among its key recommendations was the need to determine and enshrine a minimum environmental state below which water quality must not fall [[3]](cite://3/2).

The NPS was updated, and Ken Taylor, a forum member, credited it as the forum's "biggest gift to the nation," saying it forced regional councils to set actual limits on both water quality and quantity [[4]](cite://4/1).

The most significant step came in 2020, when the Labour-led government introduced what became known as the Essential Freshwater package, including an updated NPS for Freshwater Management. This introduced a concept called **Te Mana o te Wai** — placing the health and wellbeing of the waterway first, human health needs second, and social, economic, and cultural wellbeing third [[5]](cite://5/1). It also required councils to stop further degradation of waterways and wetlands, and introduced freshwater farm plans for farms above certain size thresholds [[6]](cite://6/1).

---

## The Coalition Government's Rollback (2023–present)

After the 2023 election, the National-led coalition government moved quickly to dismantle much of what Labour had built. The repeal of the Natural and Built Environment Act and the Spatial Planning Act in late 2023 was followed by the passage of the Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment Bill in October 2024 [[7]](cite://7/1).

That law:
- Excluded the Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy of obligations from resource consent processes [[7]](cite://7/2)
- Relaxed rules around stock exclusion zones and intensive winter grazing [[7]](cite://7/3)
- Paused requirements for councils to identify new Significant Natural Areas (SNAs) [[7]](cite://7/4)
- Restricted councils from notifying new freshwater plans until a replacement NPS is in place [[8]](cite://8/1)

Agriculture minister Todd McClay said the government was "backing" New Zealand farmers and that "improving primary sector profitability is key to remaining competitive internationally" [[9]](cite://9/1). Federated Farmers celebrated it as "the end of the war on farming," arguing the previous rules were "rushed through," amended eight times in three years, and unworkable [[5]](cite://5/2).

In May 2025, the government opened public consultation on sweeping proposed changes to national direction — including replacing the NPS for Freshwater Management entirely and further "rebalancing" Te Mana o te Wai to better reflect, in the government's words, "the interests of all water users" [[10]](cite://10/1).

---

## The Main Points of Disagreement

The debate cuts across several fault lines:

**Environment vs. economy**
The core tension pits environmental protections against agricultural productivity. Freshwater ecologist Mike Joy warned that most lowland rivers are no longer swimmable or fishable, and that the proposed changes would make things worse — describing the removal of wetland grazing restrictions as "suicidal" from an ecological perspective [[10]](cite://10/2). The Green Party's Lan Pham called the proposed RMA changes a "comprehensive dismantling" of environmental protections, amounting to "wholesale pollution, wholesale degradation, wholesale exploitation under the guise of growth" [[10]](cite://10/3). Labour's Rachel Brooking said the government was undoing work aimed at ensuring swimmable rivers within a generation [[10]](cite://10/4).

**Te Mana o te Wai**
The fate of this concept has become a flashpoint. Ngāi Tahu rūnanga chair Justin Tipa called its removal from resource consent processes "absolutely unacceptable," arguing that the hierarchy — which places the health of the waterway first — is "a critical protection, particularly where freshwater ecosystems are under serious threat" [[9]](cite://9/2). ACT, by contrast, wants the concept scrapped altogether, with leader David Seymour calling it "nonsensical" and "vague" [[10]](cite://10/5).

**Māori rights and water allocation**
A group of Māori landowners, Wai Manawa Whenua, took the Crown to the High Court in late 2025, arguing the existing "first in, first served" water allocation system is degrading water quality and shutting Māori out [[11]](cite://11/1). Federation of Māori Authorities chairperson Traci Houpapa said water had been fully or over-allocated in many catchments, and that Māori need to be part of designing a fair and equitable allocation system [[11]](cite://11/2).

**Central direction vs. local flexibility**
Farmers and some councils argue that nationally determined bottom lines are often unworkable at a local level, and that catchment-based, regionally tailored approaches make more sense [[12]](cite://12/1). Critics counter that the absence of binding national standards is precisely what has allowed water quality to deteriorate for decades, pointing to the Canterbury experience, where tens of thousands of permits were issued over 35 years without a compulsory management plan [[2]](cite://2/2).

**Drinking water safety**
A public health researcher at Otago University, Marnie Prickett, warned that the 2020 NPS had explicitly prioritised drinking water protection — partly in response to the deadly Havelock North campylobacter outbreak — and that proposed changes risk stripping those protections back [[13]](cite://13/1). GNS Science research found almost 60 percent of freshwater sources analysed had nitrate concentrations above 0.9 milligrams per litre, well below the current national standard but at levels some overseas studies link to bowel cancer and pre-term birth [[9]](cite://9/3).

---

## Where Things Stand in 2026

The most recent report, *Our Freshwater 2026*, paints a sobering picture. Associate professor Nick Ling of the University of Waikato said the state of freshwater "is continuing to get worse," and that decades of under-investment in wastewater infrastructure compound the problem [[14]](cite://14/1). The political consensus needed for meaningful, lasting reform remains elusive — with analysts noting that dramatic policy swings between governments, combined with the slow pace at which national direction flows through to regional plans, is itself a major barrier to improvement [[15]](cite://15/1).

Would you like to explore the specific situation in Canterbury, which holds about 63 percent of the country's irrigated agricultural land and is often described as the frontline of New Zealand's freshwater crisis?

1.text:
[Page 9] Water in New Zealand is protected by legislation, principally the Resource Management Act 1991. It provides a legal framework for using water, managing its quality, and balancing the needs of different groups who affect or use water. For example, fishers and swimmers want the lakes and rivers to be clear, while factory owners need to dispose of waste material. Regional councils throughout the country monitor water quality, and then decide how to manage land and effluent. In consultation with the local community, a council might decide to maintain high water quality in upland rivers and lakes for recreation and biodiversity, but allow some runoff and waste into lowland rivers and estuaries.

1.document_title: Water Quality in New Zealand: Comprehensive Assessment of Threats, Management Strategies, and Case Studies
1.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines water quality in New Zealand, addressing freshwater management and protection challenges. While New Zealand has high-quality freshwater by global standards, it faces significant threats from soil erosion, sewage, farm fertilizers, and algae growth. Major pollution sources include point sources (sewage pipes) and non-point sources (farm runoff), with contaminants encompassing sediments, organic matter, and dissolved chemicals like nitrate and phosphate. High nitrate levels pose particular health risks for infants. The document presents case studies of Lake Rotorua, Lake Taupō, and the Manawatū River, illustrating how human activities have degraded water quality. Management strategies outlined under the Resource Management Act 1991 include regional council monitoring, water-quality standards, and weed control methods. Key issues addressed include excessive nutrient levels causing algal blooms, invasive species like hornwort and didymo, and disease-causing organisms. Solutions involve multiple approaches: grass carp for vegetation control, restoring riparian shade, reducing nutrient inputs, improving farming practices, and implementing legislative protections. The document emphasizes voluntary farm management practices, including dairy farmer initiatives using effluent spraying and wetland treatment systems, a voluntary accord between Fonterra Co-operative Group and government entities to minimize dairying's environmental impact, and a Code of Practice for Fertiliser Use to mitigate agricultural harm.

2.text:
[Page 16] After a review of New Zealand’s soil conservation in 1964, the Water and Soil Conservation Act was passed in 1967. A Water and Soil Division was set up within the Ministry of Works and Development. Under its control were the Soil Conservation and Rivers Control Council, the Water Pollution Control Council and the Water Allocation Council. Importantly, at local level the control lay with each catchment authority, via the regional water boards. Emphasis was placed on measuring the extent and types of erosion through land inventory surveys and land capability assessments.

2.document_title: Soil Erosion and Conservation in New Zealand: Comprehensive Analysis of Causes, Types, Management, and Control Methods
2.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines soil erosion and conservation in New Zealand from the 1940s to modern times. It explains that soil contains vital nutrients essential to farming and describes natural erosion processes including wind, rain, floods, and earthquakes. The document categorizes erosion into four main types: surface erosion (sheet and wind), fluvial erosion (rill and gully), mass-movement erosion (slips and earth flows), and streambank erosion. Human activities significantly accelerated erosion—settlers cleared forests and introduced grazing animals, exposing soil. By 1997, 50% of New Zealand experienced moderate to slight erosion, with 10% severe. New Zealand loses approximately 210 million tonnes of soil annually to rivers—about 10 times the global average. Hill country erosion costs $100-150 million annually, damaging infrastructure and aquatic ecosystems. The document traces management history from early surveys (Raeside and Gibbs, 1945) through key legislation including the Soil Conservation and Rivers Control Act (1941), Water and Soil Conservation Act (1967), and Resource Management Act (1991). Conservation methods implemented since the 1940s include tree planting, aerial topdressing, new farming techniques, and dam construction. Biological control methods include reforestation with poplars and pines, riparian strips, and shelter belts. Mechanical techniques include flumes, debris dams, bulldozing, and conservation tillage. Research demonstrates that reforestation successfully controls erosion while dense pasture reduces sheet erosion but cannot prevent slips and gullies.

3.text:
[Page 1] How we use water Compared to many countries, New Zealand’s lakes and rivers are clean and clear, and the tap water is of good quality. People have contact with fresh water in many ways, including: wading in streams or rivers while tramping or fishing boating, swimming or fishing in lakes washing or drinking farm irrigation. Water quality can vary for instance, it may not be drinkable, but is usable for washing. Soil erosion When early settlers cut down the forests to make farmland, many hillsides began to erode. Soil was washed down and began to build up in rivers and lakes, sometimes smothering plants and fish. Sewage Sewage and factory waste was once piped directly into rivers and lakes. This brought unwanted nutrients, damaged the water and wildlife, and caused health problems in people. Today most sewage is treated with chemicals first. Farm fertilisers Fertilisers put onto farms contain nutrients such as nitrate and phosphate. Any that are washed into lakes and rivers upset the natural balance of nutrients in the water. Fish are harmed and some water plants (e.g. algae) grow too much. Algae and other problem plants Algae are tiny water plants. Excess nutrients in the water (e.g. from city waste or farming) can make them grow too quickly. They clog lakes and rivers, reduce water clarity and starve fish of oxygen. During low flows and high summer temperatures in the 1980s the Manawatū River had so much algae that fish were dying. There is now less pollution, but water runoff from farms still damages the water quality. Hornwort is the worst water weed. It can reach 10 metres tall underwater, smothering other plants. Protecting the water There are laws that protect New Zealand’s water, and control how it is used. The strictest standards are for drinking water. Councils test lakes and rivers for pollution, and sometimes certain fish species are used to eat up unwanted water weed. Farmers have to follow guidelines about using fertiliser and effluent, to reduce pollution in streams and lakes.
{}

[Page 15] Fluoridation Fluoride is added to some public water supplies to reduce dental decay. The Department of Health first conducted fluoride trials in Hastings in 1953. By 1978, 54% of New Zealand communities had fluoridated water; by 2016, the figure was 58%. Christchurch and New Plymouth were the only major cities without fluoridated water. A 2009 survey found that children living in fluoridated areas had 40% less severe tooth decay than children in unfluoridated areas. Local councils made decisions about the fluoridation of drinking water until the Health (Fluoridation of Drinking Water) Amendment Act 2021 transferred this responsibility to district health boards. Fluoridation illustrates how public health measures are often politicised and fiercely contested on ideological and philosophical grounds. Some people have argued that fluoridation of water supplies breaches individual rights and limits choices. In 1980 the Human Rights Commission ruled that it did not contravene human rights. In the 2010s there were further legal challenges to the fluoridation of water supplies. Consumer advocacy group, New Health New Zealand Inc., claimed in 2014 that fluoridation of water breached the right to refuse medical treatment under the Bill of Rights Act. They argued that fluoridation was a form of medical treatment that should not be compulsory. They also challenged the right of the South Taranaki District Council to add fluoride to the water supplies of Patea and Waverley. In 2018 these cases reached the Supreme Court, where a majority of judges, sometimes for different reasons, dismissed them.

Additional topics include tobacco control as a public health success story, cancer screening programmes, mental health with 20% prevalence in 12 months and 47% lifetime prevalence, water safety issues (Queenstown 1984, Havelock North 2016), and the 2017 Healthy Homes Guarantee Act addressing housing standards.

7.document_title: New Zealand Aquaculture: Industry Overview, Farming Practices, and Regulatory Framework
7.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth analysis of New Zealand's aquaculture industry, covering its development, major farming practices, and regulatory landscape. The industry, valued at $280 million by 2001, primarily focuses on three export species: green-lipped mussels, quinnat salmon, and Pacific oysters. Green-lipped mussels are cultivated using the Japanese longline system, becoming New Zealand's second most important seafood export by 2000, sold to over 60 countries. Salmon farming evolved through three methods: ocean ranching (1976), sea-cage ranching (1983) in Big Glory Bay and Marlborough Sounds, and freshwater farming in South Island hydroelectric canals, producing 8,500 tonnes in 2001 with 65% exported. Pacific oysters, cultivated starting in 1970, reached 3,500 tonnes annually by 2001 and generated $13.6 million in exports. Additional species include pāua shellfish, scallops, and sea horses. The industry operates under a dual licensing system managed by regional councils and the Ministry of Fisheries, with a government moratorium on marine farm expansion by 2002. Key challenges include regional concentration, toxic algal blooms, and tensions between farmers and Māori groups regarding seabed ownership. Despite these challenges, the industry has strong future prospects for diversifying into high-value species such as pāua, kingfish, and crayfish.

A plentiful supply is something that New Zealanders have taken for granted since the days of early settlement. Maintaining the quality has, for a long time, been largely due to the low population and the low level of contaminants from farming and urban development.

8.document_title: Water Quality in New Zealand: Comprehensive Assessment of Threats, Management Strategies, and Case Studies
8.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines water quality in New Zealand, addressing freshwater management and protection challenges. While New Zealand has high-quality freshwater by global standards, it faces significant threats from soil erosion, sewage, farm fertilizers, and algae growth. Major pollution sources include point sources (sewage pipes) and non-point sources (farm runoff), with contaminants encompassing sediments, organic matter, and dissolved chemicals like nitrate and phosphate. High nitrate levels pose particular health risks for infants. The document presents case studies of Lake Rotorua, Lake Taupō, and the Manawatū River, illustrating how human activities have degraded water quality. Management strategies outlined under the Resource Management Act 1991 include regional council monitoring, water-quality standards, and weed control methods. Key issues addressed include excessive nutrient levels causing algal blooms, invasive species like hornwort and didymo, and disease-causing organisms. Solutions involve multiple approaches: grass carp for vegetation control, restoring riparian shade, reducing nutrient inputs, improving farming practices, and implementing legislative protections. The document emphasizes voluntary farm management practices, including dairy farmer initiatives using effluent spraying and wetland treatment systems, a voluntary accord between Fonterra Co-operative Group and government entities to minimize dairying's environmental impact, and a Code of Practice for Fertiliser Use to mitigate agricultural harm.

9.text:
[Page 16] Control of water use Although water is regarded as common property, its use has been regulated to ensure that one individual or group does not adversely affect others. Under the Resource Management Act 1991, the management of water resources is the responsibility of regional and unitary councils, with a long term goal of sustainability. Maintaining or improving the water quality of lakes is of particular concern, as many lakes have shown an alarming deterioration since the 1950s.

[Page 3] Land and water Māori asserted rights over both land and water. The beds of lakes, rivers, harbours and the open sea were seen as whenua papatupu customary land. Addressing Native Minister Donald McLean and his party in the lakes district of Rotorua in 1873, Te Arawa chief Tāmihana Korokai said, ‘Haere mai e koro mā! Haere mai ki Rotorua, te whenua o Ngatiwhakaue, moana kau’ [Welcome, my friends! Welcome to Rotorua, the land of Ngatiwhakaue, which is principally water].

11.document_title: Māori Land Tenure and Customary Rights Systems
11.document_summary: This document explores the traditional Māori system of land tenure and property rights known as "take whenua." Land was historically held communally by tribal groups (hapū) with individual and family use rights for specific purposes. Key principles included discovery (whenua kite hou), ancestral rights (take tupuna), conquest (take raupatu), and gifting (take tuku). Mana whenua refers to tribal authority over land and water bodies. Continuous occupation (ahi kā), symbolized by keeping fires burning, was essential to maintain land rights. The principle of ringa kaha meant victors had to actively defend conquered lands. Abandonment caused rights to diminish from ahi kā to ahi tere to ahi mataotao. Land transfers included conditions confirmed through ceremonies and taonga (treasures). The Native Land Court, established in 1865, resolved disputes but often simplified Māori customs, preferring conquest-based claims. By 1847, Chief Justice William Martin noted Māori had appropriated all valuable land through these customary systems. The system was fluid and accommodated changing tribal relationships, with disputed lands arising from migration and inter-tribal marriage.

12.text:
[Page 15] Restoring fishing rights For many years Māori had tried without success to secure fishing rights of various kinds. In the early 1920s the government acknowledged the long standing claims of Te Arawa to traditional rights over lakes in the Rotorua region and agreed to pay compensation for the loss of fishing and burial rights in the lakes. In 1926 a similar agreement was reached with Ngāti Tūwharetoa over its rights in Lake Taupō and adjoining streams. These agreements raised Māori hopes about other treaty rights.

12.document_title: Te Tiriti o Waitangi: A Comprehensive History from 1840 to Modern Legal Recognition
12.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the history of Te Tiriti o Waitangi (Treaty of Waitangi) from its signing in 1840 through to modern legal recognition. The treaty, signed between the British Crown and over 500 Māori chiefs on 5-6 February 1840, was drafted in English and translated to Māori by missionary Henry Williams. Critical differences between versions created ongoing disputes: Article One differed on sovereignty versus governance; Article Two guaranteed chiefs "te tino rangatiratanga" (chieftainship) while giving the Crown land-buying rights; Article Three granted Māori British subject protections. From 1860-1940, the Crown systematically dishonored treaty promises through land confiscation, the Native Land Court, and legislation undermining Māori rights, despite Māori resistance through the Kīngitanga (Māori King movement), petitions, and alternative institutions. The pivotal transformation occurred with the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975, which established the Waitangi Tribunal to investigate Crown breaches. The tribunal's jurisdiction expanded in 1985 to cover all Crown actions since 1840, fundamentally changing the treaty's role from a largely ignored historical document to a central element of New Zealand law and governance. Subsequent parliamentary legislation incorporated treaty principles into law, leading to widespread legal recognition and formal settlements between the Crown and iwi.

13.text:
[Page 5] Traditional Māori communities drew their drinking water from natural sources, as did early settlers. By the 1860s growing towns required official town water supplies, so dams, reservoirs and artesian wells were constructed. Drinking fountains were also constructed in urban places in succeeding decades.

13.document_title: Tea, Coffee and Soft Drinks: A History of Beverage Consumption in New Zealand
13.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the history of beverage consumption in New Zealand from the 1800s to the 2000s, covering tea, coffee, soft drinks, mineral water, and dairy beverages. Tea, brought by European settlers, became a national staple across all social classes, with consumption declining from 3-3.5 kg per person (1910s-1960s) to 0.6 kg by the 2000s. Coffee initially faced higher taxes but gained prominence in the 1940s with American servicemen and surpassed tea consumption by 1980, reaching 4 kg per person by 2009. The document details the introduction of bottled mineral water in the 1870s, carbonated drinks including Coca-Cola and local brands like Lemon & Paeroa, fruit juices, cordials, and the evolution of milk consumption from raw to pasteurized. Key historical events include the Tea Examination Act of 1882 to ensure purity, tea rationing during WWII, and the emergence of modern café culture in the 1980s-2000s, including New Zealand's contribution to the flat white coffee invention. By 2011, New Zealanders consumed approximately 93 litres of carbonated drinks per person annually, while milk consumption remained at 90 litres per person in 2005.

14.document_title: Tangaroa and Māori Sea Traditions: Mythology, Spirituality, and Cultural Practices
14.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores the profound spiritual and cultural significance of Tangaroa, the Māori god of the sea, and its central role in Māori and Polynesian traditions. It examines creation myths depicting Tangaroa as either the son of Papatūānuku (earth mother) and Ranginui (sky father), or as Papatūānuku's husband and rival to Ranginui. The document details Māori categorizations of different water types (waikino, waitapu, waimāori, waitai) and their spiritual meanings, particularly exploring te taha wairua ('the dimension of two waters') as the spiritual plane underlying all existence. It traces the origins of carving and tattooing to underwater discoveries by Ruatepupuke and Mataora, including the legend of Ruatepupuke rescuing his son Te Manuhauturuki from Tangaroa's realm and discovering whakairo (wood carving), explaining why carved images lack speech. The document recounts the legend of Tinirau, ancestor of all fish, and his conflict with the priest Kae over the death of his pet whale Tutunui, illustrating tribal justice narratives. Throughout, it emphasizes how the sea was central to traditional Polynesian and Māori life as both a practical resource and a spiritual realm, with humans believed to have evolved from aquatic origins, reflected in traditional wood carvings with marine-like features.

16.document_title: New Zealand Rivers: Comprehensive Guide to Geography, Ecology, Culture, and Conservation
16.document_summary:
This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's extensive river systems across both the North and South Islands, covering over 180,000 kilometres of mapped rivers including the Waikato (425 km) and Clutha (largest by volume). It details river formation through high rainfall, glacial activity, and geological processes, describing distinct river types: deep, fast-flowing rivers in the North Island hills and wide, braided rivers in the South Island's east.

The document emphasizes the profound cultural significance of rivers to Māori people, including their roles in exploration, transportation, food sources, and spiritual traditions involving taniwha (river spirits). It documents European settlement impacts including military conquest, transport use, 19th-century gold rushes, and industrial/agricultural pollution.

The content examines ecological transformations over two centuries, detailing how introduced species like rainbow trout, brown trout, and salmon impacted native fish populations. It describes the creation of eight artificial lakes along the Waikato River through hydroelectric dams (1945-1970s) and habitat loss through forest clearance. Conservation efforts are discussed, from late 19th-century catchment protection through the 1941 Soil Conservation Act to the 1981 Wild and Scenic Rivers Amendment protecting 12 rivers.

Modern challenges including invasive species like didymo, dairy farming impacts on water quality, and off-road vehicle use are addressed. The document highlights Māori guardianship cases involving the Waikato and Whanganui rivers, explores rivers' cultural significance through 19th and 20th-century art, literature, and film, and examines contemporary management practices including jet boat tourism, riparian protection through native tree planting, and regional council monitoring.

17.document_title: The Waitangi Tribunal: History, Development, Structure, and Impact on New Zealand's Treaty Settlement Process
17.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines the Waitangi Tribunal's establishment in 1975 and its evolution into a significant bicultural institution. Initially limited to claims from October 1975 onwards, the tribunal's authority expanded in 1985 to include historical claims dating back to 1840. The tribunal comprises a chair, deputy chair, and diverse professional members, conducting three types of inquiries: district (location-specific), generic (national significance), and urgent (exceptional circumstances). Key achievements include protecting Te Āti Awa's shellfish gathering rights, preserving Māori eel fishery rights, and securing the first $3 million cash settlement for Ngāti Whātua. Major legislative outcomes include the Māori Language Act 1987 and the Resource Management Act 1991. Significant treaty settlements include Ngāi Tahu's $170 million compensation (1998) and Muriwhenua fishing rights. By 2009, the tribunal had produced over 100 reports. Operational reforms include the fiscal envelope policy, Rangahaua Whānui research project, casebook system (1996), and Judge Joe Williams' 'New Approach' (2000). The tribunal has been instrumental in placing the Treaty at the center of New Zealand's historical and political discourse.

However, the treaty did not guide government policy regarding lakes.

19.document_title: How to Fix the Manawatū River
19.document_summary: The Manawatū River, home to one of New Zealand's six Ramsar-listed wetlands of international significance, has become one of the country's most polluted waterways. Originally cloaked in native forests, the river's degradation began with European settlement through deforestation, industrial waste discharge, and intensive agriculture. Pollution evolved from visible sewage and industrial waste in the early 20th century to diffuse pollution from nitrogen and phosphorus runoff from farms. Current challenges include unsafe swimming conditions, sedimentation from eroded hill country, and habitat destruction for native fish species like kōaro. Key solutions include: returning nutrients to land through better farm practices and wetland restoration; upgrading sewage infrastructure to prevent wastewater discharge during heavy rainfall; retiring marginal hill country through reforestation to reduce erosion and sedimentation; and implementing stricter land-use regulations. The 2009 "worst in the west" designation prompted initiatives including Horizons Regional Council's One Plan (2010) and the Manawatū River Leaders' Forum, offering hope for restoration despite ongoing tensions between commercial enterprise, farming, and environmental protection. Climate change threatens to intensify these challenges through increased rainfall.

20.text:
[Page 26] Under existing arrangements, water users are actually encouraged to compete for water, and things soon get litigious. The Environment Court grinds through a perpetual imbroglio of allocation challenges and appeals: some freshwater plans have taken 10 years to finalise. (Horizons’ One Plan has so far cost around $9.4 million, excluding costs to the courts, submitters and appellants.) Increasingly, New Zealand’s freshwater use is being decided by lawyers and judges. Alastair Bisley thinks there’s a better way. For the past four years, he has chaired the Land and Water Forum, an assembly of water users and devotees from every conceivable quarter. His job has been, in essence, to break up the stoush, then get everyone to sit down and listen to one another. Haven for the Waikato’s duckshooters, Whangamarino wetland has also granted eel fisher Gary Watson a living for more than 30 years. In that time, he’s seen the swamp endure storms, sedimentation, peat fires, drainage, invasion by willows and koi carp. These days, his traps often come up empty; the mysid shrimps the eels once gorged on have been decimated by the introduced koi. Once a vast flooded peat system that sustained wildlife and people aplenty, Whangamarino was engineered into submission by the lower Waikato Waipa Flood Protection Scheme in 1961. Only in 2000 did the Department of Conservation finally succeed in restoring water levels with a specially built weir offering some new hope for the freshwater habitat. A former Foreign Affairs official and trade negotiator, Bisley wanted to see water “become something which draws us together, not something which pushes us apart. It’s absolutely clear that all of us regard water as critical to our lives, but there’s a big overlap around the ways we value it. It makes sense to use water as productively as possible, and in doing so, enhance its value to us.” The forum delivered three hefty reports with 158 recommendations to the Government on better ways to manage the country’s water, and in the process was held up as representing a new way of tackling our problems, through understanding, equity, barter. More importantly, perhaps, it reminded us that water was more than a commodity. Bisley believes water can yet be democratised without sidelining commercial interests, but we—all of us—have to get used to the notion and prospect of limits. The Government duly acknowledged the four years everyone had donated to the process, and gave an assurance that the forum’s “core recommendations” would be incorporated into a discussion document, Freshwater Reform 2013 and Beyond. One of the recommendations was that we urgently need to determine and enshrine a “minimum environmental state” beyond which we must not let water languish.

20.document_title: New Zealand's Water Crisis: Economic Growth, Environmental Degradation, and Governance Challenges
20.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection examines New Zealand's freshwater crisis, exploring tensions between economic development and environmental sustainability. The collection analyzes water's dual role as a natural resource and economic commodity, detailing how hydroelectric schemes and irrigation power New Zealand's agricultural economy, particularly dairy which generates $11.4 billion in exports but requires 900 liters of water per liter of milk. Key findings include: 28% of assessed lakes worsened between 2005-2009, the Manawatu River identified as the most polluted in the Western world, and 68% of freshwater fish species threatened. The documents reveal that 60% of national water usage occurs in Canterbury, with 86% dedicated to agricultural irrigation. Government policies, including the $400 million Irrigation Acceleration Fund and appointment of commissioners to bypass democratic processes, have prioritized short-term economic gains over sustainability. Water contamination with E.coli and toxic algal blooms has forced boil-water notices affecting over 880,000 New Zealanders. The collection highlights historical injustices including the 1863 Waikato land confiscation and inadequate settlements, while exploring Māori perspectives on water stewardship and cultural loss. Climate change projections indicate increased extreme weather and volatile river flows, yet governance frameworks remain inadequate. The collection presents sustainable farming practices as potential solutions while emphasizing that intensive dairy farming and healthy waterways appear mutually exclusive, requiring urgent integrated policy responses.

21.text:
[Page 22] “The Water Conservation Order was in the way,” says Snoyink, “so they had it gutted. People had the foresight to campaign for protection of that river and now, because we’ve already taken all the easy water, they’re overturning these protection orders. And DOC is nowhere to be seen—we don’t have that voice for the natural environment any more.” That’s possibly because it was Nick Smith as Minister of Conservation who facilitated the amendment, then put the application before the commissioners he had appointed at Environment Canterbury. “There is this absurd contention,” says Eugenie Sage, “that you can simply re plumb an entire region. So the rivers are reduced simply to canals to convey water from point A to point B so it can be used to grow grass.” She argues that supposedly sacrosanct measures such as Water Conservation Orders can be overturned only because New Zealand rivers still have no effective legal framework to protect them. “We need more effective regulation and binding national standards, because they have the strength of rule. Christchurch was able to clean up its air because of a national environmental standard for particulate matter. Where there’s been central government leadership on environmental quality issues, things have improved. Where there hasn’t, such as with water quality, things continue to decline.” Neil Deans, Fish & Game’s Nelson Marlborough manager, points out that the Government’s 2011 National Policy Statement, which compels councils to produce water management plans, is 30 years late. Historically, plans have not been compulsory. “We didn’t get one in Canterbury until about 2010. So what happened in the meantime? Tens of thousands of permits were allocated in that space, for 35 years. The problem is that this is effects based legislation, and the effect of one more little straw on the camel’s back is very hard to measure. But the effect of all those straws has well and truly broken the camel’s back in many of our catchments throughout New Zealand, particularly in areas like Canterbury.”

27.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection examines New Zealand's freshwater crisis, exploring tensions between economic development and environmental sustainability. The collection analyzes water's dual role as a natural resource and economic commodity, detailing how hydroelectric schemes and irrigation power New Zealand's agricultural economy, particularly dairy which generates $11.4 billion in exports but requires 900 liters of water per liter of milk. Key findings include: 28% of assessed lakes worsened between 2005-2009, the Manawatu River identified as the most polluted in the Western world, and 68% of freshwater fish species threatened. The documents reveal that 60% of national water usage occurs in Canterbury, with 86% dedicated to agricultural irrigation. Government policies, including the $400 million Irrigation Acceleration Fund and appointment of commissioners to bypass democratic processes, have prioritized short-term economic gains over sustainability. Water contamination with E.coli and toxic algal blooms has forced boil-water notices affecting over 880,000 New Zealanders. The collection highlights historical injustices including the 1863 Waikato land confiscation and inadequate settlements, while exploring Māori perspectives on water stewardship and cultural loss. Climate change projections indicate increased extreme weather and volatile river flows, yet governance frameworks remain inadequate. The collection presents sustainable farming practices as potential solutions while emphasizing that intensive dairy farming and healthy waterways appear mutually exclusive, requiring urgent integrated policy responses.

38.document_title: Government Reveals First Changes to Resource Management Act
38.document_summary: The New Zealand government announced its first changes to the Resource Management Act (RMA), effective May 2024. Minister Chris Bishop outlined five key reforms aimed at reducing regulatory burden on farming, mining, and primary industries: repealing intensive winter grazing regulations, removing low-slope maps from stock exclusion rules, suspending Significant Natural Area identification requirements for three years, removing Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy compliance for resource consents during freshwater policy review, and realigning coal mining consenting with other mining activities. Agriculture Minister Todd McClay emphasized farm-level solutions, while Associate Environment Minister Andrew Hoggard noted concerns about overly restrictive land-use regulations. Federated Farmers and Beef + Lamb New Zealand welcomed the changes as practical relief from complex, unworkable rules. However, Labour and Green Party opposition criticized the reforms as short-sighted, prioritizing profits over environmental protection and waterway health. Local Government New Zealand supported the certainty provided but called for more substantial RMA reform.

39.document_title: Canterbury Dairy Expansion: 32 New Farms as Grain Growers Switch to Milk Production
39.document_summary: Canterbury is experiencing significant dairy farm expansion with 32 new dairy discharge consents approved and 15 more in progress, potentially adding up to 25,000 dairy cows to the region's herd. Low global wheat prices and strong milk payouts are driving arable farmers to convert grain operations to dairy farming. While dairy remains profitable with 81% of surveyed farmers making profit at $9.50/kg milk solids, the arable sector struggles with only 40% profitable. The expansion follows the end of a temporary dairy conversion ban in January 2025. Concerns exist about losing critical mass in the grain industry and its supporting infrastructure. Nationally, dairy cow numbers declined 0.5% to 4.68 million in 2024/25, though milk solids production increased 2.9%.
