5.fileDescription: This comprehensive document chronicles the remarkable conservation journey of the kākāpō, New Zealand's critically endangered flightless nocturnal parrot. Once abundant throughout New Zealand's islands, the species declined dramatically to just 18 males in Fiordland by the 1980s, with only 62 birds remaining by the early 2000s due to introduced predators and historical human hunting. The breakthrough came with the discovery of a 200-strong population on Stewart Island in 1977, including the first identified female since the early 1900s. The recovery program involved relocating all surviving kākāpō to predator-free island sanctuaries including Whenua Hou, Maud Island, and Little Barrier Island between 1982-1992. Key conservation innovations include helicopter access to remote populations, hand-rearing of chicks, inter-island transfers, electronic surveillance systems, and supplementary feeding programs. The species' unique lekking courtship behavior, where males inflate and boom low-frequency calls from elaborately maintained bowl-shaped arenas, was crucial to understanding their breeding patterns. Despite their appearance as ecological relics, kākāpō demonstrate adaptability and have become marathon survivors with lifespans potentially exceeding 60 years. The dedicated recovery team has achieved significant breeding successes, transforming wild kākāpō into managed refugees in their own homeland. The long-term vision includes establishing free-living, self-sustaining populations on subantarctic islands like Campbell Island, representing an unprecedented turning point in the species' survival.

chunkHighlights.text: Over the years, this programme has been through some shaky times, partly because there are still so many unknowns about the birds, but also because of the hobbling effects of political pressure and bureaucratic constraints. Following an external review in 1994, executive control over budget, strategy, staff and all things kākāpō was put in the hands of three people: Paul Jansen, Graeme Elliott and Merton—all of whom have clocked up many years in grassroots conservation. Jansen, the programme leader, has quietly emphatic

manners and the reputation of a man who gets things done. Elliott, the team’s scientist, is a thinker and electronics tinkerer, responsible for much of the innovative technology now employed in the field. Merton, with unrivalled knowledge and experience of kākāpō, is the prime architect of the close-order management strategy for the birds, adapted from his black robin work. Since 1995, the trio has put the kākāpō on a fast track to recovery—well, fast in kākāpō terms.

In the avian world, where life is but a short sprint, kākāpō are the marathon runners—possibly the longest lived of all birds. Many of those alive today were already mature adults when they were found in the mid-1970s, and biologists estimate a typical kākāpō life span to be around 60 years, perhaps more. Like tuatara, they seem timeless. Their metabolism is so unhurried they can digest foods containing toxins that would kill humans or make them sick, like the leaves and fruit of the native tutu, and poroporo berries—both kākāpō favourites.

And still the bizarre night parrots keep surprising their caretakers. Graeme Elliott, in an effort to breathe a little more enthusiasm into the birds’ courtship, has tried injecting selected rimu trees with a hormone to induce the trees to produce more fruit—so far the most consistent kākāpō aphrodisiac. He has also developed a “boom box”—a portable, weatherproof stereo system which, placed near a lek, automatically comes on at night, blaring out the boom! boom! sound to spur the males into song.
In 1998, kākāpō bred successfully on Te Hoiere/Maud Island—but without the benefit of a boom box and without a rimu tree in sight.

The event on Maud was all the more significant for taking place in an extremely modified environment, showing that, despite appearing to be stuck in an ecological time warp, the kākāpō is an adaptable creature. Maud Island is the 309-hectare tip of a mountain that was flooded when the sea level rose. It was farmed until 1975, when the Royal New Zealand Forest and Bird Society successfully campaigned to buy it and turn it into a nature reserve. Most of the island had been cleared of its original forest, and one corner had been planted in pines. Remarkably, it
was in the radiata that the kākāpō nested.

Many kākāpō now reside on Whenua Hou, an island west of Stewart Island which was cleared of possums, weka and rats to create a safe haven. Locating the birds on the 1396-hectare scrub- and forest-covered island is a challenge made easier by the use of radio telemetry, but the method is not foolproof: the kākāpō’s transmitters can become detached, in which case dogs are brought in to sniff out the escapees.

By late December 1998, all four of Maud’s males were booming, and soon mating signs—tufts of down and feathers near the track-and-bowl area—were found. Then, on the island’s west-facing slope, where the setting sun dapples through the trees and brown pine needles muffle one’s footsteps, Merton and others discovered a nest with three eggs under sparse bracken cover on a slope so steep the subsequent track cut up it was a winding staircase of 140 steps.

The find was such a momentous event that Merton and his colleagues took no chances with the safety of their charges. The three chicks that hatched were offspring of Richard Henry, the last and only known surviving Fiordland kākāpō. “We’ve waited more than 20 years for this nest,” Merton said at the time. “It must succeed!” And so the intervention began. Every time the mother, named Flossie, left the nest to forage—generally at around 2 or 3am—a stealthy construction crew moved in.

First, a metre-high retaining wall was erected on the lower side of the nest to prevent the eggs from rolling down the hill. Next a plywood roof was added. Then a drain was dug on the upslope to divert any possible flooding. A piece of plastic pipe became an entrance tunnel, and an infra-red beam, wired to a door chime, was placed across the entrance to alert nest minders when the mother left for her nightly perambulations. A miniature video surveillance camera was placed inside the nest to keep an electronic eye on the chicks. Later, a play- ground was added. It was as if a person living in a shanty had left for a short walk and returned to find a prefab house with a sundeck, and a sand pit for the kids.

Not showing the least surprise, Flossie and the youngsters took the alterations in their goosestep stride. All the while, a roster of nest minders camped in a tent 80 metres away, ready to dash in to deal with any emergency. Electronic surveillance and nest minding would become standard procedure with all subsequent nests.

A fabric scoop on the end of a ski pole makes a useful device for extracting chicks from deep hideaways when weighing and measuring is to be carried out. Females feed young chicks (such as the 12-day-old in the bottom photograph) by regurgitating the soft parts of plants, including fruit and shoots, but older chicks are given less digested fruit and seeds.

6.fileDescription: This comprehensive document chronicles critical conservation efforts to save the kakapo, one of the world's rarest parrots, from extinction. In March 1992, with only 50 kakapo remaining and just 15 known females, the Department of Conservation launched a rescue mission on Codfish Island after El Niño-driven gales threatened chick survival. Don Merton coordinated the transfer of critically underweight chicks to Auckland Zoo for artificial rearing, including a challenging rescue of two chicks from an inaccessible nest beneath a boulder. At Auckland Zoo, Curator Mick Sibley supervised intensive hand-rearing of three chicks—Alf, BJ, and Nora's foster chick—providing round-the-clock care with specialized feeding every two hours using soya bean-based porridge. The programme achieved remarkable success in raising multiple chicks together but faced tragic setbacks, including deaths from acute respiratory problems caused by food particle inhalation. The surviving chick Hoki was successfully transferred to Maud Island, serving as a crucial research subject and potential nucleus for a captive breeding population. The recovery programme gained invaluable insights into kakapo development and breeding requirements, with the Department of Conservation recognizing that intervention, monitoring, supplementary feeding, and nest protection are essential for species survival. This conservation effort mirrors successful strategies used with black robins, offering hope that kakapo can return from the brink of extinction.

chunkHighlights.text: We left the island that afternoon in a positive frame of mind, but the old adage about counting chickens seems to have special relevance to kakapo. After receiving encouraging reports from Buckingham for nearly a month, Nora’s foster chick started to lose condition, and on May 13 it had to be rescued a second time, and transferred to Auckland Zoo to join the other two.

For the next 35 days all was well. Regular “plunket faxes” arrived in our office from the zoo, plotting steady weight gains in the three chicks. It was a time of great excitement, and some nervousness. Would these birds be the first successfully hand-reared kakapo? Would they survive the transition back to the wild? Ultimately, would they help the species “turn the corner” and escape the threat of extinction?

Louise Joyce, a Television New Zealand journalist who visited the zoo weekly for nearly three months to record the progress of the chicks, takes up the story in April, when only two chicks had been transferred . . .

Maud Island’s VIP bird, Hoki, gets a large, predator-proof aviary to herself, and plenty of attention from her caretakers. She has gourmet tastes: her favourite foods are Brazil nuts, macadamias and almonds-she turns her beak up at parrot pellets.

At the start, things had gone well. Alf had put on four times his own weight within a fortnight, and BJ had responded with a similar weight gain. Zoo staff were confident that both birds were thriving, and would soon be able to be moved to island sanctuaries.
Even so, caring for these birds was an exhaustive and time-consuming task.

The chicks were fed every two hours with a soya bean-based porridge, and were weighed regularly to check their growth rate. They were never left unattended, and were under around-the-clock observation by Mick Sibley, the zoo’s Curator of Zoological Projects, and the 11 members of his team. Lighting was dimmed in their temperature-controlled environment, and people spoke in whispers to avoid disturbing them.
Everything possible was provided for them—even a couple of hand-puppets with heads resembling an adult kakapo, and taped calls of wild kakapo played before meals to stimulate their appetite.
But always there was the worry of whether they were doing the right things to ensure the chicks’ survival.

“Unlike other birds, kakapo haven’t had years of research done on the diet and living habits of chicks at this age,” says Sibley. “It’s not as if we have textbooks to refer to. We don’t know their optimum temperature requirements, and we don’t know precisely where these chicks should be in terms of development and growth at their age.

7.fileDescription: This article by Kennedy Warne chronicles the conservation efforts to save New Zealand's critically endangered kākāpō parrot. The author recounts witnessing a male kākāpō named Lionel performing his courtship display on Whenua Hou island in 2002, when only 86 birds remained. The narrative traces the species' tragic decline from mainland forests in Fiordland during the 1980s, documented by conservation biologist Don Merton, to current recovery efforts. The article highlights innovative conservation techniques, including using rock wrens' nesting behavior to locate kākāpō, and recent successes with breeding seasons. It emphasizes the urgent need for species conservation, noting that New Zealand faces extinction risks for 4,000 endemic species. The piece balances urgency with wonder, celebrating the unique characteristics of kākāpō while advocating for continued predator-free sanctuary development and ecological restoration efforts.

chunkHighlights.text: Rare species can’t wait
By Kennedy Warne
Lessons from a big booming budgerigar.

The first time I saw a kākāpō in the wild was on a windswept ridge of an island off the west coast of Rakiura. At that time, 2002, most of the 86 living kākāpō were clustered on that one island, Whenua Hou. It was the middle of the night, and I was jammed in a tent with two wildlife rangers.

Every half an hour or so, we checked the screen of a monitor that was connected to a repurposed domestic security camera stationed 80 metres away, on the island’s summit. The camera was pointed at a shallow depression in the soil—a kākāpō courtship bowl. The bowl was empty. Whenever we turned the monitor on, all we saw were scrubby bushes flailing in the wind, and all we heard was the caterwauling cries of petrels wheeling overhead in the storm.

Then, around midnight, we heard what we had been hoping for: the sonorous boom of a kākāpō male. Three hands reached simultaneously for the video button. The screen came to life, and there, pumped up like a rugby ball, was Lionel, singing his basso profundo lovesong to the island’s 21 females. All of whom, apparently, ignored his overtures. When I checked online just now, I learned that Lionel died in 2014, apparently without siring any offspring.

It’s quite something to find every kākāpō listed by name on Wikipedia. All 123 adult birds are there, along with the recently deceased, like Lionel. And, as the story in this issue of the magazine explains, these birds don’t just have names but now also an individual genetic fingerprint—and, with that, an expectation that the species can be managed towards a more robust future.
This year has been the best-equal kākāpō breeding season ever. Whenua Hou—“new land”—is turning out to be more than a rest home for old birds; it’s a nursery for new generations.

8.fileDescription: This comprehensive document provides an overview of New Zealand's threatened species and conservation efforts. It defines threatened species as native plants and animals with critically low populations facing extinction risk, with New Zealand having 2,788 threatened species (37% of birds, 34% of plants). Main causes of decline include habitat destruction, invasive predators like rats and possums, and over-harvesting. New Zealand uses an eight-tier classification system for conservation status based on threats, endemism, vulnerability, and cultural importance. Conservation strategies include island sanctuaries, pest control, captive breeding, and habitat restoration. Notable successes include the black robin recovery (7 to 250 individuals), takahē recovery program, and tuatara reintroduction programs. The document presents case studies of endangered species including the Mahoenui giant wētā, Peraxilla mistletoes, kiwi, and tuatara. About 30% of New Zealand is protected conservation land. Recent efforts have expanded beyond visible species to include freshwater fish and plants, with a shift toward restoring entire habitats. Key challenges include funding limitations, many species poorly understood (1,455 fungi species classified as 'data deficient'), an estimated 50,000 unidentified native species potentially at risk, and preventing 'zombie species' that survive only in cultivation.

chunkHighlights.text: Private funding

In 1990 the Department of Conservation and other groups set up the Threatened Species Trust Programme to attract commercial sponsorship. This has generated more funds for saving threatened species. For example, between 1990 and 2004 the aluminium smelting company Comalco donated $1.6 million towards saving the kākāpō. The Bank of New Zealand has been a multi-million-dollar sponsor of efforts to save the kiwi since 1991.

9.fileDescription: Four male kākāpō have been relocated to Coal Island (Te Puka-Hereka) off Fiordland as part of the DOC Kākāpō Recovery Programme to address habitat shortage. The transfer aims to test whether the island can support a larger population ahead of a predicted 2026 breeding season. Only males were introduced due to the presence of stoats on the island. Coal Island was selected for its similar habitat and proximity to existing breeding islands. The Coal Island Trust has spent 20 years removing predators to create a haven for native species. This trial will help assess the island's viability for future kākāpō breeding and potentially open doors to additional sites. The programme is supported by Meridian Energy since 2016.

10.filePath: pdf/Kākāpō might not be the bird of the year, but this is the year of the kākāpō.pdf
fileAuthor: Alexia Russell - Producer of The Detail
10.fileDescription: 2026 marks a pivotal year for kākāpō conservation as the critically endangered parrot species prepares for its largest breeding boom in years. With all 237 kākāpō individually named and tracked, conservationists anticipate significant population growth following a four-year wait for the next mast year, when rimu trees will produce abundant seeds. The recovery program is shifting from intensive management methods—including egg incubation and supplementary feeding—toward minimal intervention approaches, allowing birds to breed naturally. Female kākāpō numbers have increased 400% from 21 to 84 breeding-age birds since 30 years ago. A key initiative involves the Predator Free Rakiura programme to eliminate feral cats and rats from Stewart Island, potentially enabling kākāpō reintroduction. While this reduced intervention carries risks, conservationists view it as essential for long-term sustainability and species recovery.

chunkHighlights.text:
ByAlexia Russell - Producer of The Detail
2025-11-20 06:42:08+13:00
Next year - 2026 - could be the year that the kākāpō breeding programme takes such a big leap forward that conservationists
can finally take a step [wk_audio]aca70a6e-44d5-4344-8c1b-b24cd9c093e0 Kākāpō numbers are so thin that all 237 of them have a name and a transmitter. The funny little tree-climbing, owl-like parrot has had intensive management over the last several decades, and its numbers have come back from the brink to give conservationists hope. And after a four year wait, they're preparing for what could be the biggest boom in kākāpō chicks yet, because next year is a mast year. That means rimu trees on the predator-free islands where the birds live are about to burst with seeds, the bumper year that kākāpō wait for. "You have to wait around to get a good thing from kākāpō, but this year all the stars are in alignment," says Alison Ballance, who will be continuing her Kākāpō Files podcast series from December 16. It will also mark the first time that conservationists take a step back from such intensive methods of rescuing the critically endangered population. Those methods are resource-heavy and not sustainable. So instead of incubating every egg, encouraging the females to lay more than one clutch, and providing supplementary feed, attention is turning to making sure the birds have enough room to spread their wings. The ultimate prize would be to turn Stewart Island/Rakiura into a pest-free haven. "That's why we're looking with great interest at the Predator Free Rakiura programme," says Ballance, "where the community down there alongside DoC, and Zero Invasive Predators and Ngāi Tahu are starting to begin a programme where [they're asking] can they get rid of things like feral cats and rats on Stewart Island. "And if that was the case, then we could move kākāpō back to Rakiura and just stand back and let them be kākāpō in their own time frame, without the risk of predation." Conservationists know that back
the risk of taking their eye off every egg and chick means they may lose

more than they have in the past. They say while it's nerve-wracking, it's essential. There will be fewer chick checks this season, more eggs hatching in nests rather than in incubators, and generally a move towards minimal intervention. The last mast years were in 2019 and 2022, so the big crop of chicks that arrived in 2019 will now be ready to breed. The females start from age five but it's possible some four-year-olds may also lay eggs. "There should be lots of new, young female kākāpō trying to breed this year which will be really exciting. The Department of Conservation's kākāpō recovery team tell me there's a bit of a wild card. There's 24 young females who are four years old and basically they [DoC] haven't had experience in the last 30 years of intensive kākāpō management of a breeding season that was four years apart. "So they're wondering ... maybe some of those precocious four-year-olds ... will they breed?" Thirty years ago there were 51 known kākāpō; 21 female and 30 male. Now we've got 84 females of breeding age, so that's about a 400 percent increase in potential chicks. Kākāpō are a long-lived species, although we don't know exactly how long-lived. There are definitely some birds in their late 40s and early 50s and there's speculation they could live up to 80 or even 100 - and they keep laying until the end. Check out how to listen to and follow The Detail here. You can also stay up-to-date by liking us on Facebook
or following us on Twitter.

16.fileDescription: This comprehensive document provides an overview of New Zealand's threatened species and conservation efforts. It defines threatened species as native plants and animals with critically low populations facing extinction risk, with New Zealand having 2,788 threatened species (37% of birds, 34% of plants). Main causes of decline include habitat destruction, invasive predators like rats and possums, and over-harvesting. New Zealand uses an eight-tier classification system for conservation status based on threats, endemism, vulnerability, and cultural importance. Conservation strategies include island sanctuaries, pest control, captive breeding, and habitat restoration. Notable successes include the black robin recovery (7 to 250 individuals), takahē recovery program, and tuatara reintroduction programs. The document presents case studies of endangered species including the Mahoenui giant wētā, Peraxilla mistletoes, kiwi, and tuatara. About 30% of New Zealand is protected conservation land. Recent efforts have expanded beyond visible species to include freshwater fish and plants, with a shift toward restoring entire habitats. Key challenges include funding limitations, many species poorly understood (1,455 fungi species classified as 'data deficient'), an estimated 50,000 unidentified native species potentially at risk, and preventing 'zombie species' that survive only in cultivation.

retrieved_chunks.text: No other creature in the pantheon of New Zealand’s endemic fauna has ever attracted so much attention, effort and funding, and none is more critically endangered and vulnerable. Yet for all the kākāpō’s ecological charisma and PR celebrity, few people ever get it in the wild—and not just because its sanctuaries are out of bounds to all but key personnel. You could walk its island forests and scrublands for days and never see a bird. The kākāpō evolved with blind and total faith in its perfect camouflage, and the birds blend into the foliage so well that trying to see them is like picking the 3D shapes out of Magic Eye pictures.

It's fun and it makes it easier for people to engage with these charismatic parrots. But that's not the ultimate goal of the kākāpō recovery programme, says operations manager Deirdre Vercoe. "Our vision is to restore the mauri of the kākāpō, or the life force of the kākāpō. And that vision is to have kākāpō nameless, wandering through our forests, booming from the mountains and the hilltops around our cities and towns. Not to have a transmitter on, not to have a name and a well known history." Deidre Vercoe does a nighttime kākāpō chick check So this year, for the first time in the programme's 31 year history, which began when there were just 51 birds alive, some of the new kākāpō chicks will not be named. Normally naming happens when a chick has fledged and has passed the 150 day mark since they hatched. It's then that they get added to the adult kākāpō tally. Currently there are 92 new chicks alive. They may not all make it but there is hope that the population will reach over 300 birds by the end of this year. The next question is where to put them. Home birds or wanderers? Dr Andrew Digby sits in front of a laptop in a side small room off the large hut on Whenua Hou / Codfish island. Conservation lovers glued to a black and white livestream from a remote island off the coast of New Zealand on Sunday can safely claim to be the only people to have seen a critically endangered kākāpō lay an egg in real time. The images beamed to the world from a large cavity beneath a rātā tree on Whenua Hou/Codfish Island showed 23-year-old Rakiura laying her second egg of the season, the product of a dalliance with Kōmaru a week earlier. retrieved_chunks.text: It is four in the morning, and I am sitting alone on the rain-soaked soil of an island at the edge of Foveaux Strait, hunched against the pre-dawn cold and endless southwesterlies. I have been in the thick blackness of this southern night for six hours already, waiting for the approaching dawn to silhouette the forest canopy with patches of grey. My only company lies a couple of metres away, in a tangle of rotting rata stumps and roots: a tiny grey chick which looks as cold and disconsolate as I feel. It is H2, a seven-day-old kakapo and one of the very latest additions to the embattled parrot’s population. While I shiver in layers of expensive polypropylene and synthetic fabrics, H2 has only the finest coating of grey down for warmth and resembles nothing more than a patch of mould on the forest floor. As a volunteer nest minder, I am spending two weeks looking after this fragile addition to the kakapo world while its mother, Heather, forages in the surrounding rimu forest of Codfish Island/Whenua Hou. Fatigued by 10 days of scant and intermittent sleep and up to four hours’ walking on waterlogged tracks each day, I find my biggest challenge is simply to stay awake. It’s rough and it’s raw, but what I’m doing is the reality of conservation in this country. Forget photo opportunities and cuddling one of the world’s rarest birds. Saving this species requires patience, sturdy boots and getting used to rivulets of water trickling down your neck. retrieved_chunks.text: Over the years, this programme has been through some shaky times, partly because there are still so many unknowns about the birds, but also because of the hobbling effects of political pressure and bureaucratic constraints. Following an external review in 1994, executive control over budget, strategy, staff and all things kākāpō was put in the hands of three people: Paul Jansen, Graeme Elliott and Merton—all of whom have clocked up many years in grassroots conservation. Jansen, the programme leader, has quietly emphatic manners and the reputation of a man who gets things done. Elliott, the team’s scientist, is a thinker and electronics tinkerer, responsible for much of the innovative technology now employed in the field. Merton, with unrivalled knowledge and experience of kākāpō, is the prime architect of the close-order management strategy for the birds, adapted from his black robin work. Since 1995, the trio has put the kākāpō on a fast track to recovery—well, fast in kākāpō terms. Many of those alive today were already mature adults when they were found in the mid-1970s, and biologists estimate a typical kākāpō life span to be around 60 years, perhaps more. Like tuatara, they seem timeless. Their metabolism is so unhurried they can digest foods containing toxins that would kill humans or make them sick, like the leaves and fruit of the native tutu, and poroporo berries—both kākāpō favourites. She has gourmet tastes: her favourite foods are Brazil nuts, macadamias and almonds-she turns her beak up at parrot pellets. At the start, things had gone well. Alf had put on four times his own weight within a fortnight, and BJ had responded with a similar weight gain. retrieved_chunks.text: Rare species can’t wait By Kennedy Warne Lessons from a big booming budgerigar. The first time I saw a kākāpō in the wild was on a windswept ridge of an island off the west coast of Rakiura. At that time, 2002, most of the 86 living kākāpō were clustered on that one island, Whenua Hou. It was the middle of the night, and I was jammed in a tent with two wildlife rangers. Every half an hour or so, we checked the screen of a monitor that was connected to a repurposed domestic security camera stationed 80 metres away, on the island’s summit. The camera was pointed at a shallow depression in the soil—a kākāpō courtship bowl. The bowl was empty. Whenever we turned the monitor on, all we saw were scrubby bushes flailing in the wind, and all we heard was the caterwauling cries of petrels wheeling overhead in the storm. Then, around midnight, we heard what we had been hoping for: the sonorous boom of a kākāpō male. Three hands reached simultaneously for the video button. The screen came to life, and there, pumped up like a rugby ball, was Lionel, singing his basso profundo lovesong to the island’s 21 females. All of whom, apparently, ignored his overtures. When I checked online just now, I learned that Lionel died in 2014, apparently without siring any offspring. It’s quite something to find every kākāpō listed by name on Wikipedia. All 123 adult birds are there, along with the recently deceased, like Lionel. And, as the story in this issue of the magazine explains, these birds don’t just have names but now also an individual genetic fingerprint—and, with that, an expectation that the species can be managed towards a more robust future. This year has been the best-equal kākāpō breeding season ever. Whenua Hou—“new land”—is turning out to be more than a rest home for old birds; it’s a nursery for new generations.

Next year - 2026 - could be the year that the kākāpō breeding programme takes such a big leap forward that conservationists
can finally take a step [wk_audio]aca70a6e-44d5-4344-8c1b-b24cd9c093e0 Kākāpō numbers are so thin that all 237 of them have a name and a transmitter. The funny little tree-climbing, owl-like parrot has had intensive management over the last several decades, and its numbers have come back from the brink to give conservationists hope. And after a four year wait, they're preparing for what could be the biggest boom in kākāpō chicks yet, because next year is a mast year. That means rimu trees on the predator-free islands where the birds live are about to burst with seeds, the bumper year that kākāpō wait for. "You have to wait around to get a good thing from kākāpō, but this year all the stars are in alignment," says Alison Ballance, who will be continuing her Kākāpō Files podcast series from December 16. It will also mark the first time that conservationists take a step back from such intensive methods of rescuing the critically endangered population. Those methods are resource-heavy and not sustainable. So instead of incubating every egg, encouraging the females to lay more than one clutch, and providing supplementary feed, attention is turning to making sure the birds have enough room to spread their wings. The ultimate prize would be to turn Stewart Island/Rakiura into a pest-free haven. "That's why we're looking with great interest at the Predator Free Rakiura programme," says Ballance, "where the community down there alongside DoC, and Zero Invasive Predators and Ngāi Tahu are starting to begin a programme where [they're asking] can they get rid of things like feral cats and rats on Stewart Island. "And if that was the case, then we could move kākāpō back to Rakiura and just stand back and let them be kākāpō in their own time frame, without the risk of predation." Conservati…

Eggs were incubated, and the chicks were raised and held in enclosures near Te Anau. Secondary, captive populations can be started up, often on island sanctuaries. These then form a back-up in case the original population dies out.

retrieved_chunks.text: [Page 18] “Kākāpō are extinct throughout their natural range,” he began, “and there is no way of returning them there, at least in the short to medium term. If they are to survive in a free living state, then it must be outside their former range. But where? It is fair to expect that the number of kākāpō will steadily, if slowly, increase, and that the small islands where they are being kept will soon reach their holding capacity. What are we going to do then? There aren’t many options, because kākāpō need a lot of space, and a self sustaining population of several hundred birds would require many thousands of hectares. They cannot coexist with predatory mammals, so the mainland is out, and they need a dominant masting plant species in order to breed. We’re looking at all the possi bilities—including the subantarctic.” His eyes had the gleam of a man who sees a prize which is not yet within his grasp. “Campbell?” I asked. “It’s a candidate, and a good one. It is large—over 11,000 hectares—and after last year’s rat eradication project it should now be free of all alien mammals. It has a wide variety of plants, including abundant snow tussock, which could provide the necessary high energy food to enable kākāpō to breed. The climate shouldn’t worry them. Kākāpō are adapted to cool, damp, subalpine conditions. Their down is particularly dense, and under their skin they have a layer of fat up to 15 millimetres thick.” Placing the birds so far outside their former range might seem a form of banishment, Merton admitted, but it would also be like putting our feathery treasures on term deposit in a safe offshore bank, where no calamity and no fund cutting or staff downsizing could affect them. Although kākāpō are unable to fly they have well developed wings which they use for balance when climbing—an activity at which they excel—and for braking during short downward leaps. retrieved_chunks.text: [Page 6] close to extinction, the remaining population stable but ageing, and time steadily running out. Recently, however, the tide has turned. And not a moment too soon, according to Don Merton, who has been at the forefront of the effort for the past 28 years, because, as he says: “If we can’t save the kākāpō, our flagship species and number one conser vation priority, what hope is there for all the other, less glamorous critters?” Male kākāpō use networks of tracks and bowls on display grounds called arenas during the breeding season to compete for the attention of females—a courtship behaviour known as lekking. The same tracks and bowls are thought to remain in operation for hundreds, if not thousands, of years—as long as there are birds to use them. The overgrown state of this track, in Fiordland’s Transit Valley, reflects the sad reality that kākāpō have disappeared from the area. Not until February 1974 was another kākāpō discovered. By then it had been established that the birds favoured so called kākāpō gardens—areas where the beech forest had been broken up by an avalanche, creating conditions for faster growing herbs, tussocks and berry plants to flourish. ## Two Birds, Two Paths Back from the Brink

![embed-1](embed://1)

New Zealand's kākāpō and takahē recovery programmes share a common origin story — both species were brought to the edge of extinction by introduced predators and habitat loss — but the two programmes have taken markedly different paths in how they manage their birds and measure success.

---

## Island Sanctuaries vs Wild Landscapes

Both programmes have relied heavily on predator-free islands as refuges. Kākāpō were moved to offshore sanctuaries including Whenua Hou/Codfish Island, Maud Island, and Chalky Island (Te Kākahu o Tamatea) after remnant populations were discovered in Fiordland and on Stewart Island/Rakiura in the 1970s [[1]](cite://1/1)[[2]](cite://2/1). Today the birds breed across three protected offshore islands [[3]](cite://3/1).

The takahē programme also established 'security populations' on offshore predator-free islands, but it has gone further in returning birds to mainland wild landscapes. After the species was rediscovered in the Murchison Mountains, Fiordland, in 1948, a Specially Protected Area was created there — and the wild population has since reached an estimated 220–260 birds, hitting carrying capacity [[4]](cite://4/1)[[5]](cite://5/1). More recently, takahē have been reintroduced to Kahurangi National Park, Greenstone Station in the upper Whakatipu, and the Rees Valley near Glenorchy [[5]](cite://5/2)[[6]](cite://6/1). As of June 2026, the Rees Valley has become the largest wild takahē population outside of Fiordland [[6]](cite://6/2).

Kākāpō, by contrast, remain almost entirely confined to islands. The programme is only beginning to explore mainland fenced sanctuaries (such as Sanctuary Mountain Maungatautari) and is watching with great interest the Predator Free Rakiura initiative, which could one day allow the birds to return to Stewart Island/Rakiura in a truly wild state [[7]](cite://7/1)[[8]](cite://8/1).

---

## Intensity of Hands-On Management

This is where the two programmes diverge most sharply.

The kākāpō programme has been, by its own description, among the most intensive wildlife management operations in the world [[9]](cite://9/1). Every bird has a name, a transmitter, a detailed genetic profile, and — during breeding seasons — infrared cameras and volunteer nest minders stationed at each nest [[10]](cite://10/1)[[11]](cite://11/1)[[12]](cite://12/1). Techniques have included supplementary feeding tied to rimu masting cycles, egg incubation, artificial insemination, chick hand-rearing, and the use of 'boom boxes' to stimulate male courtship behaviour [[11]](cite://11/2)[[13]](cite://13/1). The programme formally began in its current form in 1995, when just 51 birds were known to exist [[14]](cite://14/1).

The takahē programme has also involved intensive management — particularly through the Burwood Takahē Centre, created in the 1980s for captive breeding and chick rearing [[5]](cite://5/3) — but it has been more willing to establish genuinely self-sustaining wild populations in mainland settings with predator trapping rather than island isolation alone. Rangers do check every bird at least once a year, which is a significant undertaking across 50,000 hectares of Fiordland terrain, but the Murchison Mountains population is now considered robust enough that intensive monitoring can be scaled back [[4]](cite://4/2).

---

## The Shift Towards 'Lighter Touch'

Both programmes are now moving, at different speeds, towards reduced intervention — but from very different starting points.

For kākāpō, the 2026 breeding season — the biggest on record, with 92 new chicks alive as of May — has marked the first deliberate step back from intensive management. Measures introduced this season include leaving more eggs to hatch naturally in nests rather than incubators, reducing supplementary feeding, and — in a symbolic cultural gesture — allowing some chicks to remain nameless, honouring a Ngāi Tahu aspiration to return the manu to their own natural ways [[9]](cite://9/2)[[8]](cite://8/2). The ultimate vision, articulated by DOC operations manager Deirdre Vercoe, is for kākāpō to one day wander forests as 'nameless, wild birds', booming from hillsides without transmitters or human oversight [[8]](cite://8/3).

For takahē, that wild future is already partly a reality. With a population now exceeding 500 birds [[15]](cite://15/1) and new populations actively breeding in the Rees Valley and elsewhere, the programme is successfully expanding its footprint — though predator control through extensive trap lines remains absolutely essential [[5]](cite://5/4)[[6]](cite://6/3).

![embed-2](embed://2)

---

## Shared Challenges

Despite their differences, both programmes face a familiar set of pressures:

- **Predator management** remains the single biggest threat to both species in mainland settings, with stoats a particular concern for takahē [[5]](cite://5/5).
- **Space** is becoming an acute issue for kākāpō, with DOC warning it is running out of high-quality predator-free islands [[16]](cite://16/1)[[8]](cite://8/4).
- **Genetic diversity** is a challenge for kākāpō, given the species' extremely small founding population — a concern being addressed through genomic analysis and targeted artificial insemination [[17]](cite://17/1)[[13]](cite://13/2).
- Both programmes have drawn on **commercial sponsorship and community partnerships**, with Ngāi Tahu playing an active role in both, and corporate donors having contributed millions to kākāpō recovery over the decades [[18]](cite://18/1).

The kākāpō programme is perhaps best understood as a prolonged intensive care operation gradually transitioning towards rehabilitation, while the takahē programme — with a larger and more dispersed population — is already in the recovery ward, testing its legs in the wild.

1.text:
[Page 13] area. Island restoration Some islands are being restored to something resembling their original ecology, with unwanted animals entirely eradicated. Larger browsing animals such as wild cattle and goats are the first to go, followed by smaller predators cats and possums, stoats and weasels, and eventually rats. Existing patches of native vegetation are enlarged, often with the help of planting programmes. Some sparse populations have become abundant once again. Other species were reintroduced to their former homes, while some islands became sanctuaries for animals never previously found there. Kākāpō were once plentiful, but when only a few remained in Fiordland and on Stewart Island (Rakiura), they were moved to Whenua Hou/Codfish, Maud and Little Barrier islands, and in 2003 to Fiordland’s Chalky Island (Te Kākahu o Tamatea). Public sanctuaries Most conservation restrict access to prevent disturbance or the arrival of unwanted pests. But several are open to the public. Kāpiti Island near Wellington and Tiritiri Matangi near Auckland have similar histories. Once cleared for farming, they now have no animal pests, and native forest has been re established over 250,000 native trees were planted on Tiritiri Matangi. Both are refuges for saddlebacks, kōkako, stitchbirds, little spotted kiwi and takahē. Not far from Kāpiti is Mana Island, also a bird sanctuary, and noted for its ‘colony’ of concrete gannets, built to tempt real gannets to breed there. Betty gets her goats In the 1970s the government decided to kill wild goats and sheep on Arapawa Island, in the Marlborough Sounds. Protesters claimed the animals were descendants of those left by James Cook. DNA tests showed some were genetically unique. Many were culled, but others were sent to farms and wildlife parks. Betty Rowe led the rescue campaign and established a sanctuary on Arapawa Island. Marine reserves To create areas where people could not disturb the ocean, seabed and seashore, the Marine Reserves Act was passed in 1971. The first reserve was at Goat Island, north of Auckland (now Cape Rodney Ōkakari Point Marine Reserve). The second was the ocean around the Poor Knights Islands, noted for islands subtropical fish. Others include islands off the Coromandel Peninsula, Tūhua (Mayor Island) in Bay of Plenty, Kāpiti Island, Long Island in the Marlborough Sounds, Tonga Island in Abel Tasman National Park, Elizabeth Island in Fiordland and Ulva Island near Stewart Island.

1.document_title: New Zealand's Nearshore Islands: History, Conservation, and Human Settlement
1.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's over 600 nearshore islands within 50 kilometres of the main islands, covering their geological formation, historical significance, and contemporary conservation status. The islands are distributed around the North Island (Great Barrier, Rangitoto, Bay of Islands) and southern regions (Marlborough Sounds, Fiordland). Historically, Māori utilized these islands for harvesting seafood, birds, and resources like argillite rock, obsidian, and adzite, including tītī (muttonbirds). European contact began in the late 1700s-1800s with sealers, whalers, and explorers like James Cook. Island industries included 19th-century mining, farming, and the world's first regular pigeon airmail service on Great Barrier Island (1897-1908). The document details quarantine facilities on Quarantine Island (Dunedin), Ōtamahua (Christchurch), and Matiu (Wellington), which housed disease victims, leprosy patients, and wartime internees. Today, islands serve as nature reserves hosting endangered species including tuatara, kākāpō, kiwi, and rare plants like Pennantia baylisiana. Conservation efforts began with Resolution Island in 1891 and include successful eradication programs and species reintroduction initiatives.

2.document_title: New Zealand's Threatened Species: Conservation Status, Strategies, and Recovery Efforts
2.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an overview of New Zealand's threatened species and conservation efforts. It defines threatened species as native plants and animals with critically low populations facing extinction risk, with New Zealand having 2,788 threatened species (37% of birds, 34% of plants). Main causes of decline include habitat destruction, invasive predators like rats and possums, and over-harvesting. New Zealand uses an eight-tier classification system for conservation status based on threats, endemism, vulnerability, and cultural importance. Conservation strategies include island sanctuaries, pest control, captive breeding, and habitat restoration. Notable successes include the black robin recovery (7 to 250 individuals), takahē recovery program, and tuatara reintroduction programs. The document presents case studies of endangered species including the Mahoenui giant wētā, Peraxilla mistletoes, kiwi, and tuatara. About 30% of New Zealand is protected conservation land. Recent efforts have expanded beyond visible species to include freshwater fish and plants, with a shift toward restoring entire habitats. Key challenges include funding limitations, many species poorly understood (1,455 fungi species classified as 'data deficient'), an estimated 50,000 unidentified native species potentially at risk, and preventing 'zombie species' that survive only in cultivation.

4.text:
[Page 10] Managing the 70% of New Zealand that is not conservation land has major implications for threatened species. Until the 1980s this land was mainly developed for farming and other production. But in 1991 the Resource Management Act changed the focus to the sustainable management of resources. However, this only addresses the negative environmental impact of new developments, rather than restoring already degraded habitats. Still, city councils and regional councils are required to consider conservation values, and many have begun to restore certain habitats. The New Zealand Biodiversity Strategy, launched in 2000, aimed to conserve New Zealand’s diversity of species, and to include the whole community in the effort. For example, throughout New Zealand there are local schemes to control predators in areas of native bush. The strategy also recognised that these projects must cut across map boundaries, and should not be the sole responsibility of the Department of Conservation. For example, the black billed gull, considered to be in serious decline, nests on South Island riverbeds which are not conservation lands. The regional council, Environment Canterbury, is now involved in saving the gull, among other species.

6.document_title: Stewart Island/Rakiura: Comprehensive Guide to New Zealand's Third Largest Island
6.document_summary: Stewart Island/Rakiura is New Zealand's third largest island located south of the South Island. The Māori name "Rakiura" means "glowing skies," referencing the aurora australis, while the English name honors William Stewart, first mate of the sealer Pegasus. Covering 1,680 square kilometers with approximately 85% protected as Rakiura National Park (established 2002), the island features diverse vegetation zones from coastal shrublands to alpine tussock lands, with over half covered by podocarp and hardwood forests. The island supports exceptional biodiversity including 15,000 southern tokoeka (Stewart Island kiwi), kākāpō, three penguin species, fur seals, and sea lions, with 21 endemic alpine plant species. Historically, Polynesians reached the island by the late 1200s, with permanent Māori settlement following primarily around coastal areas for fishing and harvesting tītī (muttonbirds). European contact began with James Cook in 1770, followed by sealers, whalers, and missionaries. Since the 1850s, the island's economy has centered on sheep farming, timber milling, and fishing, with fishing becoming dominant by 2013. Tourism evolved from the 1890s to a major industry attracting 30,000 annual visitors. Key geographic features include Paterson Inlet (8,900 hectares), Mason Bay with 200-metre dunes, Ulva Island (predator-free scenic reserve), Port Pegasus with granite domes, and the Southern Circuit tramping track (71.5 km). Oban (Halfmoon Bay) serves as the main township with 378 residents in 2013.

8.document_title: New Zealand Wading Birds: A Comprehensive Guide to Species, Conservation, and Migration
8.document_summary: This comprehensive guide explores New Zealand's diverse wading bird species, including oystercatchers, stilts, dotterels, plovers, wrybills, snipes, and bar-tailed godwits. It details their physical adaptations—such as varying leg and beak lengths suited to different feeding zones—and feeding behaviors in coastal and inland habitats. The guide covers three oystercatcher species and two stilt species, including the critically endangered black stilt (kakī). Notable migration patterns are highlighted, particularly the bar-tailed godwit's remarkable 11,000-kilometre non-stop journey from Alaska to New Zealand in 8-9 days, with 80,000-100,000 godwits arriving annually. The document addresses conservation concerns for endangered species like the Chatham Island oystercatcher and New Zealand dotterel, discussing threats from predators, human activity, and habitat loss. 9.text:
[Page 9] Kāpiti Island was reserved as a native bird sanctuary in 1897 but the name was a misnomer. The place was overrun with introduced animals that killed native species. The Royal Forest and Bird Protection Society and others organised the destruction of these invaders. Goats were eradicated from the island in 1928, followed by cats, deer, sheep, cattle, pigs and dogs. Possums were gone by 1986, and rats a decade later. Native species have thrived, providing an impression of forest life before humans arrived in Aotearoa. In 1923, angered by the destruction of Kāpiti Island’s natural ecosystem, Val Sanderson founded what became the Royal Forest and Bird Protection Society (later Forest and Bird). Since then the society has lobbied governments to protect endangered animal species and wild places. In 2011 its management team included lawyers, a marketing manager and a professional lobbyist. It had 50 branches, and 70,000 members and supporters.

9.document_title: Interest Groups and Lobbying in New Zealand: A Comprehensive Analysis
9.document_summary: This comprehensive document analyzes interest groups, lobbying, and advocacy in New Zealand across multiple sectors. It covers the definition and functions of interest groups (advocacy, policy formulation, and membership support) and their four main categories: economic groups (trade unions, business organizations like Federated Farmers), cause groups (environmental and values-based organizations), consumer groups, and community/recreational groups. The document traces activism evolution from early temperance and scenery preservation movements through 1960s-70s environmental, Māori rights, and feminist movements. It details economic interest groups including Federated Farmers (formed 1945), the liquor lobby, Business New Zealand, and the New Zealand Business Roundtable, highlighting their influence on government policy. Notable examples include Percy Coyle's lobbying for the liquor industry in the 1930s and Telecom's $30 million campaign to protect its broadband monopoly. Cause interest groups discussed include the Women's Christian Temperance Union (1885), environmental organizations like Forest and Bird, and moral conservative groups. Consumer advocacy organizations include Consumer New Zealand, HOBANZ, and welfare-focused groups like ASH, FOE, Alcohol Action NZ, and CPAG. Community groups covered include Grey Power, iwi groups, and sports organizations. Interest groups employ various tactics including direct action, petitions, demonstrations, and media campaigns, with Wellington serving as the lobbying hub. 15.document_title: Step away from the kākāpō
15.document_summary: The 2019 kākāpō breeding season achieved record success but was marred by an aspergillosis fungal disease outbreak on Codfish Island/Whenua Hou, infecting 21 birds and killing nine. Genetic analysis revealed all birds contracted the same fungal strain, likely introduced by humans through supplementary food. The same strain appeared on Anchor Island but caused no illness there. Researchers attribute the outbreak partly to hot, dry summer conditions that coincided with vulnerable chick stages. In response, DOC's recovery programme implemented enhanced biosecurity measures including food freezing, nest ventilation, and reduced direct chick handling. The team is transitioning toward less intensive management with remote monitoring and hands-off breeding sites, recognizing that while intensive management has prevented kākāpō extinction, stepping back represents the future direction for the species' recovery.

17.document_title: Kākāpō get busy
17.document_summary: On Whenua Hou island sanctuary, kākāpō breeding is triggered by rimu tree masting events. Scientists predict masting based on temperature patterns and fruit development on branch tips. In autumn, 47% of rimu branch tips bore fruit, signaling a record-breaking 2019 breeding season. Ripe red fruit carpeted the ground, and kākāpō mothers fed it to their chicks, which grew faster than usual. Nearly every nest contained two or three chicks—unprecedented in observations. This mega-mega-mast event is exceptionally rare, combining simultaneous beech and rimu masting with unusually widespread distribution, resulting in almost every kākāpō bird breeding.

18.document_title: Kākāpō: Bird on the Brink - Conservation Efforts and Recovery Success
18.document_summary: This comprehensive document chronicles the remarkable conservation journey of the kākāpō, New Zealand's critically endangered flightless nocturnal parrot. Once abundant throughout New Zealand's islands, the species declined dramatically to just 18 males in Fiordland by the 1980s, with only 62 birds remaining by the early 2000s due to introduced predators and historical human hunting. The breakthrough came with the discovery of a 200-strong population on Stewart Island in 1977, including the first identified female since the early 1900s. The recovery program involved relocating all surviving kākāpō to predator-free island sanctuaries including Whenua Hou, Maud Island, and Little Barrier Island between 1982-1992. Key conservation innovations include helicopter access to remote populations, hand-rearing of chicks, inter-island transfers, electronic surveillance systems, and supplementary feeding programs. The species' unique lekking courtship behavior, where males inflate and boom low-frequency calls from elaborately maintained bowl-shaped arenas, was crucial to understanding their breeding patterns. Despite their appearance as ecological relics, kākāpō demonstrate adaptability and have become marathon survivors with lifespans potentially exceeding 60 years. The dedicated recovery team has achieved significant breeding successes, transforming wild kākāpō into managed refugees in their own homeland. The long-term vision includes establishing free-living, self-sustaining populations on subantarctic islands like Campbell Island, representing an unprecedented turning point in the species' survival.

20.document_title: Feathering the Nest: Restoring Maungatautari
20.document_summary: This article profiles Chris Smuts-Kennedy, an ecologist leading species reintroductions at Maungatautari Ecological Island Trust in New Zealand's Waikato region. The project has enclosed 4,300 hectares with 47 km of predator-proof fencing to restore native wildlife. Recent successes include releasing 79 stitchbirds and 60 whiteheads, with takahe, kaka, and kiwi also reintroduced and breeding. Smuts-Kennedy, with 43 years of experience in New Zealand fauna, aspires to reintroduce kakapo to the mountain, viewing it as an ideal habitat due to its rimu trees and stable fruiting patterns. He discusses potential candidates including Sirocco, a human-raised kakapo ambassador, and other birds unsuitable for breeding. [Page 1] Rare species can’t wait By Kennedy Warne Lessons from a big booming budgerigar. The first time I saw a kākāpō in the wild was on a windswept ridge of an island off the west coast of Rakiura. At that time, 2002, most of the 86 living kākāpō were clustered on that one island, Whenua Hou. It was the middle of the night, and I was jammed in a tent with two wildlife rangers. Every half an hour or so, we checked the screen of a monitor that was connected to a repurposed domestic security camera stationed 80 metres away, on the island’s summit. The camera was pointed at a shallow depression in the soil—a kākāpō courtship bowl. The bowl was empty. Whenever we turned the monitor on, all we saw were scrubby bushes flailing in the wind, and all we heard was the caterwauling cries of petrels wheeling overhead in the storm. Then, around midnight, we heard what we had been hoping for: the sonorous boom of a kākāpō male. Three hands reached simultaneously for the video button. The screen came to life, and there, pumped up like a rugby ball, was Lionel, singing his basso profundo lovesong to the island’s 21 females. All of whom, apparently, ignored his overtures. When I checked online just now, I learned that Lionel died in 2014, apparently without siring any offspring. It’s quite something to find every kākāpō listed by name on Wikipedia. All 123 adult birds are there, along with the recently deceased, like Lionel. And, as the story in this issue of the magazine explains, these birds don’t just have names but now also an individual genetic fingerprint—and, with that, an expectation that the species can be managed towards a more robust future. This year has been the best equal kākāpō breeding season ever. Whenua Hou—“new land”—is turning out to be more than a rest home for old birds; it’s a nursery for new generations.

21.document_title: Rare species can't wait
21.document_summary: This article by Kennedy Warne chronicles the conservation efforts to save New Zealand's critically endangered kākāpō parrot. The author recounts witnessing a male kākāpō named Lionel performing his courtship display on Whenua Hou island in 2002, when only 86 birds remained. The narrative traces the species' tragic decline from mainland forests in Fiordland during the 1980s, documented by conservation biologist Don Merton, to current recovery efforts. The article highlights innovative conservation techniques, including using rock wrens' nesting behavior to locate kākāpō, and recent successes with breeding seasons. It emphasizes the urgent need for species conservation, noting that New Zealand faces extinction risks for 4,000 endemic species. The piece balances urgency with wonder, celebrating the unique characteristics of kākāpō while advocating for continued predator-free sanctuary development and ecological restoration efforts.

22.text:
[Page 13] Over the years, this programme has been through some shaky times, partly because there are still so many unknowns about the birds, but also because of the hobbling effects of political pressure and bureaucratic constraints. Following an external review in 1994, executive control over budget, strategy, staff and all things kākāpō was put in the hands of three people: Paul Jansen, Graeme Elliott and Merton—all of whom have clocked up many years in grassroots conservation. Jansen, the programme leader, has quietly emphatic manners and the reputation of a man who gets things done. Elliott, the team’s scientist, is a thinker and electronics tinkerer, responsible for much of the innovative technology now employed in the field. Merton, with unrivalled knowledge and experience of kākāpō, is the prime architect of the close order management strategy for the birds, adapted from his black robin work. Since 1995, the trio has put the kākāpō on a fast track to recovery—well, fast in kākāpō terms. In the avian world, where life is but a short sprint, kākāpō are the marathon runners—possibly the longest lived of all birds. Many of those alive today were already mature adults when they were found in the mid 1970s, and biologists estimate a typical kākāpō life span to be around 60 years, perhaps more. Like tuatara, they seem timeless. Their metabolism is so unhurried they can digest foods containing toxins that would kill humans or make them sick, like the leaves and fruit of the native tutu, and poroporo berries—both kākāpō favourites. And still the bizarre night parrots keep surprising their caretakers. Graeme Elliott, in an effort to breathe a little more enthusiasm into the birds’ courtship, has tried injecting selected rimu trees with a hormone to induce the trees to produce more fruit—so far the most consistent kākāpō aphrodisiac. He has also developed a “boom box”—a portable, weatherproof stereo system which, placed near a lek, automatically comes on at night, blaring out the boom! boom! sound to spur the males into song. In 1998, kākāpō bred successfully on Te Hoiere/Maud Island—but without the benefit of a boom box and without a rimu tree in sight. The event on Maud was all the more significant for taking place in an extremely modified environment, showing that, despite appearing to be stuck in an ecological time warp, the kākāpō is an adaptable creature. Maud Island is the 309 hectare tip of a mountain that was flooded when the sea level rose. It was farmed until 1975, when the Royal New Zealand Forest and Bird Society successfully campaigned to buy it and turn it into a nature reserve. Most of the island had been cleared of its original forest, and one corner had been planted in pines. Remarkably, it was in the radiata that the kākāpō nested. Many kākāpō now reside on Whenua Hou, an island west of Stewart Island which was cleared of possums, weka and rats to create a safe haven. Locating the birds on the 1396 hectare scrub and forest covered island is a challenge made easier by the use of radio telemetry, but the method is not foolproof: the kākāpō’s transmitters can become detached, in which case dogs are brought in to sniff out the escapees. By late December 1998, all four of Maud’s males were booming, and soon mating signs—tufts of down and feathers near the track and bowl area—were found. Then, on the island’s west facing slope, where the setting sun dapples through the trees and brown pine needles muffle one’s footsteps, Merton and others discovered a nest with three eggs under sparse bracken cover on a slope so steep the subsequent track cut up it was a winding staircase of 140 steps. The find was such a momentous event that Merton and his colleagues took no chances with the safety of their charges. The three chicks that hatched were offspring of Richard Henry, the last and only known surviving Fiordland kākāpō. “We’ve waited more than 20 years for this nest,” Merton said at the time. “It must succeed!” And so the intervention began. Every time the mother, named Flossie, left the nest to forage—generally at around 2 or 3am—a stealthy construction crew moved in. First, a metre high retaining wall was erected on the lower side of the nest to prevent the eggs from rolling down the hill. Next a plywood roof was added. Then a drain was dug on the upslope to divert any possible flooding. A piece of plastic pipe became an entrance tunnel, and an infra red beam, wired to a door chime, was placed across the entrance to alert nest minders when the mother left for her nightly perambulations. A miniature video surveillance camera was placed inside the nest to keep an electronic eye on the chicks. Later, a play ground was added. It was as if a person living in a shanty had left for a short walk and returned to find a prefab house with a sundeck, and a sand pit for the kids. Not showing the least surprise, Flossie and the youngsters took the alterations in their goosestep stride. All the while, a roster of nest minders camped in a tent 80 metres away, ready to dash in to deal with any emergency. Electronic surveillance and nest minding would become standard procedure with all subsequent nests. A fabric scoop on the end of a ski pole makes a useful device for extracting chicks from deep hideaways when weighing and measuring is to be carried out. Females feed young chicks (such as the 12 day old in the bottom photograph) by regurgitating the soft parts of plants, including fruit and shoots, but older chicks are given less digested fruit and seeds.

[Page 1] It is four in the morning, and I am sitting alone on the rain soaked soil of an island at the edge of Foveaux Strait, hunched against the pre dawn cold and endless southwesterlies. I have been in the thick blackness of this southern night for six hours already, waiting for the approaching dawn to silhouette the forest canopy with patches of grey. My only company lies a couple of metres away, in a tangle of rotting rata stumps and roots: a tiny grey chick which looks as cold and disconsolate as I feel. It is H2, a seven day old kakapo and one of the very latest additions to the embattled parrot’s population. While I shiver in layers of expensive polypropylene and synthetic fabrics, H2 has only the finest coating of grey down for warmth and resembles nothing more than a patch of mould on the forest floor. As a volunteer nest minder, I am spending two weeks looking after this fragile addition to the kakapo world while its mother, Heather, forages in the surrounding rimu forest of Codfish Island/Whenua Hou. Fatigued by 10 days of scant and intermittent sleep and up to four hours’ walking on waterlogged tracks each day, I find my biggest challenge is simply to stay awake. It’s rough and it’s raw, but what I’m doing is the reality of conservation in this country. Forget photo opportunities and cuddling one of the world’s rarest birds. Saving this species requires patience, sturdy boots and getting used to rivulets of water trickling down your neck. 23.document_title: Minders: The Kakapo Caregivers of Codfish Island - Conservation and Intensive Management
23.document_summary: This comprehensive document chronicles the extraordinary kakapo conservation efforts on Codfish Island/Whenua Hou, focusing on the landmark 2002 breeding season. Over 100 volunteer nest minders from around the world participated in intensive 24-hour surveillance of 24 nests, resulting in 26 chicks hatching with 24 surviving—a 39% increase in the world kakapo population from 62 to 86 birds. The nest minders maintained constant vigilance, acted as surrogate parents during female foraging periods, and used innovative equipment like heat pads and infrared monitoring systems. The Department of Conservation-led intervention programme involved detailed monitoring, video surveillance, nightly chick weighing, and hand-rearing of struggling chicks. Despite harsh conditions—steep boggy tracks, cold nights, and minimal sleep—volunteers found the opportunity invaluable. The document profiles individual kakapo mothers (Heather, Ruth, Nora, Flossie) and their distinct parenting behaviors. A 1999 aerial poison drop eradicated rats, dramatically improving nesting success. With a chick mortality rate of just 8%, the 2002 season represented the most significant breakthrough for kakapo recovery since their rediscovery in 1977, demonstrating that intensive human intervention can successfully secure this endangered species' survival.

24.text:
[Page 1] On this tender genetic thread hung the future of the entire species. For four decades, conservationists have focused on the fortunes of the remaining individuals, increasing the population to 155. Today, as deputy editor Rebekah White reveals in this issue, scientists have turned their attention back to that frail genetic thread, analysing it in cross section to reveal the fabric of the kākāpō genome, and the specific genes of every kākāpō in the population, to breed the population back to health.

24.document_title: A New Hope
24.document_summary: This essay explores New Zealand's conservation efforts and the potential of genetic technology to restore extinct species. The author reflects on receiving a ceramic replica of a huia feather—a bird hunted to extinction over a century ago—as a symbol of what modernity has destroyed. The piece highlights successful conservation efforts, particularly the kākāpō bird, whose population has been increased from 50 to 155 individuals through dedicated conservation work and genome analysis. It discusses the South Island kōkako's potential extinction and the North Island kōkako's near-extinction. The essay presents palaeobiologist Jeffrey Yule's philosophical framework for ethical species cloning, which proposes that extinct species like the huia, thylacine, and passenger pigeon could be restored if specific criteria are met. Ultimately, the author suggests that genetic technology offers hope for repairing past environmental mistakes and restoring public faith in conservation efforts.

25.text:
[Page 1] If we’re serious about Predator Free 2050—about ridding New Zealand of every last rat, stoat and possum—then Fiordland poses its sternest backcountry test. If we can pull it off here, we can pull it off in any of our national parks. What makes this land so difficult—and so important? Lining up a limb, DOC biodiversity ranger Bex Jackson readies to fire a lead sinker into the canopy of a beech tree, site of a long tailed bat roost in the Iris Burn. Behind her, senior ranger Emmanuel Oyston holds the fishing line the pair will use to haul a climbing rope up to the roost. Since DOC began rodent control in 2014, this bat colony at Rocky Point has doubled in size. Looking at this part of the country, I’m not so sure. Fiordland National Park—12,600 square kilometres, barely scratched by road or track, suffering some of the planet’s foulest meteorology. It will be raining here for more than half the year—eight metres of rain disembogues annually over Milford Sound. Chill southerlies mean the forest is defeated at just 1000 metres of altitude: above is gaunt granite, some of the oldest rock in the land. The single biggest problem with pests in this park is getting to them. Glaciers have carved a confusing coastline—is that a passage or a peninsula? An island or an isthmus? You’ll need a boat, a good one—or a helicopter, and lots of fuel. Any endeavour here has to plan for immensity, hindrance, contingency and the consent of that funereal firmament.

25.document_summary: This comprehensive document chronicles New Zealand's ambitious Predator Free 2050 initiative, with Fiordland National Park serving as the ultimate test case for eliminating invasive predators including rats, stoats, and possums. The narrative follows DOC rangers conducting fieldwork across challenging terrain, documenting conservation successes in long-tailed bat monitoring, whio (blue duck) recovery, and wildlife protection efforts. Despite receiving less than 1% of DOC's budget while occupying 15% of the conservation estate, Fiordland has achieved measurable results through aerial 1080 drops, sustained rat trapping, and innovative pest management strategies. Key programs include Andrew Smart's whio recovery programme using trained detection dogs, Lindsay Wilson's stoat and rat control operations across 65,000+ hectares using Goodnature A24 traps, and the Zero Invasive Predators (ZIP) initiative's "remove and protect" strategy. Success stories include doubled bat populations at Rocky Point (2014-2017) and increased kākā populations following aerial drops in Waitutu Forest. The document emphasizes that success depends on community support, social license, and local commitment alongside technological innovation, arguing that if conservation goals can be achieved in Fiordland's harsh conditions, they can succeed anywhere in New Zealand.

26.text:
[Page 6] anything, but give it a go.’” The organisers decided to base Te Korowai on the Fiordland Marine Guardians experience. Fiordland is considered the prototype of community driven marine protection. Developed over 10 years, the Fiordland marine conservation strategy became enshrined in legislation in 2005. [sidebar 1] One of the principles developed by Fiordland was the ‘egg’ organisational model, in which local interests (tourism, fishing, conservation, runanga) form the central decision making yolk, while statutory agencies (councils, ministries, wider iwi, the Department of Conservation) occupy a supporting role as the surrounding white. This structure puts the stewardship responsibility squarely on the community. Another Fiordland principle bequeathed to Te Korowai was the idea of gifts and gains. Each interest group gives concessions in order to gain a desired outcome, expressed in Te Korowai’s vision of “a flourishing, rich and healthy environment where opportunities abound”—a.k.a. “more fish”. In Fiordland, commercial lobster fishers agreed to stop setting pots in the inner fjords and recreational fishers conceded lower bag limits. Perhaps the most important piece of advice Fiordland’s guardians gave the Kaikoura group was that to get buy in, you have to consult widely, listen carefully and not impose a time frame on the process. Nine years on, Kaikoura has the most innovative combination of marine protections anywhere in the country. [Chapter Break] It also has the strangest shaped marine reserve. It looks like an AK47 with its muzzle resting on State Highway 1, just north of Goose Bay.

26.document_title: Sea Change: Marine Management and Conservation in Aotearoa New Zealand
26.document_summary: This comprehensive collection examines New Zealand's marine resource management, conservation, and governance challenges. Key topics include Kaikoura's successful community engagement process resulting in marine protection legislation (2014) with whale and seal sanctuaries; Te Korowai and no-take reserves effectiveness; collaborative community-based management in Otago through taiapure customary areas; and marine biosecurity challenges from invasive species like Undaria seaweed and Mediterranean fanworms. The collection addresses the global fishing crisis where 75-85% of world fisheries are fully exploited or depleted, analyzing New Zealand's Quota Management System as a rare success with unintended consequences. Case studies illustrate how building trust across Māori, Pākehā, and tourism operators through shared dialogue enables sustainable coastal management. The documents emphasize New Zealand's fragmented marine governance (18 statutes, 14 agencies, six strategies) and advocate for integrated ocean policy, positioning ocean management as a defining environmental challenge.

27.document_title: Hiker Navigating Fiordland Trail

28.text:
[Page 1] Backyard explorers By discoveryexpeditions.co.nz Within our New Zealand bubble are some of the most dramatic, breathtaking landscapes in the world. Fiordland and Rakiura/Stewart Island offer an insight into the world as it once was: raw, pristine, largely uninhabited. Recognised by UNESCO World Heritage status, Fiordland National Park is characterised by steep, jumbled topography, a rugged coastline, dense rainforest and a dynamic climate. Further south, most of Rakiura/Stewart Island is part of Rakiura National Park, with settlement confined mainly to Oban, the only township. The island’s densely forested hills, tiny population and untouched coastline of rocky outcrops and golden sand beaches make it a natural refuge for marine and bird life. Few people venture to these isolated parts of the deep south, but leading tourism operator Real Journeys explores Fiordland and Rakiura/Stewart Island on Discovery Expeditions, sea voyages ranging from four to seven days. Some expeditions retrace Captain James Cook’s 1773 voyage around the Fiordland coastline and visit Māori and European historical sites that have played a part in New Zealand’s history. On Fiordland voyages, passengers have the opportunity to catch glimpses of the region’s abundant wildlife: bottlenose dolphins, Fiordland crested penguins and the occasional whale. Each voyage offers plenty of opportunities to disembark the vessel with daily nature hikes, kayaking, or tender craft activities. Throughout the trip, on board nature guides, who are experts on southern New Zealand, share knowledge of the flora, fauna and history of these regions. Travel in these parts is never predictable: the elements shape each trip, but being flexible yields rewards. Days are spent in isolated wilderness, taking in the sights and wildlife along the way.

[Page 20] Inevitably, conversation turned to the national park. Schofield, a former deer culler and forester with the Department of Internal Affairs and then chief ranger of Fiordland National Park, has made a number of submis sions to the Conservation Authority concerning the park. He argues that rather than wasting money on piecemeal pest control efforts on the main island, it would be better to create more pest free refuges (such as Ulva and Codfish Islands) on the many small islands off the coast. He is also concerned that the national park might assume de facto control of surrounding sea areas, although the park boundaries will not extend below the mean high water mark. In Fiordland National Park, he says, the consent process for tourism concessions treats the adjacent waters as if they are part of the park itself. “There, a protectionist attitude to the sea has little effect on the economic prosperity of Te Anau or Manapouri, which derive income from farming, but the effects of such an approach on Halfmoon Bay could be devastating.”
