9.fileName: 'Always exciting' - Bumper season for kākāpō breeding.pdf
9.filePath: pdf/'Always exciting' - Bumper season for kākāpō breeding.pdf
9.fileDescription: The Department of Conservation announces the first kākāpō breeding season in four years, potentially the largest in decades. With remote monitoring detecting mating activity from December 29, the season marks the 13th breeding cycle since the recovery programme began 30 years ago. The current population stands at 236 birds, including 83 breeding-age females, up from just 51 in the programme's inception. This season introduces lower-intervention strategies across three protected offshore islands, including prioritizing genetically valuable eggs, reducing incubator use, and minimizing nest interference. Ngāi Tahu representatives emphasize the importance of returning kākāpō to natural behaviors and expanding safe habitats. First chicks are expected to hatch mid-February, with success measured not just by numbers but by creating self-sustaining, thriving populations.

chunkHighlights.text:
DOC Operations Manager for Kākāpō Recovery Deidre Vercoe said the
milestone felt particularly significant for the species this year. "It's always exciting when the breeding season officially begins, but this year it feels especially long-awaited after such a big gap since the last season in 2022," she said. "Now it is underway, we expect more mating over the next month, and we are preparing for what might be the biggest breeding season since the programme began 30 years ago." Through its longstanding Kākāpō Recovery programme, DOC had worked with Ngāi Tahu to rebuild the population from 51 manu (31 males, 20 females) through 12 breeding seasons. The population peaked at 252 in 2022. The flightless, nocturnal parrots breed once every two to four years, when the rimu trees mast. The kākāpō are among the most intensively managed species in the world. Prior to the breeding season, the total population sits at 236, including 83 breeding-age females. This year would be the 13th breeding season in the 30 years since the programme began. It could also see the most chicks since records began, although success could no longer be measured in mere numbers, Vercoe said. "Kākāpō are still critically endangered, so we'll keep working hard to increase numbers, but looking ahead, chick numbers are not our only measure of success. "We want to create healthy, self-sustaining populations of kākāpō that are thriving, not just surviving. This means with each successful breeding season, we're aiming to reduce the level of intensive, hands-on management to return to a more natural state. "We're working towards the goal of returning them to their former range

around New Zealand so that one day, hearing a kākāpō boom might be a normal part of naturing." A range of lower-intervention strategies would be introduced this season, across the three protected offshore breeding islands. These include prioritising checks for genetically valuable eggs and chicks, leaving more eggs to hatch in nests rather than incubators, reduce nest interference for mothers raising multiple chicks, and reducing supplementary feeding. The Kākāpō Recovery Group's Te Rūnanga o Ngāi Tahu representative Tāne Davis said growth brought both advantages and challenges. "As part of the more hands-off approach to enhance the mauri of the species, a Ngāi Tahu aspiration is also for a percentage of the chicks hatched this year to remain nameless, acknowledging the beginning of returning the manu to their own natural ways," he said. "The predicted scale of this season also reminds us of the need for more safe homes, like a predator-free Rakiura, for this taonga species." The first chicks were expected to start hatching from mid-February. Sign up for Ngā Pitopito Kōrero, a daily newsletter curated by our editors and delivered straight to your inbox every weekday. 10.fileDescription: This comprehensive document chronicles the remarkable conservation journey of the kākāpō, New Zealand's critically endangered flightless nocturnal parrot. Once abundant throughout New Zealand's islands, the species declined dramatically to just 18 males in Fiordland by the 1980s, with only 62 birds remaining by the early 2000s due to introduced predators and historical human hunting. The breakthrough came with the discovery of a 200-strong population on Stewart Island in 1977, including the first identified female since the early 1900s. The recovery program involved relocating all surviving kākāpō to predator-free island sanctuaries including Whenua Hou, Maud Island, and Little Barrier Island between 1982-1992. Key conservation innovations include helicopter access to remote populations, hand-rearing of chicks, inter-island transfers, electronic surveillance systems, and supplementary feeding programs. The species' unique lekking courtship behavior, where males inflate and boom low-frequency calls from elaborately maintained bowl-shaped arenas, was crucial to understanding their breeding patterns. Despite their appearance as ecological relics, kākāpō demonstrate adaptability and have become marathon survivors with lifespans potentially exceeding 60 years. The dedicated recovery team has achieved significant breeding successes, transforming wild kākāpō into managed refugees in their own homeland. The long-term vision includes establishing free-living, self-sustaining populations on subantarctic islands like Campbell Island, representing an unprecedented turning point in the species' survival.

chunkHighlights.text: Female kākāpō are devoted mothers, but since they are all solo parents they must leave their eggs and chicks unguarded for long periods each night while they forage. Before the advent of mammalian predators, their absences were of little consequence, but ground-level nests of eggs or chicks are like fast-food outlets to rats and their ilk, and now the only safe place for kākāpō to breed is on predator-free islands. Even in these havens, kākāpō workers take no chances, installing infrared movement sensors and surveillance cameras at all nests.

11.fileDescription: This comprehensive document chronicles the remarkable conservation journey of the kākāpō, New Zealand's critically endangered flightless nocturnal parrot. Once abundant throughout New Zealand's islands, the species declined dramatically to just 18 males in Fiordland by the 1980s, with only 62 birds remaining by the early 2000s due to introduced predators and historical human hunting. The species' unique lekking courtship behavior, where males inflate and boom low-frequency calls from elaborately maintained bowl-shaped arenas, was crucial to understanding their breeding patterns. Despite their appearance as ecological relics, kākāpō demonstrate adaptability and have become marathon survivors with lifespans potentially exceeding 60 years. The dedicated recovery team has achieved significant breeding successes, transforming wild kākāpō into managed refugees in their own homeland. The long-term vision includes establishing free-living, self-sustaining populations on subantarctic islands like Campbell Island, representing an unprecedented turning point in the species' survival.

chunkHighlights.text: Over the years, this programme has been through some shaky times, partly because there are still so many unknowns about the birds, but also because of the hobbling effects of political pressure and bureaucratic constraints. Following an external review in 1994, executive control over budget, strategy, staff and all things kākāpō was put in the hands of three people: Paul Jansen, Graeme Elliott and Merton—all of whom have clocked up many years in grassroots conservation. Jansen, the programme leader, has quietly emphatic

manners and the reputation of a man who gets things done. Elliott, the team’s scientist, is a thinker and electronics tinkerer, responsible for much of the innovative technology now employed in the field. Merton, with unrivalled knowledge and experience of kākāpō, is the prime architect of the close-order management strategy for the birds, adapted from his black robin work. Since 1995, the trio has put the kākāpō on a fast track to recovery—well, fast in kākāpō terms.

In the avian world, where life is but a short sprint, kākāpō are the marathon runners—possibly the longest lived of all birds. Many of those alive today were already mature adults when they were found in the mid-1970s, and biologists estimate a typical kākāpō life span to be around 60 years, perhaps more. Like tuatara, they seem timeless. Their metabolism is so unhurried they can digest foods containing toxins that would kill humans or make them sick, like the leaves and fruit of the native tutu, and poroporo berries—both kākāpō favourites.

And still the bizarre night parrots keep surprising their caretakers. Graeme Elliott, in an effort to breathe a little more enthusiasm into the birds’ courtship, has tried injecting selected rimu trees with a hormone to induce the trees to produce more fruit—so far the most consistent kākāpō aphrodisiac. He has also developed a “boom box”—a portable, weatherproof stereo system which, placed near a lek, automatically comes on at night, blaring out the boom! boom! sound to spur the males into song.
In 1998, kākāpō bred successfully on Te Hoiere/Maud Island—but without the benefit of a boom box and without a rimu tree in sight.

The event on Maud was all the more significant for taking place in an extremely modified environment, showing that, despite appearing to be stuck in an ecological time warp, the kākāpō is an adaptable creature. Maud Island is the 309-hectare tip of a mountain that was flooded when the sea level rose. It was farmed until 1975, when the Royal New Zealand Forest and Bird Society successfully campaigned to buy it and turn it into a nature reserve. Most of the island had been cleared of its original forest, and one corner had been planted in pines. Remarkably, it
was in the radiata that the kākāpō nested.

Many kākāpō now reside on Whenua Hou, an island west of Stewart Island which was cleared of possums, weka and rats to create a safe haven. Locating the birds on the 1396-hectare scrub- and forest-covered island is a challenge made easier by the use of radio telemetry, but the method is not foolproof: the kākāpō’s transmitters can become detached, in which case dogs are brought in to sniff out the escapees.

By late December 1998, all four of Maud’s males were booming, and soon mating signs—tufts of down and feathers near the track-and-bowl area—were found. Then, on the island’s west-facing slope, where the setting sun dapples through the trees and brown pine needles muffle one’s footsteps, Merton and others discovered a nest with three eggs under sparse bracken cover on a slope so steep the subsequent track cut up it was a winding staircase of 140 steps.

The find was such a momentous event that Merton and his colleagues took no chances with the safety of their charges. The three chicks that hatched were offspring of Richard Henry, the last and only known surviving Fiordland kākāpō. “We’ve waited more than 20 years for this nest,” Merton said at the time. “It must succeed!” And so the intervention began. Every time the mother, named Flossie, left the nest to forage—generally at around 2 or 3am—a stealthy construction crew moved in.

First, a metre-high retaining wall was erected on the lower side of the nest to prevent the eggs from rolling down the hill. Next a plywood roof was added. Then a drain was dug on the upslope to divert any possible flooding. A piece of plastic pipe became an entrance tunnel, and an infra-red beam, wired to a door chime, was placed across the entrance to alert nest minders when the mother left for her nightly perambulations. A miniature video surveillance camera was placed inside the nest to keep an electronic eye on the chicks. Later, a play- ground was added. It was as if a person living in a shanty had left for a short walk and returned to find a prefab house with a sundeck, and a sand pit for the kids.

Not showing the least surprise, Flossie and the youngsters took the alterations in their goosestep stride. All the while, a roster of nest minders camped in a tent 80 metres away, ready to dash in to deal with any emergency. Electronic surveillance and nest minding would become standard procedure with all subsequent nests.

A fabric scoop on the end of a ski pole makes a useful device for extracting chicks from deep hideaways when weighing and measuring is to be carried out. Females feed young chicks (such as the 12-day-old in the bottom photograph) by regurgitating the soft parts of plants, including fruit and shoots, but older chicks are given less digested fruit and seeds.

12.filePath: pdf/Minders: the kakapo caregivers of Codfish Island.pdf
12.fileDescription: This comprehensive document chronicles the extraordinary kakapo conservation efforts on Codfish Island/Whenua Hou, focusing on the landmark 2002 breeding season. Over 100 volunteer nest minders from around the world participated in intensive 24-hour surveillance of 24 nests, resulting in 26 chicks hatching with 24 surviving—a 39% increase in the world kakapo population from 62 to 86 birds. The nest minders maintained constant vigilance, acted as surrogate parents during female foraging periods, and used innovative equipment like heat pads and infrared monitoring systems. The Department of Conservation-led intervention programme involved detailed monitoring, video surveillance, nightly chick weighing, and hand-rearing of struggling chicks. Despite harsh conditions—steep boggy tracks, cold nights, and minimal sleep—volunteers found the opportunity invaluable. The document profiles individual kakapo mothers (Heather, Ruth, Nora, Flossie) and their distinct parenting behaviors. A 1999 aerial poison drop eradicated rats, dramatically improving nesting success. With a chick mortality rate of just 8%, the 2002 season represented the most significant breakthrough for kakapo recovery since their rediscovery in 1977, demonstrating that intensive human intervention can successfully secure this endangered species' survival.

chunkHighlights.text: It is four in the morning, and I am sitting alone on the rain-soaked soil of an island at the edge of Foveaux Strait, hunched against the pre-dawn cold and endless southwesterlies.
I have been in the thick blackness of this southern night for six hours already, waiting for the approaching dawn to silhouette the forest canopy with patches of grey.

My only company lies a couple of metres away, in a tangle of rotting rata stumps and roots: a tiny grey chick which looks as cold and disconsolate as I feel. It is H2, a seven-day-old kakapo and one of the very latest additions to the embattled parrot’s population.
While I shiver in layers of expensive polypropylene and synthetic fabrics, H2 has only the finest coating of grey down for warmth and resembles nothing more than a patch of mould on the forest floor.

As a volunteer nest minder, I am spending two weeks looking after this fragile addition to the kakapo world while its mother, Heather, forages in the surrounding rimu forest of Codfish Island/Whenua Hou. Fatigued by 10 days of scant and intermittent sleep and up to four hours’ walking on waterlogged tracks each day, I find my biggest challenge is simply to stay awake.

It’s rough and it’s raw, but what I’m doing is the reality of conservation in this country. Forget photo opportunities and cuddling one of the world’s rarest birds. Saving this species requires patience, sturdy boots and getting used to rivulets of water trickling down your neck.
Nest minders, including the author (viewing a video monitor connected to an infrared camera at the nest).
The cables, batteries and electronic gadgetry involved in the project had to be kept operational in the demanding outdoor conditions by Kakapo Recovery Programme scientist Graeme Elliott.

13.fileName: Scientists use artificial insemination to boost kākāpō numbers.pdf
13.filePath: pdf/Scientists use artificial insemination to boost kākāpō numbers.pdf
13.fileDescription: A new study demonstrates that artificial insemination is effectively improving kākāpō fertility, with German scientists from the University of Giessen collaborating with New Zealand's Department of Conservation. Kākāpō populations have recovered from just 51 birds in the 1990s to 242 today. The technique involves capturing males, extracting sperm through massage, transporting it to females, and performing insemination—a challenging process in the wild. Dr. Andrew Digby explains the method helps preserve genes of unsuccessful males and addresses the species' low genetic diversity. While this is a short-term conservation measure, the team aims for natural breeding. Kākāpō breed every two to four years, with 2026 expected to be a significant breeding season.

chunkHighlights.text:
A new study has discovered the use of artificial insemination is
improving the fertility of kākāpō. It isn't the first time scientists have
tried the method, with the first trial in 2009. But this time a team of German scientists from the University of Giessen was called in to help out. Kākāpō numbers have bounced back from just 51 birds in the 1990s, to 242 today. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/morni ngreport/audio/2018988066/scientists-using-artificial-insemination-to-sa ve-kakap Co-author of the study and Department of Conservation's science advisor Dr Andrew Digby told Morning Report the team members have been refining their methods since the first success in 2019, but the method was not easy. "Doing it in the wild is actually really, really difficult," he said. "First of all, you've got to find and catch the male that you want, and then you've got to get the sperm from him, and you use a massage technique for that. "Then we've got to get the sperm to the female, and that's not an easy task because sometimes the female can be quite a long way away." Next they've got to catch the female and inseminate her, which can be hard if she is up a tree for example, Dr Digby said. Kākāpō numbers have bounced back from just 51 birds in the 1990s, to 242 today. Dr Digby explained these challenges are why it has been quite a long time between the team being successful with the method. Kākāpō have a low genetic diversity, which is one of the reasons Dr Digby and his team are using artificial insemination to help grow numbers. "We've got some males who have been trying to mate for decades, but they've never been successful," he said. "We are giving them a bit of a helping hand to ensure that their genes carry on into future generations." Dr Digby said his team have been working with scientists from around the world, as the skills required to do the work are "incredibly specialised". "This German team have got a lot of experience with inseminating parrots, but even they found that the kākāpō is quite different to all of the other parrots. "Ultimately this is a relatively short-term measure. We want to be as
natural as possible, we want them to do it for themselves." Kākāpō only

breed every two to four years, and Dr Digby was confident 2026 would be a very big breeding season as it will be four years since the last one. Sign up for Ngā Pitopito Kōrero, a daily newsletter curated by our editors and delivered straight to your inbox every weekday. Related

14.fileName: Our Changing World: Return of The Kākāpō Files.pdf
14.filePath: pdf/Our Changing World: Return of The Kākāpō Files.pdf
14.fileDescription: This article covers the anticipated 2025-2026 kākāpō breeding season on Whenua Hou/Codfish Island, with preparations underway for what may be the largest breeding season ever. The kākāpō population has grown from just 51 birds in 1995 to 237 today, thanks to the Department of Conservation's Kākāpō Recovery Programme. Male kākāpō attract females through boom and ching calls while preparing mating grounds. The breeding season is tied to rimu tree fruiting cycles, and this year's rimu mast is the largest on record at 63 percent, compared to the previous record of 47 percent in 2019. With 84 adult females capable of breeding, 2026 has potential to be a turning point for this iconic species. However, challenges remain including disease risks, bird flu concerns, and the possibility of rimu fruit failing to ripen. DOC is implementing a new "lighter touch" approach on two breeding islands to sustain long-term conservation efforts. Alison Ballance will document the season through the second season of The Kākāpō Files podcast.

chunkHighlights.text:
The males stay in one spot and attract the females through their boom
and ching calls. On the small, bush-clad, Whenua Hou / Codfish Island
preparations are underway. People and supplies are being dropped in by
helicopter. Food hoppers are being filled. Transmitters are being
checked. And come nighttime, a booming sound has begun to fill the air.
Anticipation is high, and building, for what may turn out to be the
biggest kākāpō breeding season ever. [wk_audio]909a5748-727a-404d-bdaa-509e8cd712a4 Follow Our Changing World on Apple, Spotify, iHeartRadio or wherever you listen to your podcasts Today there are 237 kākāpō. "The first male who was heard booming this year was Faulkner, in late November," Alison Ballance said, having heard the news from Department of Conservation's Kākāpō Recovery Programme members, who are keeping a close eye on developments. "Faulkner is 9 years old, coming on 10. So this will be his first booming season. And over the weeks that have followed, lots of other males have joined in now." Kākāpō are 'lek' breeders. The males stay in one spot and attract the females to them through their boom and ching calls. They also prepare a pathway and shallow depressions for the ladies to admire, says Alison. "The boys have been doing lots of housework, which is always good to hear. So the male kākāpō have been tidying up their track and bowl systems." The earliest mating can happen around Christmas Day, but most of the action takes place a week or two after, over the New Year. Well known for The Kākāpō Files podcast released in 2019 during her time as Our Changing World host and producer, Alison's association with kākāpō goes back much further than that - to her days working in natural history filmmaking. It started in 1995, when she found herself filming kākāpō nests on Whenua Hou "That was a real high point for me in my life journey really, getting involved with kākāpō. But that point in time was a real low point for the kākāpō population." At that time there were just 51 known birds. 1995 was also the year that the Kākāpō Recovery Programme began in its current form. In the 10 years running up to 1995 there had only been three kākāpō chicks that survived to adulthood. So

the newly formed programme aimed to change those odds. In the late
80s and early 90s every known wild kākāpō was uplifted and transferred to predator free offshore islands to try halt their decline. Whenua Hou became the new 'kākāpō central', and the most important breeding site for this attempted comeback. Fast forward 30 years and today there are 237 kākāpō. It has been a huge conservation effort, with continuous tracking and monitoring of the birds, and it gets stepped up even further when a breeding season happens to include artificial insemination, egg incubation, supplementary feeding and chick hand-rearing. So a lot of work when breeding happens, but that's not every year, says Alison. "The one thing you need to know about kākāpō is you have to be very, very patient…. because they only breed every two to four years, and the last time they bred was four years ago". Their breeding is tied to the rimu tree fruiting, called a mast. These birds are tuned in to the rimu cycle, and after careful years of study, DOC's kākāpō recovery team is too. By counting the growing tips on the rimu branches a full year in advance, they can know if the parrots will breed. And, says Alison, the numbers stack up for this to be a bumper year "The previous biggest mast on record was 2019, when we did the first season of The Kākāpō Files. And the autumn count on Whenua Hou at that time was 47 percent. Well, this year the autumn count on Whenua Hou was 63 percent. So it's by far and away the biggest rimu fruiting season on record." However, no one is willing to count their chicks 'before they fledge'. "Unfortunately lots of things could happen," says Alison, "The rimu fruit might not ripen, it often doesn't. And in that case, chicks might starve." Disease is always a concern too. The 2019 breeding season saw an outbreak of a fungal infection called aspergillosis which killed both adults and chicks. Plus, there's the ongoing concern about the arrival of the highly pathogenic strain of bird flu that's been sweeping the globe. There is something new happening this year too, says Alison. Now, with the numbers up and the kākāpō spread across three breeding islands, DOC is keen to take a new 'lighter touch' approach on two of those
islands. "They're trying to do themselves out of a job really… In the last
30 years it's been important to increase numbers as quickly as possible,
but you can't keep up this intensity of effort for this many birds." Across
this season Alison will be collaborating with DOC's Kākāpō Recovery
Programme team members to get updates from the breeding islands -
when the birds mate, when eggs are laid, how many chicks hatch safely,

and whether they are healthy and growing - and she will be bringing them to RNZ audiences once again through the second season of The Kākāpō Files. She thinks this season, with its hands-off approach, will bring a 'very different vibe'. And with 84 adult female kākāpō that could breed, 2026 has the potential to be real turning point for this iconic manu. 17.fileDescription: This essay explores New Zealand's conservation efforts and the potential of genetic technology to restore extinct species. The author reflects on receiving a ceramic replica of a huia feather—a bird hunted to extinction over a century ago—as a symbol of what modernity has destroyed. The piece highlights successful conservation efforts, particularly the kākāpō bird, whose population has been increased from 50 to 155 individuals through dedicated conservation work and genome analysis. It discusses the South Island kōkako's potential extinction and the North Island kōkako's near-extinction. The essay presents palaeobiologist Jeffrey Yule's philosophical framework for ethical species cloning, which proposes that extinct species like the huia, thylacine, and passenger pigeon could be restored if specific criteria are met. Ultimately, the author suggests that genetic technology offers hope for repairing past environmental mistakes and restoring public faith in conservation efforts.

chunkHighlights.text: On this tender genetic thread hung the future of the entire species. For four decades, conservationists have focused on the fortunes of the remaining individuals, increasing the population to 155. Today, as deputy editor Rebekah White reveals in this issue, scientists have turned their attention back to that frail genetic thread, analysing it in cross-section to reveal the fabric of the kākāpō genome, and the specific genes of every kākāpō in the population, to breed the population back to health.

18.fileDescription: This comprehensive document provides an overview of New Zealand's threatened species and conservation efforts. It defines threatened species as native plants and animals with critically low populations facing extinction risk, with New Zealand having 2,788 threatened species (37% of birds, 34% of plants). Main causes of decline include habitat destruction, invasive predators like rats and possums, and over-harvesting. New Zealand uses an eight-tier classification system for conservation status based on threats, endemism, vulnerability, and cultural importance. Conservation strategies include island sanctuaries, pest control, captive breeding, and habitat restoration. Notable successes include the black robin recovery (7 to 250 individuals), takahē recovery program, and tuatara reintroduction programs. The document presents case studies of endangered species including the Mahoenui giant wētā, Peraxilla mistletoes, kiwi, and tuatara. About 30% of New Zealand is protected conservation land. Recent efforts have expanded beyond visible species to include freshwater fish and plants, with a shift toward restoring entire habitats. Key challenges include funding limitations, many species poorly understood (1,455 fungi species classified as 'data deficient'), an estimated 50,000 unidentified native species potentially at risk, and preventing 'zombie species' that survive only in cultivation.

chunkHighlights.text: Private funding

In 1990 the Department of Conservation and other groups set up the Threatened Species Trust Programme to attract commercial sponsorship. This has generated more funds for saving threatened species. For example, between 1990 and 2004 the aluminium smelting company Comalco donated $1.6 million towards saving the kākāpō. The Bank of New Zealand has been a multi-million-dollar sponsor of efforts to save the kiwi since 1991.

retrieved_chunks.text:
area. Island restoration Some islands are being restored to something
resembling their original ecology, with unwanted animals entirely eradicated. Larger browsing animals such as wild cattle and goats are the first to go, followed by smaller predators – cats and possums, stoats and weasels, and eventually rats. Existing patches of native vegetation are enlarged, often with the help of planting programmes. Some sparse populations have become abundant once again. Other species were reintroduced to their former homes, while some islands became sanctuaries for animals never previously found there. Kākāpō were once plentiful, but when only a few remained in Fiordland and on Stewart Island (Rakiura), they were moved to Whenua Hou/Codfish, Maud and Little Barrier islands, and in 2003 to Fiordland’s Chalky Island (Te Kākahu-o-Tamatea). Public sanctuaries Most conservation restrict access to prevent disturbance or the arrival of unwanted pests. But several are open to the public. Kāpiti Island near Wellington and Tiritiri Matangi near Auckland have similar histories. Once cleared for farming, they now have no animal pests, and native forest has been re-established – over 250,000 native trees were planted on Tiritiri Matangi. Both are refuges for saddlebacks, kōkako, stitchbirds, little spotted kiwi and takahē. Saving this species requires patience, sturdy boots and getting used to rivulets of water trickling down your neck. Fiordland is considered the prototype of community driven marine protection. Developed over 10 years, the Fiordland marine conservation strategy became enshrined in legislation in 2005. [sidebar 1] One of the principles developed by Fiordland was the ‘egg’ organisational model, in which local interests (tourism, fishing, conservation, runanga) form the central decision making yolk, while statutory agencies (councils, ministries, wider iwi, the Department of Conservation) occupy a supporting role as the surrounding white. This structure puts the stewardship responsibility squarely on the community. Another Fiordland principle bequeathed to Te Korowai was the idea of gifts and gains. Each interest group gives concessions in order to gain a desired outcome, expressed in Te Korowai’s vision of “a flourishing, rich and healthy environment where opportunities abound”—a.k.a. “more fish”. In Fiordland, commercial lobster fishers agreed to stop setting pots in the inner fjords and recreational fishers conceded lower bag limits. Perhaps the most important piece of advice Fiordland’s guardians gave the Kaikoura group was that to get buy in, you have to consult widely, listen carefully and not impose a time frame on the process. [Page 1] Backyard explorers By discoveryexpeditions.co.nz Within our New Zealand bubble are some of the most dramatic, breathtaking landscapes in the world. Fiordland and Rakiura/Stewart Island offer an insight into the world as it once was: raw, pristine, largely uninhabited. Recognised by UNESCO World Heritage status, Fiordland National Park is characterised by steep, jumbled topography, a rugged coastline, dense rainforest and a dynamic climate. Further south, most of Rakiura/Stewart Island is part of Rakiura National Park, with settlement confined mainly to Oban, the only township. The island’s densely forested hills, tiny population and untouched coastline of rocky outcrops and golden sand beaches make it a natural refuge for marine and bird life. Few people venture to these isolated parts of the deep south, but leading tourism operator Real Journeys explores Fiordland and Rakiura/Stewart Island on Discovery Expeditions, sea voyages ranging from four to seven days. Some expeditions retrace Captain James Cook’s 1773 voyage around the Fiordland coastline and visit Māori and European historical sites that have played a part in New Zealand’s history. On Fiordland voyages, passengers have the opportunity to catch glimpses of the region’s abundant wildlife: bottlenose dolphins, Fiordland crested penguins and the occasional whale. Each voyage offers plenty of opportunities to disembark the vessel with daily nature hikes, kayaking, or tender craft activities. Throughout the trip, on board nature guides, who are experts on southern New Zealand, share knowledge of the flora, fauna and history of these regions. Travel in these parts is never predictable: the elements shape each trip, but being flexible yields rewards. Days are spent in isolated wilderness, taking in the sights and wildlife along the way.

response.response_text:
## Two of a Kind — But Different Roads to Recovery

Both the kākāpō and takahē are flightless New Zealand birds that were once on the very edge of extinction, and both have been the subject of intensive, decades-long recovery efforts. Yet the two programmes have taken notably different approaches to bringing these taonga (treasured) species back from the brink.

![embed-1](embed://1)

## The Kākāpō Programme: Islands, Intensity, and a Lighter Touch

The kākāpō recovery story is fundamentally one of relocation and radical intervention. When predators — cats, rats, stoats, and ferrets — decimated mainland populations, all 61 surviving Stewart Island/Rakiura birds were caught between 1982 and 1992 and transferred to predator-free offshore sanctuaries including Whenua Hou/Codfish Island, Te Hoiere/Maud Island, and Hauturu/Little Barrier Island. [[1]](cite://1/1) A massive aerial poison drop over Whenua Hou in 1999 eradicated rats and helped create what was described as a 'kākāpōrium' — the safest possible haven for the birds. [[2]](cite://2/1)

From that point, management became extraordinarily hands-on. The Kākāpō Recovery Programme, established in its current form in 1995 when just 51 birds remained, introduced continuous monitoring, supplementary feeding tied to rimu mast cycles, egg incubation, chick hand-rearing, artificial insemination, inter-island transfers, and strict quarantine and hygiene procedures at all breeding sites. [[3]](cite://3/1)[[4]](cite://4/1) Every single bird carries a transmitter and has a name. [[5]](cite://5/1)

Today, with the population at around 235–237 birds spread across three breeding islands, the programme is deliberately evolving. [[5]](cite://5/2)[[3]](cite://3/2) The 2026 breeding season — the biggest on record — has been used to trial a 'lighter touch' approach: leaving more eggs to hatch in nests rather than incubators, reducing nest interference, cutting back supplementary feeding, and establishing more hands-off breeding sites. [[6]](cite://6/1)[[7]](cite://7/1) The ultimate vision is to restore kākāpō as nameless, wild birds booming through New Zealand forests, with Predator Free Rakiura identified as a key future goal. [[5]](cite://5/3)[[8]](cite://8/1)

## The Takahē Programme: Captive Breeding, Wild Populations, and Landscape-Scale Pest Control

The takahē programme shares common ground with kākāpō — island sanctuaries, intensive management, and translocation — but its architecture is quite different. After takahē were rediscovered in the Murchison Mountains, Fiordland, in 1948, the focus in the early 1980s shifted to understanding breeding requirements and reducing chick mortality, including egg incubation and raising chicks in enclosures near Te Anau. [[9]](cite://9/1)

Central to the takahē effort has been the Burwood Takahē Centre near Te Anau, a dedicated semi-captive breeding facility where birds are raised in predator-proof pens — typically two adults and two chicks per pen. [[10]](cite://10/1) Burwood now produces around 25 chicks a year, with a similar number produced at some 20 other sanctuary sites around the country. [[11]](cite://11/1)

![embed-2](embed://2)

Crucially, the takahē programme has maintained a wild mainland population — something kākāpō management moved away from entirely. The Murchison Mountains remain a core site, and in recent years the programme has worked to establish additional wild populations: in Kahurangi National Park from 2018, and in the Upper Whakatipu (Greenstone Station and Rees Valley) from 2023. [[12]](cite://12/1) The Murchison Mountains population reached capacity in 2025, with an estimated 220–260 birds, allowing DOC to step back and redirect resources to new sites. [[13]](cite://13/1)

## Where the Approaches Diverge

The sharpest difference between the two programmes lies in their relationship with the mainland and predator control. The takahē programme has always grappled with the challenge of protecting birds in large, open landscapes — the Murchisons, the Gouland Downs in Kahurangi, and now the Whakatipu valleys — where stoats, cats, and ferrets remain a persistent threat. The response has been extensive trap lines, aerial 1080 operations, and careful site selection. [[11]](cite://11/2)[[12]](cite://12/2) Stoats remain the takahē's greatest foe, and in beech mast years can kill up to 40 percent of adults in the Murchison Mountains alone. [[11]](cite://11/3)

The kākāpō programme, by contrast, essentially gave up on the mainland decades ago, concentrating all birds on a small number of fully predator-free islands. [[1]](cite://1/2)[[14]](cite://14/1) The current challenge is that the programme is running out of high-quality predator-free island sites as the population grows, pushing interest toward fenced mainland ecosanctuaries and large-scale predator eradication projects. [[5]](cite://5/4)[[15]](cite://15/1)

Both programmes also differ in scale of public engagement: takahē have been placed in urban sanctuaries like Zealandia in Wellington, Willowbank, and Orokonui — making them accessible to city visitors — while kākāpō remain largely confined to remote, restricted offshore islands. [[16]](cite://16/1)[[17]](cite://17/1)

## Shared DNA

For all their differences, both programmes reflect the same hard-won understanding: without sustained intervention against introduced predators, neither species would have survived. Both have used island refuges as stepping stones, both have employed captive breeding as insurance, and both are now — from positions of cautious optimism — beginning to ease their grip, trusting the birds to take more of their own future into their own wings.

Would you like to dig deeper into the future habitat challenges facing the kākāpō programme — particularly the Predator Free Rakiura ambitions?

1.document_title: New Zealand's Threatened Species: Conservation Status, Strategies, and Recovery Efforts
1.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an overview of New Zealand's threatened species and conservation efforts. It defines threatened species as native plants and animals with critically low populations facing extinction risk, with New Zealand having 2,788 threatened species (37% of birds, 34% of plants). Main causes of decline include habitat destruction, invasive predators like rats and possums, and over-harvesting. New Zealand uses an eight-tier classification system for conservation status based on threats, endemism, vulnerability, and cultural importance. Conservation strategies include island sanctuaries, pest control, captive breeding, and habitat restoration. Notable successes include the black robin recovery (7 to 250 individuals), takahē recovery program, and tuatara reintroduction programs. The document presents case studies of endangered species including the Mahoenui giant wētā, Peraxilla mistletoes, kiwi, and tuatara. About 30% of New Zealand is protected conservation land. Recent efforts have expanded beyond visible species to include freshwater fish and plants, with a shift toward restoring entire habitats. Key challenges include funding limitations, many species poorly understood (1,455 fungi species classified as 'data deficient'), an estimated 50,000 unidentified native species potentially at risk, and preventing 'zombie species' that survive only in cultivation.

2.text:
[Page 9] Conservation programme The Department of Conservation raises chicks in captivity in three aviaries, and releases them into the wild. Predators are trapped, to safeguard birds in the wild. Project River Recovery was launched in 1991 in partnership with Meridian Energy, restoring some of the Mackenzie Basin habitat by controlling weeds and predators, and digging ponds. This has also benefited other native plants and animals.

2.document_title: New Zealand Wading Birds: A Comprehensive Guide to Species, Conservation, and Migration
2.document_summary: This comprehensive guide explores New Zealand's diverse wading bird species, including oystercatchers, stilts, dotterels, plovers, wrybills, snipes, and bar-tailed godwits. It details their physical adaptations—such as varying leg and beak lengths suited to different feeding zones—and feeding behaviors in coastal and inland habitats. The guide covers three oystercatcher species and two stilt species, including the critically endangered black stilt (kakī). Notable migration patterns are highlighted, particularly the bar-tailed godwit's remarkable 11,000-kilometre non-stop journey from Alaska to New Zealand in 8-9 days, with 80,000-100,000 godwits arriving annually. The document addresses conservation concerns for endangered species like the Chatham Island oystercatcher and New Zealand dotterel, discussing threats from predators, human activity, and habitat loss. Conservation programs, habitat restoration, predator management, and captive breeding initiatives are emphasized as crucial for species survival. The guide also includes Māori cultural perspectives on wading birds and their significance in traditional beliefs and poetry.

3.text:
[Page 8] Private funding In 1990 the Department of Conservation and other groups set up the Threatened Species Trust Programme to attract commercial sponsorship. This has generated more funds for saving threatened species. For example, between 1990 and 2004 the aluminium smelting company Comalco donated $1.6 million towards saving the kākāpō. The Bank of New Zealand has been a multi million dollar sponsor of efforts to save the kiwi since 1991.

4.document_summary: Stewart Island/Rakiura is New Zealand's third largest island located south of the South Island. The Māori name "Rakiura" means "glowing skies," referencing the aurora australis, while the English name honors William Stewart, first mate of the sealer Pegasus. Covering 1,680 square kilometers with approximately 85% protected as Rakiura National Park (established 2002), the island features diverse vegetation zones from coastal shrublands to alpine tussock lands, with over half covered by podocarp and hardwood forests. The island supports exceptional biodiversity including 15,000 southern tokoeka (Stewart Island kiwi), kākāpō, three penguin species, fur seals, and sea lions, with 21 endemic alpine plant species. Historically, Polynesians reached the island by the late 1200s, with permanent Māori settlement following primarily around coastal areas for fishing and harvesting tītī (muttonbirds). European contact began with James Cook in 1770, followed by sealers, whalers, and missionaries. Since the 1850s, the island's economy has centered on sheep farming, timber milling, and fishing, with fishing becoming dominant by 2013. Tourism evolved from the 1890s to a major industry attracting 30,000 annual visitors. Key geographic features include Paterson Inlet (8,900 hectares), Mason Bay with 200-metre dunes, Ulva Island (predator-free scenic reserve), Port Pegasus with granite domes, and the Southern Circuit tramping track (71.5 km). Oban (Halfmoon Bay) serves as the main township with 378 residents in 2013.

5.text:
[Page 13] area. Island restoration Some islands are being restored to something resembling their original ecology, with unwanted animals entirely eradicated. Larger browsing animals such as wild cattle and goats are the first to go, followed by smaller predators cats and possums, stoats and weasels, and eventually rats. Existing patches of native vegetation are enlarged, often with the help of planting programmes. Some sparse populations have become abundant once again. Other species were reintroduced to their former homes, while some islands became sanctuaries for animals never previously found there. Kākāpō were once plentiful, but when only a few remained in Fiordland and on Stewart Island (Rakiura), they were moved to Whenua Hou/Codfish, Maud and Little Barrier islands, and in 2003 to Fiordland’s Chalky Island (Te Kākahu o Tamatea). Public sanctuaries Most conservation restrict access to prevent disturbance or the arrival of unwanted pests. But several are open to the public. Kāpiti Island near Wellington and Tiritiri Matangi near Auckland have similar histories. Once cleared for farming, they now have no animal pests, and native forest has been re established over 250,000 native trees were planted on Tiritiri Matangi. Both are refuges for saddlebacks, kōkako, stitchbirds, little spotted kiwi and takahē. Not far from Kāpiti is Mana Island, also a bird sanctuary, and noted for its ‘colony’ of concrete gannets, built to tempt real gannets to breed there. Betty gets her goats In the 1970s the government decided to kill wild goats and sheep on Arapawa Island, in the Marlborough Sounds. Protesters claimed the animals were descendants of those left by James Cook. DNA tests showed some were genetically unique. Many were culled, but others were sent to farms and wildlife parks. Betty Rowe led the rescue campaign and established a sanctuary on Arapawa Island. Marine reserves To create areas where people could not disturb the ocean, seabed and seashore, the Marine Reserves Act was passed in 1971. The first reserve was at Goat Island, north of Auckland (now Cape Rodney Ōkakari Point Marine Reserve). The second was the ocean around the Poor Knights Islands, noted for islands subtropical fish. Others include islands off the Coromandel Peninsula, Tūhua (Mayor Island) in Bay of Plenty, Kāpiti Island, Long Island in the Marlborough Sounds, Tonga Island in Abel Tasman National Park, Elizabeth Island in Fiordland and Ulva Island near Stewart Island.

5.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's over 600 nearshore islands within 50 kilometres of the main islands, covering their geological formation, historical significance, and contemporary conservation status. The islands are distributed around the North Island (Great Barrier, Rangitoto, Bay of Islands) and southern regions (Marlborough Sounds, Fiordland). Historically, Māori utilized these islands for harvesting seafood, birds, and resources like argillite rock, obsidian, and adzite, including tītī (muttonbirds). European contact began in the late 1700s-1800s with sealers, whalers, and explorers like James Cook. Island industries included 19th-century mining, farming, and the world's first regular pigeon airmail service on Great Barrier Island (1897-1908). The document details quarantine facilities on Quarantine Island (Dunedin), Ōtamahua (Christchurch), and Matiu (Wellington), which housed disease victims, leprosy patients, and wartime internees. Today, islands serve as nature reserves hosting endangered species including tuatara, kākāpō, kiwi, and rare plants like Pennantia baylisiana. Conservation efforts began with Resolution Island in 1891 and include successful eradication programs and species reintroduction initiatives.

6.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores native plants in New Zealand across historical, horticultural, and commercial contexts. It traces native plant use from Māori cultivation of rengarenga lilies and karaka trees through European settlement, highlighting early advocates like Leonard Cockayne and J.G. McKenzie. A pivotal shift occurred in the 1970s-1980s when gardeners like Muriel Fisher and Lawrie Metcalf transformed public perception, demonstrating native plants were attractive and easy to cultivate. The document covers diverse native plant categories including ornamental grasses, tree ferns, alpine species, and specialist plants, with over 800 cultivars of hebes, flax, and mānuka produced through breeding. It emphasizes native garden design principles focusing on form, texture, and foliage. Modern revegetation practices use locally sourced native plants for ecological restoration, with approximately 300 commercial native plant nurseries operating by the late 1990s. Key initiatives include subalpine shrubland, forest revegetation, swamp restoration, and sand dune projects. Commercial applications include historical fiber cultivation of New Zealand flax, pharmaceutical extraction attempts, native food crops like kōkihi, and growing export markets for native foliage plants, particularly Pittosporum, with 1.4 million stems exported in 2003-4.

7.document_title: Seaweed: Ecology, Traditional Uses, and Modern Applications in New Zealand
7.document_summary: This comprehensive guide explores seaweed species found in New Zealand, their ecological importance, and diverse applications spanning traditional and modern uses. The document covers three main groups of seaweed classified by color: green, brown, and red seaweeds, with detailed information on their distribution, structure, and life cycles. Green seaweeds thrive in shallow, sunlit waters; brown seaweeds include kelps that form underwater forests over 20 metres tall; red seaweeds grow at greater depths and comprise 550 species in New Zealand. Kelp forests, particularly bladder kelp and common kelp, are vital marine ecosystems supporting numerous species and serving as fundamental food sources and habitats for marine creatures. The document details traditional Māori uses of seaweeds, including karengo as a nutritious food source and bull kelp (rimurapa) for storage in pōhā bags. Modern applications include agar extraction for bacterial cultivation and food preservation, cosmetic thickeners, food seasoning production, shellfish farming support, and potential uses in reducing livestock methane emissions. The document also addresses invasive species like Asian kelp, which threaten native marine habitats, while highlighting New Zealand's abundant seaweed resources and potential for developing a thriving seaweed industry despite current challenges in competing with Asian producers due to labour-intensive harvesting methods.

9.document_title: Canterbury Region: Comprehensive Geography, History, Culture, and Development
9.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an extensive overview of Canterbury, New Zealand's South Island region, covering geography, history, culture, economy, and governance. Geographically, Canterbury features vast plains, the Southern Alps, braided rivers, and Christchurch, the "garden city." The region's geology was shaped by volcanic activity (Banks Peninsula 15-12 million years ago) and glaciation, with significant seismic activity including devastating earthquakes in 2010-2011 (6.3 magnitude, 185 deaths) and 2016 (7.8 magnitude Kaikōura). Historically, Ngāi Tahu Māori settled the region 600-700 years ago, establishing centers like Kaiapoi. European settlement began with Captain Cook (1770) and intensified after the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), with the Canterbury Association organizing settlement from 1850. The region developed strong agricultural heritage, transitioning from large estates to family farms, with sheep farming dominant (3.15 million head by 1885, 11% of national flock in 2012), supplemented by wheat production (62.5% of national) and expanding dairy operations (115% increase 2002-2012). Major irrigation schemes, including the Rangitātā diversion race (1945) and Central Plains Water scheme (2015), enabled intensive farming. Industrial development centered on farm-related processing and manufacturing, maintaining 11% of national manufacturing employment by 2013. Tourism accounted for 8.4% of jobs in 2010 but was severely impacted by the 2011 earthquake, with recovery underway by 2014. Transport infrastructure evolved significantly with the Lyttelton rail tunnel (1867), road tunnel (1964), Ōtira tunnel (1923), and Christchurch airport (opened 1940, first international airport 1950). Culturally, Canterbury developed a rich artistic heritage with notable figures including Samuel Butler, Denis Glover, Allen Curnow, and Rita Angus. The region has a strong sporting tradition, including rugby (Crusaders), tennis (Anthony Wilding), and hosted the 1974 Commonwealth Games. Governance evolved from provincial abolition (1876) through the Canterbury Regional Council (1989) to the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority (CERA) post-2011. In 2013, Canterbury had 478,623 residents (11.3% of New Zealand's population), predominantly European (86.2%), with recovery efforts including the Christchurch Central Recovery Plan (July 2012) and ongoing reconstruction.

10.document_title: Kaitiakitanga: Māori Guardianship, Environmental Stewardship, and Traditional Conservation Practices
10.document_summary: Kaitiakitanga is a foundational Māori concept of guardianship and environmental stewardship rooted in the worldview that humans are part of nature. A kaitiaki is a guardian recognized by tangata whenua to care for natural areas such as lakes, forests, and waterways. Traditional conservation practices include temporary rāhui (resource restrictions), use of the lunar calendar (maramataka) for planting and harvesting, sustainable hunting and fishing, and blessing of mauri stones by tohunga (priests). Key spiritual concepts include mana (spiritual power), tapu (spiritual restriction), and mauri (life force). Today, kaitiakitanga is experiencing renewal as iwi (tribes) restore ecosystems and apply traditional knowledge in modern contexts. Practical examples include Ngāi Tahu's guardianship of pounamu resources, Ngāti Toa's fishery restoration at Pukerua Bay, and multi-tribal efforts to stop river pollution and protect endangered species. The document outlines challenges in collaborating with non-Māori stakeholders and details legislative frameworks such as the Resource Management Act 1991 and Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 that incorporate kaitiakitanga principles. Kaitiakitanga offers perspectives on environmental stewardship and kinship with nature, enabling Māori to fulfill ancestral responsibilities while contributing to broader environmental sustainability.

11.document_title: New Zealand's Threatened Species: Conservation Status, Strategies, and Recovery Efforts
11.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an overview of New Zealand's threatened species and conservation efforts. It defines threatened species as native plants and animals with critically low populations facing extinction risk, with New Zealand having 2,788 threatened species (37% of birds, 34% of plants). Main causes of decline include habitat destruction, invasive predators like rats and possums, and over-harvesting. New Zealand uses an eight-tier classification system for conservation status based on threats, endemism, vulnerability, and cultural importance. Conservation strategies include island sanctuaries, pest control, captive breeding, and habitat restoration. Notable successes include the black robin recovery (7 to 250 individuals), takahē recovery program, and tuatara reintroduction programs. The document presents case studies of endangered species including the Mahoenui giant wētā, Peraxilla mistletoes, kiwi, and tuatara. About 30% of New Zealand is protected conservation land. Recent efforts have expanded beyond visible species to include freshwater fish and plants, with a shift toward restoring entire habitats. Key challenges include funding limitations, many species poorly understood (1,455 fungi species classified as 'data deficient'), an estimated 50,000 unidentified native species potentially at risk, and preventing 'zombie species' that survive only in cultivation.

14.document_title: Māori and Museums: Evolution of Cultural Engagement, Governance, and Repatriation in New Zealand (1769-2008)
14.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the complex relationship between Māori and museums in New Zealand from 1769 to 2008. It examines how taonga (treasures) were initially collected as exotic curiosities by European collectors, then reframed through colonial lenses as cultural artifacts and ethnographic specimens. The document details Māori engagement across multiple periods: early collaboration from the 1870s-1970s to preserve heritage, pioneering efforts by Apirana Ngata on the Dominion Museum board in the 1930s, and the transformative Te Māori exhibition (1984-87) that revolutionized museum practice by interpreting taonga as ancestors. This pivotal exhibition, co-curated by Hirini Mead and toured internationally with Māori elders conducting ceremonial openings, catalyzed national awareness of biculturalism and Treaty of Waitangi obligations, directly influencing the creation of Te Papa Tongarewa (1998). Post-Te Māori developments include kaumātua advisory committees, Māori management positions at major institutions, bicultural frameworks, and professional organizations like Kaitiaki Māori establishing ethical codes for taonga interpretation. Key institutional developments include Te Papa's operational marae, Karanga Aotearoa Repatriation Programme, the 1996 Auckland Museum Amendment Act, and the emergence of Māori-led institutions. Contemporary solutions include bicultural institutions, shared governance models, iwi-led museums, and tertiary-qualified Māori advancing through new museum studies programs.

17.document_title: Step away from the kākāpō
17.document_summary: The 2019 kākāpō breeding season achieved record success but was marred by an aspergillosis fungal disease outbreak on Codfish Island/Whenua Hou, infecting 21 birds and killing nine. Genetic analysis revealed all birds contracted the same fungal strain, likely introduced by humans through supplementary food. The same strain appeared on Anchor Island but caused no illness there. Researchers attribute the outbreak partly to hot, dry summer conditions that coincided with vulnerable chick stages. In response, DOC's recovery programme implemented enhanced biosecurity measures including food freezing, nest ventilation, and reduced direct chick handling. The team is transitioning toward less intensive management with remote monitoring and hands-off breeding sites, recognizing that while intensive management has prevented kākāpō extinction, stepping back represents the future direction for the species' recovery.

The core of the Waikaremoana kiwi project is the control of predators, primarily stoats, by trapping. The Lake Waikaremoana Hapu Restoration Trust (LWHRT) has a four person team for undertaking predator management, as well as tasks such as the construction of an anti dispersal fence (see below) and kiwi enclosure, maintenance of a worm farm and assisting with kiwi monitoring. Predator control for the most part entails trapping stoats in covered Fenn traps baited with white hens’ eggs. The lures need to be changed regularly, particularly in summer, and the traps set and maintained. Some 1400 traps have been laid along 67 km of trap lines throughout the 1500 ha Puketukutuku Peninsula and the neighbouring Pukehou area. Weasels and a large number of rats are caught in the traps, and the team also undertakes cage trapping of larger predators, including ferrets and feral cats. Pigs have to be controlled to prevent them from stealing the hens’ eggs and turning over the trap covers in the process, thereby exposing the traps—a danger to kiwi and other bird life. The Waikaremoana Pig Hunting Club and a professional hunter contracted to DOC both remove pigs from Puketukutuku Peninsula, and the trust team has recently replaced the open bottomed trap covers originally used with a fully en closed design. 19.document_title: Iwi Kiwi: Waikaremoana Hapū's Kiwi Recovery Programme
19.document_summary: This article describes the kiwi recovery project at Lake Waikaremoana, initiated in 1992 by Dr. John McLennan to study predation as the primary cause of kiwi decline. The Waikaremoana hapū have been instrumental in the project, managing predator control through trapping stoats, weasels, rats, and cats across 1,500 hectares. Key achievements include increasing the kiwi population from 24 birds in 1993 to 76 by 2005 through intensive predator management and captive breeding programs. The Lake Waikaremoana Hapū Restoration Trust operates a four-person team conducting trapping, monitoring, and conservation work. An anti-dispersal fence prevents juvenile kiwi from dispersing into predator-dense areas. The hapū seek full management responsibility for the program to ensure long-term sustainability and protect it from funding cuts. This collaborative effort between iwi, DOC, and conservation organizations demonstrates successful inter-generational environmental restoration benefiting all New Zealanders.

20.text:
[Page 9] Feral cats had developed a taste for kākāpō, and within five years these bushwise and feisty predators halved the remaining kākāpō population. Just as in Fiordland, searchers realised they were riding a bow wave of extinction. This time, however, they would take more radical measures. Between 1982 and 1992, all 61 surviving Stewart Island kākāpō were caught and transferred to safe island sanctuaries: Whenua Hou, Te Hoiere/Maud Island and Hauturu/Little Barrier Island, in the Hauraki Gulf . The kākāpō’s wild days were over. From now on, constant inter island transfers and airlifts out of trouble would become the norm in kākāpō life. While a long term solution to their predicament was being sought, the birds would remain refugees in their own homeland. One evening in early April 1999, as the seasons were turning and winter storms were edging in from the Southern Ocean, I walked with photographer Rod Morris through wet rimu forest down from the summit of Whenua Hou. We each carried a plastic cat box housing a kākāpō. The boxes were heavy, and every few hundred metres we stopped to swap hands and to catch a glimpse of the birds: a youngster named Sirocco in Morris’s cage, a female called Hoki in mine. The birds had just been ferried in from Pearl Island—at the entrance of Port Pegasus, on the eastern side of Stewart Island—their temporary home while 1396 hectare Whenua Hou Nature Reserve was being purged of any remaining vermin. Back in the mid 1980s, possums had been eradicated from Whenua Hou, and even egg stealing weka removed, and now, having been blitzed with 22 air dropped tonnes of poison pellets, the island had been declared a predator free “kākāpōrium”—the safest haven the birds would ever know. At the release site I opened the grille door of my cage and Hoki stomped out angrily, dragging her brown tail like a hand baggage trolley, and vanished in the undergrowth. Hoki was the star of several media appearances in the early 1990s when, rescued as a starving chick from Whenua Hou, she became the first ever kākāpō to be successfully hand reared. (She also featured on the cover of Issue 15 of New Zealand Geographic.) She is a free agent now, and tends to shun human company.

20.document_title: Kākāpō: Bird on the Brink - Conservation Efforts and Recovery Success
20.document_summary: This comprehensive document chronicles the remarkable conservation journey of the kākāpō, New Zealand's critically endangered flightless nocturnal parrot. Once abundant throughout New Zealand's islands, the species declined dramatically to just 18 males in Fiordland by the 1980s, with only 62 birds remaining by the early 2000s due to introduced predators and historical human hunting. The breakthrough came with the discovery of a 200-strong population on Stewart Island in 1977, including the first identified female since the early 1900s. The recovery program involved relocating all surviving kākāpō to predator-free island sanctuaries including Whenua Hou, Maud Island, and Little Barrier Island between 1982-1992. Key conservation innovations include helicopter access to remote populations, hand-rearing of chicks, inter-island transfers, electronic surveillance systems, and supplementary feeding programs. The species' unique lekking courtship behavior, where males inflate and boom low-frequency calls from elaborately maintained bowl-shaped arenas, was crucial to understanding their breeding patterns. Despite their appearance as ecological relics, kākāpō demonstrate adaptability and have become marathon survivors with lifespans potentially exceeding 60 years. The dedicated recovery team has achieved significant breeding successes, transforming wild kākāpō into managed refugees in their own homeland. The long-term vision includes establishing free-living, self-sustaining populations on subantarctic islands like Campbell Island, representing an unprecedented turning point in the species' survival.

21.text:
[Page 3] So far, the fates of 93 nests have been documented. Nesting success at sites with predator control has been 80 per cent or higher, compared to 38 per cent at three sites without predator control. Predation on nesting females has been 5 per cent at sites with predator control compared to 65 per cent at unprotected sites. There seems to be little doubt that pest control makes a difference. However, for mainland island style pest control to be useful in conserving kaka we need to know if improvements in nesting success and female survival are large enough to actually reverse the decline of kaka populations. Female survival is the key to the health of kaka populations. Because female kaka spend long periods inside the nest chamber they are much more vulnerable to predators, such as stoats, than males are. Consequently, females are often in short supply, and it is this shortage that is driving populations to extinction. For a kaka population to increase, the numbers of young females surviving to adulthood must exceed the number of adult females lost to predation or other causes. This has been the case at all sites with predator control, but not at a single site without it. In other words, mainland island style pest control does appear capable of actually reversing the decline of kaka populations. Numbers aside, perhaps the most tangible evidence of the difference predator control can make for a kaka population was the sighting of a group of young kaka in the village of St Arnaud, adjacent to Nelson Lakes National Park, in the autumn of 1998. These birds had fledged within the neighbouring Rotoiti Nature Recovery Project area, a mainland island and a kaka study area. It was the first time in many years that locals had seen a group of young kaka in the village. Since then, young kaka have become regular visitors to St Arnaud. Now that there is hard evidence that predator control can reverse the decline of kaka, perhaps flocks of the boisterous birds will start to be

21.document_title: Counting Kaka: Evaluating Predator Control for Native Parrot Conservation in New Zealand
21.document_summary: This article examines a nationwide study tracking approximately 150 kaka (native New Zealand parrots) to determine if large-scale pest control can reverse their population decline. Over five years, researchers used radio transmitters and video surveillance to monitor 93 nests across mainland islands. Results show nesting success at predator-controlled sites reached 80% or higher, compared to 38% at uncontrolled sites. Predation on nesting females was 5% with control versus 65% without. The study demonstrates that mainland island-style pest management significantly improves female survival—the key factor for population recovery. Evidence of success includes young kaka reappearing in St Arnaud village near Nelson Lakes National Park, indicating that predator control can effectively reverse kaka population decline on mainland New Zealand.

22.text:
[Page 13] Creating a stoat proof enclave for kiwi was a priority for McLennan, and he chose Puketukutuku because, like a fortress, it could be easily defended. Across the narrow neck of the peninsula he ran a double trapline, and then, with the help of a professional hunter, eradicated all the stoats inside the enclosure. He thus effectively turned the peninsula into a predator free island, a kiwi haven. In 1998, all of his chicks survived. [chapter break] The concept of island sanctuaries is not new. In 1894, Richard Henry masterminded the transfer of some 750 kiwi and kakapo to Resolution Island, in Fiordland. But he underestimated the enemy. Stoats swam across from the mainland, and 14 years of work was undone. Despite that setback, many of our offshore islands have now been turned into refuges for species that elsewhere are either extinct or extremely rare. Some of them were natural sanctuaries on account of their distance from the mainland or their inaccessibility, and only needed to have landings strictly controlled. Others, in the fashion of McLennan’s peninsula, have had to be restored through painstaking trapping of noxious animals and subsequent vigilance against reinvasion. Whatever their past, these islands now serve as insular aviaries, genetic safe houses which offer endangered species an evolutionary second chance, the opportunity of an assisted comeback. For kiwi, there is no more telling example than Kapiti, a sliver of mountainous, rain soused land lying off the west coast north of Wellington. Former home of Te Rauparaha, then the site of a whaling station, then a ne’er do well sheep farm, in 1897 the island was turned into a wildlife sanctuary. The cleared forest slowly grew back, and the resident caretakers methodically eradicated the vermin. Between 1980 and 1986, 22,500 possums were removed from this 2000 ha island, and a week before my visit the reserve was officially declared rat free.

22.document_title: Kiwi Conservation in New Zealand: Endangered Species, Predators, and Recovery Initiatives
22.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines the critical conservation challenges facing New Zealand's iconic kiwi bird and efforts to ensure its survival. The kiwi, once abundant with an estimated 12 million birds 1200 years ago, has declined to approximately 70,000 by 1995-96, declining at six percent annually. Key threats include introduced predators, particularly stoats (introduced in the 1880s), which are highly efficient hunters. Young kiwi face extreme vulnerability, with only 5% of chicks surviving their first few months until reaching 1200g at approximately 40 weeks. Conservation strategies encompass predator-free island sanctuaries (exemplified by Kapiti Island hosting over 1000 little spotted kiwi), mainland predator control grids targeting rats, mustelids, and feral cats, Operation Nest Egg captive breeding programs, and community-driven initiatives. Successful examples include Trounson Forest (over 200 kiwi since 1996) and Project Kiwi on the Coromandel Peninsula (improving chick survival from 5% to 87%). The document emphasizes ecosystem restoration over single-species protection, highlighting the resilience of North Island brown kiwi and the potential for coexistence between kiwi and human populations through targeted conservation strategies and public awareness campaigns.

23.text:
[Page 1] It is four in the morning, and I am sitting alone on the rain soaked soil of an island at the edge of Foveaux Strait, hunched against the pre dawn cold and endless southwesterlies. I have been in the thick blackness of this southern night for six hours already, waiting for the approaching dawn to silhouette the forest canopy with patches of grey. My only company lies a couple of metres away, in a tangle of rotting rata stumps and roots: a tiny grey chick which looks as cold and disconsolate as I feel. It is H2, a seven day old kakapo and one of the very latest additions to the embattled parrot’s population. While I shiver in layers of expensive polypropylene and synthetic fabrics, H2 has only the finest coating of grey down for warmth and resembles nothing more than a patch of mould on the forest floor. As a volunteer nest minder, I am spending two weeks looking after this fragile addition to the kakapo world while its mother, Heather, forages in the surrounding rimu forest of Codfish Island/Whenua Hou. Fatigued by 10 days of scant and intermittent sleep and up to four hours’ walking on waterlogged tracks each day, I find my biggest challenge is simply to stay awake. It’s rough and it’s raw, but what I’m doing is the reality of conservation in this country. Forget photo opportunities and cuddling one of the world’s rarest birds. Saving this species requires patience, sturdy boots and getting used to rivulets of water trickling down your neck. Nest minders, including the author (viewing a video monitor connected to an infrared camera at the nest). The cables, batteries and electronic gadgetry involved in the project had to be kept operational in the demanding outdoor conditions by Kakapo Recovery Programme scientist Graeme Elliott.

23.document_title: Minders: The Kakapo Caregivers of Codfish Island - Conservation and Intensive Management
23.document_summary: This comprehensive document chronicles the extraordinary kakapo conservation efforts on Codfish Island/Whenua Hou, focusing on the landmark 2002 breeding season. Over 100 volunteer nest minders from around the world participated in intensive 24-hour surveillance of 24 nests, resulting in 26 chicks hatching with 24 surviving—a 39% increase in the world kakapo population from 62 to 86 birds. The nest minders maintained constant vigilance, acted as surrogate parents during female foraging periods, and used innovative equipment like heat pads and infrared monitoring systems. The Department of Conservation-led intervention programme involved detailed monitoring, video surveillance, nightly chick weighing, and hand-rearing of struggling chicks. Despite harsh conditions—steep boggy tracks, cold nights, and minimal sleep—volunteers found the opportunity invaluable. The document profiles individual kakapo mothers (Heather, Ruth, Nora, Flossie) and their distinct parenting behaviors. A 1999 aerial poison drop eradicated rats, dramatically improving nesting success. With a chick mortality rate of just 8%, the 2002 season represented the most significant breakthrough for kakapo recovery since their rediscovery in 1977, demonstrating that intensive human intervention can successfully secure this endangered species' survival.

24.text: Female kākāpō are devoted mothers, but since they are all solo parents they must leave their eggs and chicks unguarded for long periods each night while they forage. Before the advent of mammalian predators, their absences were of little consequence, but ground-level nests of eggs or chicks are like fast-food outlets to rats and their ilk, and now the only safe place for kākāpō to breed is on predator-free islands. Even in these havens, kākāpō workers take no chances, installing infrared movement sensors and surveillance cameras at all nests. The image shows an infrared movement sensor and surveillance setup in a forest clearing, with a kākāpō egg visible on the ground.
