15.document_title: European Discovery of New Zealand
15.document_summary: This document traces the European discovery and exploration of New Zealand from the 13th century through the mid-19th century. Polynesian navigators reached the islands in the 13th century, but Abel Tasman was the first confirmed European visitor in 1642. After a violent encounter with Māori in Golden Bay, Tasman departed without further exploration. James Cook's three Pacific voyages (1768-79) definitively mapped New Zealand's coastline with assistance from naturalist Joseph Banks. Cook's first voyage aboard the Endeavour (1768-71) combined scientific observation with British imperial expansion. Subsequent explorers including French navigators, George Vancouver, and Alessandro Malaspina used New Zealand as a base for further exploration. Notable French explorers included Jean François de Surville and Marc Joseph Marion du Fresne, whose expedition ended tragically when he and 24 crew were killed by Māori. Later French explorers like d'Entrecasteaux (1793), Duperrey (1822-1825), and Dumont d'Urville (1826-1827) continued mapping efforts. The definitive charting of New Zealand's coasts occurred between 1848-1855 by British ships Acheron and Pandora, resulting in the first New Zealand Pilot (1856). Major peaks were named after explorers, with Mt Cook (Aoraki) now bearing dual names honoring both European discovery and Māori heritage.

19.document_title: A Gulf in my Thinking

He observes a growing movement of individuals taking environmental responsibility into their own hands, becoming "ministers of the environment" by caring for wetlands, forests, and oceans. 21.document_title: Eyes in the Land: Dune Lakes, Wetlands, and Indigenous Stewardship in Northland
21.document_summary: This comprehensive collection explores New Zealand's dune lakes and wetlands in Northland, examining their ecological significance and cultural importance to iwi communities. The articles document indigenous stewardship and scientific conservation efforts, featuring Lake Ngatu and NIWA scientist Paul Champion's research on unique flora including kuta sedge and tuatara plants. Key threats include invasive species such as hornwort, Egeria densa, Gambusia affinis, and grass carp. The collection emphasizes kaitiakitanga (environmental stewardship) as the foundation for restoration, incorporating ecological and cultural dimensions. Monitoring strategies using the LakeSPI bio-assessment tool are detailed, alongside management approaches including herbicide applications and freshwater mussel restoration. The narrative incorporates the Māori proverb "Te roto tāpokopoko, he wai whakahuihui, he pukenga ora" (a dune lake is an oasis that gathers and grows life) and explores te mana o te repo (the mana of wetlands) as intermediaries between Tāne (forests) and Tangaroa (seas). Community engagement initiatives like "Get to Know Your Dune Lake" days link lake conservation to Māori traditions and reconnect communities with their ancestral lands.

22.text:
[Page 9] If everyone foraged, would we strip the land? Wellington author Johanna Knox (Ngāti Tukorehe, Ngāti Raukawa ki te Tonga, Ngāti Ranginui, Tangata Tiriti), who wrote the book on foraging in New Zealand, thinks that eating the environment is a pretty good way of reconnecting with it. She reckons foraging could resurrect the idea of the commons—not just the tragedy of it. It could bring back the concept of places that are used and maintained by people for each other—and for future generations. That idea has been largely lost from the Pākehā world, but it’s remained intact in te ao Māori. Despite the destruction of traditional food gathering areas, despite the theft of land, the depletion of resources, and the loss of kōrero about how different species are prepared—despite all of that, the philosophy of how to gather food sustainably remains intact. It’s the concept of kaitiakitanga. “A big difference between Western environmentalism and Māori kaitiakitanga is how they see humans in the environment,” says Knox. “So in Pākehā conservation, it’s like, ‘We must keep these areas pristine. Nobody can take anything from here,’ but in te ao Māori it’s like, ‘People are part of the landscape. It’s a reciprocal relationship, so of course we’re taking stuff.’ McKenzie and Mikhail Shatura, head chef at downtown Auckland restaurant Ahi, taste the morning’s foraging. Shatura assembles a dish of quail, chickweed, huruhuru whenua and ureure. Foraged ingredients don’t form the bulk of a dish, says McKenzie, but they bring the flavours of a place onto the plate. “These are supporting characters,” he says. “So I come at foraging from the perspective that if you get right out there and involve yourself in the landscape—which means taking what you can, but respectfully and sustainably and at the same time giving back—that’s just a really good way to do things.” Raglan ecologist and rongoā practitioner Mahuru Wilcox (Ngāti Awa, Ngāti Ranginui) echoes Knox. She forages native plants traditionally used for medicinal purposes for her small business, Hau Botanicals. “How can you teach people to value something if you can’t connect to it?” she asks. “These [plants] are valued because they were important as kai or as rongoā or they were important as ancestors, as tūpuna. If you’re really thinking of our world around us as our tūpuna, as our ancestors, how would you respect your tūpuna? So using those principles for how you connect.” Even in the most densely populated parts of the city, plants move through the cycles of the year. Retreating into their roots to conserve water, springing forth with new shoots. Exploding into colour for a week or two. “It’s such a reminder in your daily life as a human that everything has a season,” says Wilcox. Over time, you start to see it: the living calendar, the shifts in weather and sunlight reflected in the plants changing, day by day, in all the gaps between the fixed and immobile parts of the city.

26.document_title: Blue Carbon in New Zealand: Fiords, Coastal Wetlands, and Seagrass Restoration
26.document_summary: This comprehensive collection examines New Zealand's blue carbon ecosystems and their role in climate regulation. New Zealand's fiords, particularly Doubtful Sound and Dusky Sound, store approximately 2.24 billion tonnes of carbon—about one percent of the world's seabed carbon. These fiords bury organic carbon faster than similar ecosystems worldwide due to unique geography, steep valleys, heavy rainfall, and anaerobic mud conditions. Scientists at the Cawthron Institute are pioneering seed-based seagrass restoration methods, discovering that Zostera muelleri flowers more frequently than previously believed. Seagrass ecosystems capture carbon 55 times faster than tropical rainforests and store four times more carbon per hectare in soils. Coastal wetland restoration projects like Te Wahapū o Waihī integrate mātauranga Māori with coastal ecology, with five iwi collaborating on restoration efforts. Seaweed research reveals varying decomposition rates in deep-sea environments, though scientists raise concerns about accurately measuring seaweed's carbon removal potential. The research emphasizes protecting natural carbon sinks while addressing legal complexities involving Māori rights and rangatiratanga, highlighting kaitiakitanga (stewardship) and cultural significance of coastal ecosystem restoration.

27.text:
[Page 16] [Chapter Break] On an autumn afternoon in early March, I pull off State Highway 6 just south of Hokitika, into the carpark at Mananui Bush. Powerlines stretch overhead, curving north across fields of fodder beet. Lake Mahinapua lies across the highway to the east, hidden by thick coastal bush. Through the open window, in the quiet after I switch off the engine, I hear the faint boom and hiss of Te Tai o Rehua, the Tasman Sea. A group of Pākehā men and women stand waiting in the small clearing beneath a fierce sun. Between the laughter and the bags of kai lined up in the back of a nearby van, they could be friends on a package tour except for the hefty spiral bound books in their hands and the two huge maps spread on the ground. Clifton is kneeling on the ground, pointing at the map. The others, ranged in a semicircle, are conservation ecologist Bill Lee, veteran conservation leader Jo Breese, archaeologist Katharine Watson and landscape architect Philip Blakely. COVID related work disruptions have kept mātauranga expert Marama Muru Lanning (Waikato, Ngāti Maniapoto, Ngāti Whātua) in Auckland today. On paper their depth of experience is intimidating; in person they’re attentive and intelligent, though a little fatigued. It’s their final day together in the field—they’ve visited around 90 per cent of the stewardship land parcels, and flown over those too big to take in on foot. They’ve travelled from southern Kohaihai in Kahurangi right down to Fiordland. I ask how it’s been. “Intense,” several say at once. “Bill is our resident scientist,” Breeze says, “and he’s been recording our entrances and exits to vehicles. Our record is 54 movements in a day.” “Be careful how you phrase that,” Lee says to me, straight faced. The grazed area in the photograph above is stewardship land, at the mouth of the Karamea River, at Māori Point. It’s blocks like these that are potential candidates for an assessment of low or no conservation values, which could lead to their sale. Climate advocates argue such blocks should be reforested instead. That intensity has largely come from the volume of complex information. “We rely heavily on these,” Neil says, brandishing his Conservation Value Report for the area: a compendium of DOC’s information about each block, grouped into sections such as mātauranga, ecology, landscape, recreation and heritage. Depending on the dominant values in a block, different experts have taken the lead, as the group analyses the values against what they find on the ground, debates the merits of different classifications, talks the issues through with local DOC rangers. I ask how it worked if they needed more information.

27.document_title: Stewardship Land Reclassification in New Zealand: Conservation, Māori Rights, and the Old Ghost Road
27.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection examines New Zealand's stewardship land—nine percent of Aotearoa's total land area—through interconnected narratives spanning conservation policy, indigenous rights, and economic development. The collection begins with the Old Ghost Road project in the Mokihinui Gorge, illustrating how stewardship land's lower protection status both threatened and enabled conservation initiatives, ultimately generating $4 million annually for local communities after Meridian Energy abandoned its proposed dam project. The documents trace the government's 2021 fast-tracked reclassification process, which proposed appointing expert panels to assess stewardship land within eight months. This initiative sparked significant controversy, particularly from Ngāi Tahu iwi, who filed urgent High Court proceedings citing consultation breaches and Treaty of Waitangi violations. The historical context reveals how the Crown's 1859 acquisition of the West Coast from Poutini Ngāi Tahu for £300 left the iwi with only 4,000 hectares despite claiming 151,757 hectares, with 87% of their territory now managed by DOC with minimal iwi input. The collection explores the tension between traditional conservation frameworks and contemporary approaches that integrate mātauranga (Māori knowledge) and recognize Māori cultural values extending beyond preservation to include economic and commercial use on ancestral land. Through case studies such as Lake Mahinapua, the documents examine how mana whenua and national assessment panels are collaboratively developing integrated conservation models that respect rangatiratanga while addressing concerns about mining interests and the Stockton Coal Mine on Denniston Plateau.

[Page 1] Māori AI expert Dr Karaitiana Taiuru shares his favourite whakataukī 2024 03 18 22:44:07+13:00 Dr Karaitiana Taiuru. Tino rangatiratanga: mō tātou, ā, mō kā uri ā muri ake nei. It is the whakataukī (Māori proverb) that means most to Māori data, AI and technology ethicist Dr Karaitiana Taiuru (Ngāi Tahu, Ngāti Kahungunu, Ngāti Toa). Translated to English, it means "the ability to create and control our destiny for generations to come". It links in well with his work and family life, Taiuru told RNZ Nights. For his work, it reminded Taiuru why he still does what he does and that there was a new generation of children who will not know life without AI and it was "our role to create the new normal for them". Taiuru applies a te ao Māori perspective to AI. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/nig new generation of children who will not know life without AI and it was "our role to create the new normal for them". Taiuru applies a te ao Māori perspective to AI. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/nig hts/audio/2018930609/whakatauki of the week with karaitiana taiuru Listen to the full interview on Nights "We already know that internationally, there's bias against minority peoples so what I do, in conjunction with international best practices with artificial intelligence and other technologies, is bring that Māori voice and Te Tiriti o Waitangi considerations to play." There were "a number" of cultural values that needed to be considered in terms of AI, he said. Many Māori have moko (facial tattoos) so understanding how that was considered with facial technologies was a big factor. In his personal life, the whakataukī applied to his whānau. "For me, I consider that I have an opportunity to create wealth and opportunities for my children and also for my grandchildren. "I live by that rule. I make that sure my children have the opportunities that I didn't always have, make sure they have access to education, financial resources, a home, and part of my planning in life is that my grandchildren will also have the same access and all going well in life, I should see my great grandchildren and maybe great great grandchildren whom I will also ensure that they have equal access. "And I know my children also that they consider the same sort of philosophies in life where they want to protect their whānau as well for the future." Taiuru said the whakataukī came out of working groups around the South Island when Ngāi Tahu was trying to identify a new tribal vision that would be carried into the future. It came after settlements with the Crown in 1996. "That whakataukī was the key whakataukī that came out of those hui." Related

[Page 1] 2024 01 29 21:53:12+13:00 Anton Matthews is the director of Hustle Group, a company operating a bunch of restaurants and catering companies in Ōtautahi Christchurch. He's also a big advocate for people learning te reo Māori, also running online course Normalising Te Reo Māori. In the next in a weekly series, he shares a favourite whakataukī, or traditional Māori aphorism, with Emile Donovan. Ko te amorangi ki mua, ko te hāpai ō ki muri The leader at the front and the workers behind the scenes This simple whakataukī, or Māori proverb, is a multi layered favourite of Matthews. While he was fortunate to grow up immersed in te ao Māori, including being educated at kohanga reo and kura kaupapa, Matthews tells Nights anyone exposed to a lot of te reo Māori quickly learns that it’s a language rich in metaphor. “There’s the literal meaning of whatever has been said, but it often takes a couple of years (sometimes it never actually dawns on us), but there is a hidden meaning there as well. “That’s what I love about whakataukī is that yep, there's that kind of surface layer literally, what is the person saying? But what's the hidden meaning? What are they really trying to explain or what sort of message or idea are they trying to convey when they use the whakataukī? That's the beauty of language, not just te reo Māori, but any language has those kinds of beautiful nuances, I think.” Matthews says he loves all sorts of different whakataukī for different reasons and occasions, but his favourite is particularly appropriate to his work in the hospitality sector. Ko te amorangi ki mua, ko te hāpai ō ki muri has two parts to it, Matthews says. Amorangi is a term that refers to recognised iwi leaders, the ones who are front and centre when leading a pōwhiri, or welcome, onto the marae. “These are the familiar faces that everyone kind of knows… these people are highly respected. They have a lot of mana. We look to them when we need guidance.” Te hāpai ō referred to in the second part of the whakataukī is the complete opposite, Matthews says.

43.document_title: Whakataukī of the Week: Ko te amorangi ki mua, ko te hāpai ō ki muri
43.document_summary: Anton Matthews, director of Hustle Group and advocate for te reo Māori, shares his favorite whakataukī (Māori proverb): "Ko te amorangi ki mua, ko te hāpai ō ki muri" (The leader at the front and the workers behind the scenes). This multi-layered aphorism illustrates the duality and balance fundamental to te ao Māori. The amorangi represents recognized iwi leaders at the front, while te hāpai ō (food carriers) work behind the scenes. Matthews emphasizes that both roles are equally important and worthy of mana, requiring constant communication and interdependence. He applies this philosophy to hospitality, arguing that all staff—whether in the kitchen or front-of-house—develop skills valued on the marae and contribute equally to organizational success. The whakataukī demonstrates that everyone has a vital place, and no role is more important than another.

[Page 1] As well as being an award winning and critically acclaimed novelist and short story writer, Witi Ihimaera is also chair of Te Kaituhi Māori, the Māori writers' organisation within the New Zealand Society of Authors. Te Kaituhi Māori have just opened applications for its 2025 Kupu Kaitiaki and Kaituhi Māori programmes, fostering emerging and developing Māori writers. It's a "mighty mentor programme," Ihimaera told RNZ's Nights. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/nights/audio/201897 7273/whakatauki of the week with witi ihimaera "In the past people like Paula Morris, people like Emma Hislop, Steph Matuku and Tanya Roxborogh have been the mentors. "And so, whoever goes in for this Māori mentor programme, they get the best teaching, and we hope will become the best in the next 20 years." Such mentor programmes didn't exist when Ihimaera was himself a young writer, but that may have helped him find his voice, he said. "I had to begin my career from a Māori perspective, and a Māori point of view. "Had I possibly had help from Pākehā institutions, then I possibly could have started to write in Pākehā ways and according to Pākehā frameworks." The Kaituhi Māori mentorship programme happened for the first time in 2024. When Ihimaera read through the work produced it brought him great joy, he said. "It was so incredibly awesome that, there are times when I almost wept with excitement and with joy, because I'm an old writer, I'm now 81 and to be able to see that there was a cohort of new rangatahi writers, fresh voices, refreshing ideas of who we were and people you know were mentoring them with so much generosity. 45.document_title: Māori Landowners Take Crown to High Court Over Freshwater Rights
45.document_summary: Approximately 60 Māori Land Trusts, representing over 150,000 landowners, hapū, and iwi have filed proceedings in the High Court against the Crown over freshwater rights. The claimants argue the Crown has broken promises and failed to uphold Te Tiriti o Waitangi obligations regarding Māori proprietary and kaitiaki rights in freshwater and geothermal resources. They seek immediate action to stop water degradation, recognition of tikanga Māori rights, and a fair water allocation system enabling Māori to exercise kaitiakitanga. The case follows over a decade of Crown inaction despite 2012-2013 acknowledgments of Māori rights. The claimants criticize the current "first-in, first-served" allocation system and the dismantling of Te Mana o te Wai framework. Kingi Smiler, representing the claimant group, emphasizes the urgency of restoring balance and protecting waterways for future generations. The legal process is expected to take two to three years.

46.text:
[Page 1] From Tangata Whenua to Tangata Tiriti, from seasoned attendees to first time visitors, their visions for Aotearoa share a common theme kotahitanga. Waka mana wāhine inspire the next gen Out on the moana, Tanya Rogers stands as the kaihautū (captain) of Tī Eke Waka o Te Arawa, one of the few waka exclusively paddled by wāhine. Representing Ngāti Whakaue and Taranaki, she said the journey to Waitangi was hard work, but ultimately rewarding. "We practiced all through winter, through dry land paddles. For most of us, this was our first time paddling here, and it was absolutely magical," But she said their mission extends beyond the water. "Our job is to bring our rangatahi up. We hope we've been an inspiration to them so they can reach their aspirations of being wāhine toa." What she hopes for the future of Aotearoa she said, is kotahitanga. "I'd like to see more unity, more coming together, to see our Māori people standing together, being strong and taking us into the future. And again, our rangatahi are doing that." 'Paving the way for our mokopuna' Kataraina WiHongi, attending Waitangi with her mokopuna, envisions a future grounded in peace and justice. "If we aim for justice and peace for our tamariki and mokopuna, with their whakapapa and whakaaro, i raro i te humārie the humbleness and the peace then kia tau te rangimārie i roto i ngā mea katoa," While watching the waka celebrations with her mokopuna, she reflected on how much the space has changed. "When I was a little girl, I just swam here, because it was a Pākehā space. But now, it is very Māori. Our tamariki are growing up with te reo in kōhanga, in kura kaupapa and we need to embrace that." A space for all New Zealanders Pat Gray, Agnes Hermans, Ange Jones and Margo Irvine are representatives of Whangārei Network Waitangi, an organisation they said has spent decades educating Pākehā on Treaty issues. Their focus now is on constitutional transformation, guided by Matike Mai, a report envisioning a future where tino rangatiratanga is honoured. "We believe that an Aotearoa that upholds Te Tiriti benefits all New Zealanders," Hermans said. "A constitution based on Matike Mai would create a future for all of us." Jones added, "For us, tino rangatiratanga, honouring te tiriti is good for all New Zealand. Te ao Māori, the values, the values system care for the environment etcetera, this is what makes Aotearoa great." While being at Waitangi, kitted out in their 'Tangata Tiriti' kākahu, Hermans said they have received "lots of aroha and lots of support." "Particularly from tangata whenua, saying 'kia ora thank you for showing up' 'we really appreciate you being here." But they also received a lot of nods and smiles from Pākehā too, she said. "I think we are being a witness to something that is bigger than just the few of us, there is real base support." For Margo Irvine, attending Waitangi is an experience every New Zealander should have at least once. "I wish that all New Zealanders could experience the atmosphere here the passion, the fun, the colour, the kotahitanga. It is a very special thing." A first time visitor's whakaaro For one first time visitor from Tāmaki Makaurau, Waitangi was an unforgettable experience. "Waitangi is absolutely wonderful, it's inclusive, it's welcoming, I understand now why its so popular for Tangata Whenua and Pākehā like myself... Lifes an adventure and this is part of it." Looking ahead, she hoped for "a more cohesive society, one that respects tangata whenua." 47.document_title: Kotahitanga in Action: Hundreds Gather at Treaty Grounds with Kiingitanga and Rātana
47.document_summary: On February 4, 2024, hundreds of Māori gathered at the Waitangi Treaty Grounds in a powerful display of kotahitanga (unity). Led by Kiingi Tuuheitia and Rātana Tumuaki Manuao, iwi leaders from across the country assembled to voice concerns about the government's proposed Treaty principles bill. The pōwhiri featured speeches emphasizing unity and peaceful resistance, with leaders like Ngāpuhi Rangatira Matua Hone Sadler urging iwi to remain peaceful while standing firm. Bayden Barber referenced the 1990s kotahitanga movement, calling for continued strategic planning. Te Taepa Kameta criticized Minister Shane Jones's absence, while Rāhui Papa emphasized mobilizing under mana motuhake and ensuring He Whakaputanga receives equal standing with Te Tiriti. The gathering concluded with Tainui representatives singing in harmony, marking a historic moment of Māori solidarity.

1.fileDescription: Kaitiakitanga is a foundational Māori concept of guardianship and environmental stewardship rooted in the worldview that humans are part of nature. A kaitiaki is a guardian recognized by tangata whenua to care for natural areas such as lakes, forests, and waterways. Traditional conservation practices include temporary rāhui (resource restrictions), use of the lunar calendar (maramataka) for planting and harvesting, sustainable hunting and fishing, and blessing of mauri stones by tohunga (priests). Key spiritual concepts include mana (spiritual power), tapu (spiritual restriction), and mauri (life force). Today, kaitiakitanga is experiencing renewal as iwi (tribes) restore ecosystems and apply traditional knowledge in modern contexts. Practical examples include Ngāi Tahu's guardianship of pounamu resources, Ngāti Toa's fishery restoration at Pukerua Bay, and multi-tribal efforts to stop river pollution and protect endangered species. The document outlines challenges in collaborating with non-Māori stakeholders and details legislative frameworks such as the Resource Management Act 1991 and Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 that incorporate kaitiakitanga principles. Kaitiakitanga offers perspectives on environmental stewardship and kinship with nature, enabling Māori to fulfill ancestral responsibilities while contributing to broader environmental sustainability.

chunkHighlights.text: By Te Ahukaramū Charles Royal

Understanding kaitiakitanga Kaitiakitanga means guardianship and
protection. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the Māori world view. A kaitiaki is a guardian. This can be a person or group that cares for an area such as a lake or forest. They are given that role by the local iwi . Māori world view In the Māori world view, people are closely connected to the land and nature. Kaitiakitanga is based on this idea of humans as part of the natural world. Traditional practices In the past, people followed traditional practices when they were hunting, fishing, growing or finding food. These helped them to care for the environment. They included: temporary bans (rāhui) on taking food from an area using the lunar calendar (maramataka) to decide when to plant and harvest taking only what was needed hunting and fishing only for food, not as sport using bird snares at the right time – for example, not when the birds were breeding. Mana, tapu and mauri Mana means spiritual power. If a forest has mana , it will have plenty of flowers, fruit and birds. Tapu can mean spiritual restriction. Sometimes rāhui (restrictions) are needed to help the mana of the forest. A rāhui might stop people taking birds, fish or fruit from a certain area, or at a certain time. Mauri means life force. This must be protected in forests, rivers, gardens, lakes and the sea. Special mauri stones, which tohunga (priests) said prayers over, were used to preserve this force. Kaitiakitanga today Today there is growing interest in kaitiakitanga. Iwi are restoring their environment and culture, and using traditional ideas in the modern world. Ngāi Tahu are guardians of pounamu (greenstone) in the South Island. Te Āti Awa ki Taranaki made a claim to the government to stop pollution in their fishing areas. Four iwi (Ngāti Kahungunu, Rangitāne, Muaūpoko and Ngāti Raukawa) have come together to stop the Manawatū River being polluted. The Te Rarawa people are working to save the kūkupa (New Zealand pigeon). Kaitiakitanga has also been included in some laws,
such as the Resource Management Act 1991.

7.fileDescription: This comprehensive document collection explores the ecological, cultural, and conservation significance of kōura (New Zealand freshwater crayfish) through multiple interconnected narratives. It traces the historical role of kōura in Māori diet and culture, documenting how Māori ancestors practiced kaitiakitanga (environmental stewardship) by translocating crayfish across the country for centuries to ensure food security. The document examines kōura's ecological importance as ecosystem engineers that control invasive species and restore waterway health. It details the dramatic decline of kōura populations due to trout predation, forest clearing, invasive species (particularly brown bullhead catfish and marron), and water quality degradation, with some populations experiencing up to 99% decline. The collection highlights contemporary restoration efforts led by iwi and freshwater biologists using adapted traditional harvesting methods like the tau kōura technique. It features innovative approaches including John Hollows' professional kōura farming operations in Southland wetlands, which demonstrate sustainable aquaculture, and Kāti Huirapa rūnanga's initiatives to reconnect whānau with traditional food sources. The document emphasizes that mātauranga (Māori knowledge) remains essential for freshwater conservation and advocates for transferring ecosystem management responsibility back to indigenous communities.

chunkHighlights.text: For Māori, shifting kōura around was about more than shoring up the food supply; it was part of kaitiakitanga, stewardship of the land and the species they shared it with. When, for example, Māori found waterways that had been overfished or cleaned out by a flood, they’d top them up again with kōura from elsewhere in the catchment.

8.fileDescription: Kennedy Warne reflects on his deep personal connection to the Hauraki Gulf in New Zealand, tracing memories from childhood through his grandfather's swordfishing boat. He explores the concept of guardianship and stewardship through the Inuit legend of the mother of the sea—a story about how people's disrespect for the ocean causes the sea's bounty to disappear until a shaman restores harmony by combing her hair. Warne connects this ancient wisdom to the Māori concept of kaitiakitanga, arguing it represents a profound stewardship that goes beyond mere resource management. He observes a growing movement of individuals taking environmental responsibility into their own hands, becoming "ministers of the environment" by caring for wetlands, forests, and oceans. The essay emphasizes humanity's forgotten relationship with the sea and calls for a return to reverence and respect for the natural world.

chunkHighlights.text: And that, I think, is what kaitiakitanga is about—a kind of stewardship far deeper than the resource management that politicians and bureaucrats understand. It is about revering the world and holding it dear.

chunkHighlights.text: Legislation

Kaitiakitanga has been included in some legislation. The Resource Management Act 1991 aims to enable sustainable management of environmental resources. It states that people managing resources under the act must take kaitiakitanga into account.

The gods of the natural world were considered to be the original kaitiaki – for instance, Tāne, god of the forest, was the kaitiaki of the forest. All other kaitiaki emulate those original ones. Many hapū (sub-tribes) and whānau (families) care for a place such as a lake or forest. They work to conserve the natural heritage, address environmental problems and reclaim traditional knowledge.

retrieved_chunks.text: Kaitiakitanga can also apply to valued items. These include family heirlooms such as korowai (cloaks), mere pounamu (jade clubs) and books about whakapapa (genealogy). An item that belongs to a person later becomes the property of all their descendants. It is cared for by an individual kaitiaki on behalf of the group. The kaitiaki is responsible for bringing the object to important occasions such as funerals, and for holding information about it.

retrieved_chunks.text: Legislation Kaitiakitanga has been included in some legislation. The Resource Management Act 1991 aims to enable sustainable management of environmental resources. It states that people managing resources under the act must take kaitiakitanga into account. The act defines kaitiakitanga as ‘the exercise of guardianship by the tangata whenua of an area in accordance with tikanga Māori in relation to natural and physical resources; and includes the ethic of stewardship’. Kaitiakitanga was also included in the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004, where it has the same meaning.

It could bring back the concept of places that are used and maintained by people for each other—and for future generations. Despite the destruction of traditional food gathering areas, despite the theft of land, the depletion of resources, and the loss of kōrero about how different species are prepared—despite all of that, the philosophy of how to gather food sustainably remains intact. It’s the concept of kaitiakitanga. “A big difference between Western environmentalism and Māori kaitiakitanga is how they see humans in the environment,” says Knox. “So in Pākehā conservation, it’s like, ‘We must keep these areas pristine. retrieved_chunks.text: [Page 1] From Tangata Whenua to Tangata Tiriti, from seasoned attendees to first time visitors, their visions for Aotearoa share a common theme kotahitanga. Waka mana wāhine inspire the next gen Out on the moana, Tanya Rogers stands as the kaihautū (captain) of Tī Eke Waka o Te Arawa, one of the few waka exclusively paddled by wāhine. Representing Ngāti Whakaue and Taranaki, she said the journey to Waitangi was hard work, but ultimately rewarding. "We practiced all through winter, through dry land paddles. For most of us, this was our first time paddling here, and it was absolutely magical," But she said their mission extends beyond the water. "Our job is to bring our rangatahi up. We hope we've been an inspiration to them so they can reach their aspirations of being wāhine toa." What she hopes for the future of Aotearoa she said, is kotahitanga. ## Te Tikanga o Kaitiakitanga

Ko **kaitiakitanga** tētahi kupu Māori e māramatia ana ko te *guardianship* — arā, te tiaki, te manaaki, te ārai, me te tautiaki i ngā taonga o te taiao. [[1]](cite://1/1) He ara whakahaere i te taiao, ā, i ahu mai i te tirohanga ao Māori, i ngā tikanga tūpuna. [[1]](cite://1/2)

He mārama anō te tikanga i roto i te Resource Management Act (RMA) 1991, e kī ana: ko kaitiakitanga ko 'the exercise of guardianship by the tangata whenua of an area in accordance with tikanga Māori in relation to natural and physical resources; and includes the ethic of stewardship.' [[2]](cite://2/1)

## Ko Wai te Kaitiaki?

Ko te *kaitiaki* he tangata, he rōpū rānei e ārahina ana e te tangata whenua hei tiaki i tētahi wāhi — pērā i te roto, i te ngahere rānei. [[3]](cite://3/1) Ko te kupu *kai* e tohu ana i tētahi nā te mea e mahi ana — nō reira, ko te kaitiaki he kaitiaki, he kaimanaaki, he kaitautiaki. [[4]](cite://4/1)

I te ao tawhito, ko ngā atua o te taiao ngā kaitiaki tuatahi. Ko Tāne, ko ia te kaitiaki o te ngahere. Nō reira, ko ngā kaitiaki katoa i muri mai e aro ana ki ērā tūāhuatanga. [[4]](cite://4/2)

## Ngā Tikanga Tūpuna i Raro i Kaitiakitanga

I ngā rā o mua, i whai ngā tūpuna i ēnei tikanga hei tiaki i te taiao: [[1]](cite://1/3)

- **Rāhui** — he aukati ā-wā ki tētahi rohe kia ora anō ai ngā rauemi
- **Maramataka** — te āta titiro ki ngā wā tika mō te mahi māra me te hauhake
- Te tango i ngā mea e hiahiatia ana anake
- Te hī ika, te mahi kimi kai hei oranga noa iho, kaua hei hākinakina

## Ngā Ariā Hōhonu

E toru ngā ariā nui e hāngai ana ki kaitiakitanga: [[1]](cite://1/4)

- **Mana** — te mana wairua o te ngahere, o ngā awa, o ngā taonga katoa
- **Tapu** — ngā here wairua me ngā rāhui hei ārai i te kino
- **Mauri** — te mauri o ngā mea katoa — me tiaki, me manaaki

## Kaitiakitanga i Tēnei Rā

He nui ake ngā kaitiaki e mahi ana i ēnei rā, arā, ngā iwi e whakahoki ana i ō rātou taiao, ō rātou tikanga. [[5]](cite://5/1) I tāpirihia anō a kaitiakitanga ki roto i ētahi ture, pērā i te RMA 1991 me te Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004. [[2]](cite://2/2)

He kupu whakamāramatanga pai tā Kennedy Warne: he momo tiaki kaitiakitanga 'far deeper than the resource management that politicians and bureaucrats understand. It is about revering the world and holding it dear.' [[6]](cite://6/1)

Mō ngā tāngata Māori, ko kaitiakitanga tētahi ara e tutuki ai ngā tūmanako o ō rātou tūpuna — ā, mō ngā tāngata kē anō, he ara whakaaro mō te hononga o te tangata ki te taiao i tēnei ao kua mate haere. [[7]](cite://7/1)

Ka hiahia koe kia kōrero anō mō ngā tikanga tūpuna — pērā i te rāhui — i raro i kaitiakitanga?

1.text:
[Page 1] By Te Ahukaramū Charles Royal Understanding kaitiakitanga Kaitiakitanga means guardianship and protection. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the Māori world view. A kaitiaki is a guardian. This can be a person or group that cares for an area such as a lake or forest. They are given that role by the local iwi . Māori world view In the Māori world view, people are closely connected to the land and nature. Kaitiakitanga is based on this idea of humans as part of the natural world. Traditional practices In the past, people followed traditional practices when they were hunting, fishing, growing or finding food. These helped them to care for the environment. They included: temporary bans (rāhui) on taking food from an area using the lunar calendar (maramataka) to decide when to plant and harvest taking only what was needed hunting and fishing only for food, not as sport using bird snares at the right time for example, not when the birds were breeding. Mana, tapu and mauri Mana means spiritual power. If a forest has mana , it will have plenty of flowers, fruit and birds. Tapu can mean spiritual restriction. Sometimes rāhui (restrictions) are needed to help the mana of the forest. A rāhui might stop people taking birds, fish or fruit from a certain area, or at a certain time. Mauri means life force. This must be protected in forests, rivers, gardens, lakes and the sea. Special mauri stones, which tohunga (priests) said prayers over, were used to preserve this force. Kaitiakitanga today Today there is growing interest in kaitiakitanga. Iwi are restoring their environment and culture, and using traditional ideas in the modern world. Ngāi Tahu are guardians of pounamu (greenstone) in the South Island. Te Āti Awa ki Taranaki made a claim to the government to stop pollution in their fishing areas. Four iwi (Ngāti Kahungunu, Rangitāne, Muaūpoko and Ngāti Raukawa) have come together to stop the Manawatū River being polluted. The Te Rarawa people are working to save the kūkupa (New Zealand pigeon). Kaitiakitanga has also been included in some laws, such as the Resource Management Act 1991. Kaitiakitanga means guardianship, protection, preservation or sheltering. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the traditional Māori world view.

1.document_title: Kaitiakitanga: Māori Guardianship, Environmental Stewardship, and Traditional Conservation Practices
1.document_summary: Kaitiakitanga is a foundational Māori concept of guardianship and environmental stewardship rooted in the worldview that humans are part of nature. A kaitiaki is a guardian recognized by tangata whenua to care for natural areas such as lakes, forests, and waterways. Traditional conservation practices include temporary rāhui (resource restrictions), use of the lunar calendar (maramataka) for planting and harvesting, sustainable hunting and fishing, and blessing of mauri stones by tohunga (priests). Key spiritual concepts include mana (spiritual power), tapu (spiritual restriction), and mauri (life force). Today, kaitiakitanga is experiencing renewal as iwi (tribes) restore ecosystems and apply traditional knowledge in modern contexts. Practical examples include Ngāi Tahu's guardianship of pounamu resources, Ngāti Toa's fishery restoration at Pukerua Bay, and multi-tribal efforts to stop river pollution and protect endangered species. The document outlines challenges in collaborating with non-Māori stakeholders and details legislative frameworks such as the Resource Management Act 1991 and Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 that incorporate kaitiakitanga principles. Kaitiakitanga offers perspectives on environmental stewardship and kinship with nature, enabling Māori to fulfill ancestral responsibilities while contributing to broader environmental sustainability.

2.text:
[Page 11] Legislation Kaitiakitanga has been included in some legislation. The Resource Management Act 1991 aims to enable sustainable management of environmental resources. It states that people managing resources under the act must take kaitiakitanga into account. The act defines kaitiakitanga as ‘the exercise of guardianship by the tangata whenua of an area in accordance with tikanga Māori in relation to natural and physical resources; and includes the ethic of stewardship’. Kaitiakitanga was also included in the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004, where it has the same meaning.

4.document_title: New Zealand Rivers: Comprehensive Guide to Geography, Ecology, Culture, and Conservation
4.document_summary:
This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's extensive river systems across both the North and South Islands, covering over 180,000 kilometres of mapped rivers including the Waikato (425 km) and Clutha (largest by volume). It details river formation through high rainfall, glacial activity, and geological processes, describing distinct river types: deep, fast-flowing rivers in the North Island hills and wide, braided rivers in the South Island's east.

The document emphasizes the profound cultural significance of rivers to Māori people, including their roles in exploration, transportation, food sources, and spiritual traditions involving taniwha (river spirits). It documents European settlement impacts including military conquest, transport use, 19th-century gold rushes, and industrial/agricultural pollution.

The content examines ecological transformations over two centuries, detailing how introduced species like rainbow trout, brown trout, and salmon impacted native fish populations. It describes the creation of eight artificial lakes along the Waikato River through hydroelectric dams (1945-1970s) and habitat loss through forest clearance. Conservation efforts are discussed, from late 19th-century catchment protection through the 1941 Soil Conservation Act to the 1981 Wild and Scenic Rivers Amendment protecting 12 rivers.

Modern challenges including invasive species like didymo, dairy farming impacts on water quality, and off-road vehicle use are addressed. The document highlights Māori guardianship cases involving the Waikato and Whanganui rivers, explores rivers' cultural significance through 19th and 20th-century art, literature, and film, and examines contemporary management practices including jet boat tourism, riparian protection through native tree planting, and regional council monitoring.

11.document_title: Māori Housing in New Zealand: Historical Evolution, Challenges, and Contemporary Solutions
11.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of Māori housing from pre-colonial times through the early 21st century in New Zealand. Traditionally, Māori lived in family-based kāinga (villages) with rectangular wharepuni (sleeping houses) constructed from natural materials. European settlers introduced European-style housing from the early 1800s, though most Māori initially maintained traditional dwellings. From the late 1800s, poor sanitary conditions—including inadequate water, sewerage, and overcrowding—led to disease outbreaks, prompting government intervention that resulted in the demolition of 1,256 houses and construction of 2,103 cottages by 1909. The 1918 influenza epidemic devastated Māori communities and prompted new housing initiatives including the Native Housing Act 1935. Post-WWII urbanization saw Māori migrate to cities like Auckland and Wellington, facing discrimination from landlords and living in overcrowded subdivided apartments. State housing policies effectively excluded Māori through discriminatory practices until 1944, while housing designs ignored Māori cultural values (tikanga), contributing to assimilation policies. By the 1980s-90s, Māori home ownership remained significantly lower than the general population (29-49% vs. 50-73%). Persistent problems in the early 21st century included substandard, cold, damp housing; overcrowding (23% of Māori in 2006 vs. 4% for Europeans); and poor health outcomes. Modern solutions emerged through iwi-led initiatives including papakāinga schemes, rural housing programs, and the government's Whānau Ora scheme (2010), which combines housing with health, education, and legal support, representing a shift toward Māori self-determination.

Traditional conservation practices include temporary rāhui (resource restrictions), use of the lunar calendar (maramataka) for planting and harvesting, sustainable hunting and fishing, and blessing of mauri stones by tohunga (priests). The document details family structures, housing trends showing declining home ownership (from 73.8% in 1991 to 67.8% in 2001), and rising single-parent families (31% in 2001). Gender dynamics highlight women's improved economic and social status since the 1980s, alongside New Zealand's progressive LGBTQ+ rights stance, including decriminalization of homosexuality (1986), civil unions (2005), and same-sex marriage (2013). The education system provides free, compulsory state schooling from ages 6-16, with special initiatives like kōhanga reo and kura kaupapa Māori for language preservation. Religion remains important with approximately half the population identifying as Christian, though church attendance is low and religious diversity has increased through immigration. The document traces cultural evolution including the transformation of cuisine from British traditions to cosmopolitan cooking, beverage consumption shifts from beer to wine and coffee, and relaxed dress codes reflecting global influences. 15.document_title: Bay of Plenty Region: Comprehensive Geography, History, Culture, and Development (1840-2013)
15.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an extensive overview of the Bay of Plenty region in New Zealand from its geographical foundations through 2013. The region, located on the eastern North Island between Cape Runaway and the Coromandel Peninsula, features white sandy beaches, volcanic islands (Mayor Island, Whale Island, White Island), and mountain ranges (Kaimai, Raukūmara). Geologically, the landscape includes western volcanic ranges and eastern greywacke mountains with swift-flowing rivers. The region's volcanic ash-enriched soils support productive horticulture, particularly kiwifruit production, holding 77.7% of New Zealand's kiwifruit by 2012. Māori heritage is deeply rooted, with nine tribes inhabiting the region for approximately 700 years via legendary canoe voyages. The document traces European contact beginning with Captain James Cook's 1769 voyage, missionary activity from 1820, and significant conflicts including the 1864 battles at Gate Pā and Te Ranga. Economic development evolved from dairy farming in the early 1900s through timber industry dominance in the 1950s-60s to kiwifruit becoming the primary economic driver from the 1970s onward. Infrastructure improvements including railways (1908-1921) and Tauranga's port expansion transformed the region. Population grew from approximately 10,000 in 1840 to 205,971 by 2013, with Māori comprising 24.4% of the population. The region developed distinct divisions between western areas (Tauranga-dominated, more Pākehā, higher incomes) and eastern areas (higher Māori proportion, lower incomes). Education, culture, and community life flourished with secondary schools established from 1946 onwards, rugby competitions since the 1880s, and cultural institutions including The Elms mission station and the Tauranga Repertory Society (1936).

16.document_title: Linguistics in New Zealand: Research, Contributions, and International Impact
16.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores linguistics in New Zealand, tracing its development as an academic discipline from the 1950s at Auckland and Victoria Universities to its current international prominence. Major research areas include Austronesian and Malayo-Polynesian languages, te reo Māori (where New Zealand linguists led world research), and New Zealand English as a distinctive colonial variety. The document examines sociolinguistics research on social dialects where ethnicity and gender are more significant than social class, featuring distinctive elements like the Southland 'burr' and pragmatic particle 'eh'. It traces attitudes toward New Zealand English from early 20th-century negativity to modern pride. New Zealand's lexicographic tradition spans from William Williams' 1844 English-Māori dictionary to Harry Orsman's Dictionary of New Zealand English. Internationally prominent New Zealand linguists profiled include Eric Partridge (English slang expert), Robert Burchfield (Oxford English Dictionary editor-in-chief), Jack Richards (English-language teaching author), and Bernard Spolsky (language policy specialist). 17.document_title: Pilgrim at Oakley Creek: Urban Nature, Memory, and Human Flourishing
17.document_summary: This comprehensive collection of interconnected essays by Kennedy Warne explores the transformative power of Oakley Creek (Te Auaunga) in Auckland, New Zealand, examining it through multiple lenses: personal pilgrimage, human psychology, historical memory, and place attachment. The work chronicles Warne's six-month photographic journey from winter to summer solstice, inspired by contemplative writers and Zen philosophy, demonstrating how mindful observation of urban nature fosters deep ecological connection. The essays apply Maslow's hierarchy of needs to show how urban green spaces fulfill fundamental human requirements—from physiological exercise and emotional security to social belonging and self-actualization—while highlighting the critical importance of preserving these spaces as Auckland's open space availability declines. Through archival research and personal narrative, Warne traces the layered histories converging at Oakley Creek, including indigenous Māori heritage, colonial discoveries, the legacy of Carrington Psychiatric Hospital, and the story of patient Rolfe Hattaway whose artistic vision inspired modernist artists. The collection advocates for kaitiakitanga (guardianship) and "locaphilia"—binding oneself to place through loving attention, storytelling, and ceremonial engagement—demonstrating how individuals can expand a place's narrative and experience meaningful homecoming through relationship-based environmental engagement.

18.text:
[Page 9] If everyone foraged, would we strip the land? Wellington author Johanna Knox (Ngāti Tukorehe, Ngāti Raukawa ki te Tonga, Ngāti Ranginui, Tangata Tiriti), who wrote the book on foraging in New Zealand, thinks that eating the environment is a pretty good way of reconnecting with it. She reckons foraging could resurrect the idea of the commons—not just the tragedy of it. It could bring back the concept of places that are used and maintained by people for each other—and for future generations. That idea has been largely lost from the Pākehā world, but it’s remained intact in te ao Māori. Despite the destruction of traditional food gathering areas, despite the theft of land, the depletion of resources, and the loss of kōrero about how different species are prepared—despite all of that, the philosophy of how to gather food sustainably remains intact. It’s the concept of kaitiakitanga. “A big difference between Western environmentalism and Māori kaitiakitanga is how they see humans in the environment,” says Knox. “So in Pākehā conservation, it’s like, ‘We must keep these areas pristine. Nobody can take anything from here,’ but in te ao Māori it’s like, ‘People are part of the landscape. It’s a reciprocal relationship, so of course we’re taking stuff.’ McKenzie and Mikhail Shatura, head chef at downtown Auckland restaurant Ahi, taste the morning’s foraging. Shatura assembles a dish of quail, chickweed, huruhuru whenua and ureure. Foraged ingredients don’t form the bulk of a dish, says McKenzie, but they bring the flavours of a place onto the plate. “These are supporting characters,” he says. “So I come at foraging from the perspective that if you get right out there and involve yourself in the landscape—which means taking what you can, but respectfully and sustainably and at the same time giving back—that’s just a really good way to do things.” Raglan ecologist and rongoā practitioner Mahuru Wilcox (Ngāti Awa, Ngāti Ranginui) echoes Knox. She forages native plants traditionally used for medicinal purposes for her small business, Hau Botanicals. “How can you teach people to value something if you can’t connect to it?” she asks. “These [plants] are valued because they were important as kai or as rongoā or they were important as ancestors, as tūpuna. If you’re really thinking of our world around us as our tūpuna, as our ancestors, how would you respect your tūpuna? So using those principles for how you connect.” Even in the most densely populated parts of the city, plants move through the cycles of the year. Retreating into their roots to conserve water, springing forth with new shoots. Exploding into colour for a week or two. “It’s such a reminder in your daily life as a human that everything has a season,” says Wilcox. Over time, you start to see it: the living calendar, the shifts in weather and sunlight reflected in the plants changing, day by day, in all the gaps between the fixed and immobile parts of the city.

20.document_title: Morepork: New Zealand's Native Owl - Adaptations, Behavior, and Conservation
20.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection explores the morepork (ruru), New Zealand's native nocturnal owl. The first section provides personal observations of morepork hunting behavior, detailing their diet of insects, small birds, mice, and geckos through pellet analysis, with regional variations across different islands. Moreporks inhabit diverse environments including native bush, pine forests, and suburban areas, maintaining 3-5 hectare territories and navigating by memory. The second section examines remarkable sensory and behavioral adaptations enabling nocturnal hunting, including specialized night vision with rod-cell-dominated retinas 100 times more sensitive than pigeons' eyes, asymmetrical skull structures for precise sound localization, and silent flight through specialized feather structures. Research suggests moreporks may detect infrared light to locate warm-blooded prey. The third section details the complete life cycle, focusing on chick development from fledging through independence and territorial behavior. The collection highlights a significant conservation success story involving a nearly-extinct Norfolk Island boobook successfully bred with New Zealand moreporks, resulting in a growing population with potential reintroduction to Lord Howe Island. Additionally, the collection addresses Māori cultural perspectives, where moreporks held spiritual significance as ancestral guardians and messengers.

24.document_title: Stewardship Land Reclassification in New Zealand: Conservation, Māori Rights, and the Old Ghost Road

The documents trace the government's 2021 fast-tracked reclassification process, which proposed appointing expert panels to assess stewardship land within eight months. 25.document_title: Blue Carbon in New Zealand: Fiords, Coastal Wetlands, and Seagrass Restoration
25.document_summary: This comprehensive collection examines New Zealand's blue carbon ecosystems and their role in climate regulation. New Zealand's fiords, particularly Doubtful Sound and Dusky Sound, store approximately 2.24 billion tonnes of carbon—about one percent of the world's seabed carbon. These fiords bury organic carbon faster than similar ecosystems worldwide due to unique geography, steep valleys, heavy rainfall, and anaerobic mud conditions. Scientists at the Cawthron Institute are pioneering seed-based seagrass restoration methods, discovering that Zostera muelleri flowers more frequently than previously believed. Seagrass ecosystems capture carbon 55 times faster than tropical rainforests and store four times more carbon per hectare in soils. Coastal wetland restoration projects like Te Wahapū o Waihī integrate mātauranga Māori with coastal ecology, with five iwi collaborating on restoration efforts. Seaweed research reveals varying decomposition rates in deep-sea environments, though scientists raise concerns about accurately measuring seaweed's carbon removal potential. 26.document_title: New Zealand's Eel Crisis: Conservation, Māori Guardianship, and the Fight to Restore Tuna Migration
26.document_summary: This comprehensive collection examines the critical decline of New Zealand's eel populations (tuna) and conservation efforts to restore migration pathways. Eels, which have sustained Māori culture for generations as relations and ancestors, face unprecedented threats from hydroelectric dams, river barriers, turbines, and water intakes. Key narratives include researchers monitoring glass eel migrations on the Ashley River, Kāti Huirapa and Kāti Irakehu whānau's traditional guardianship at Wairewa/Lake Forsyth, and Ngāti Manawa iwi's struggle to protect tuna in the Rangitāiki River despite multiple dams. The articles detail mitigation strategies including trap-and-transfer programs, fish-friendly turbines, bypass pipes, gravity gates, and community-led fish ladder installations. They highlight dedicated individuals like Maurice Toetoe and Willie Tai, who have rescued and transported thousands of eels annually. A central tension emerges between New Zealand's renewable energy goals—seeking 70% increased production by 2050—and the imperative to protect culturally significant eel populations. The collection emphasizes that eels represent integral aspects of Māori identity, spirituality, and survival, requiring power companies and policymakers to implement lasting solutions beyond temporary interventions.

[Page 1] Māori AI expert Dr Karaitiana Taiuru shares his favourite whakataukī 2024 03 18 22:44:07+13:00 Dr Karaitiana Taiuru. Tino rangatiratanga: mō tātou, ā, mō kā uri ā muri ake nei. It is the whakataukī (Māori proverb) that means most to Māori data, AI and technology ethicist Dr Karaitiana Taiuru (Ngāi Tahu, Ngāti Kahungunu, Ngāti Toa). Translated to English, it means "the ability to create and control our destiny for generations to come". It links in well with his work and family life, Taiuru told RNZ Nights. For his work, it reminded Taiuru why he still does what he does and that there was a new generation of children who will not know life without AI and it was "our role to create the new normal for them". Taiuru applies a te ao Māori perspective to AI. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/nig new generation of children who will not know life without AI and it was "our role to create the new normal for them". Taiuru applies a te ao Māori perspective to AI. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/nig hts/audio/2018930609/whakatauki of the week with karaitiana taiuru Listen to the full interview on Nights "We already know that internationally, there's bias against minority peoples so what I do, in conjunction with international best practices with artificial intelligence and other technologies, is bring that Māori voice and Te Tiriti o Waitangi considerations to play." There were "a number" of cultural values that needed to be considered in terms of AI, he said. Many Māori have moko (facial tattoos) so understanding how that was considered with facial technologies was a big factor. In his personal life, the whakataukī applied to his whānau. "For me, I consider that I have an opportunity to create wealth and opportunities for my children and also for my grandchildren. "I live by that rule. I make that sure my children have the opportunities that I didn't always have, make sure they have access to education, financial resources, a home, and part of my planning in life is that my grandchildren will also have the same access and all going well in life, I should see my great grandchildren and maybe great great grandchildren whom I will also ensure that they have equal access. "And I know my children also that they consider the same sort of philosophies in life where they want to protect their whānau as well for the future." Taiuru said the whakataukī came out of working groups around the South Island when Ngāi Tahu was trying to identify a new tribal vision that would be carried into the future. It came after settlements with the Crown in 1996. "That whakataukī was the key whakataukī that came out of those hui." Related

Linguists note this represents the evolving and distinctive nature of New Zealand English.

[Page 1] 'No one should go home hungry' Manaakitanga on full display at Tuurangawaewae ByPokere Paewai Māori issues reporter 2024 09 04 05:46:28+12:00 Thousands of people have gathered at Tuurangawaewae Marae to pay their respects to Kiingi Tuheitia, but local iwi have ensured that nobody has gone hungry. One of the core beliefs at Tuurangawaewae Marae is that 'no one should go home hungry', and the people of Tainui have epitomised the Māori value of Manaakitanga or hospitality during the tangihanga of Kiingi Tuheitia. The death of Kiingi Tuheitia has been a shock, but once it was announced, they flocked to the marae. They might be in the kitchen making sandwiches, outside directing traffic or operating the livestream. Dr Rangi Mātāmua who arrived with his iwi Tūhoe said Tainui were made to host events of this scale. "I know my own people would struggle to do what they do. They don't just do it for just one event, they do this kind of national massive gatherings to continue to unite us year after year. How many events like this occur here, and they do it on the aroha and hard work of the people of Tainui." It showed their love for the kaupapa and for the other iwi who attended, he said. "They are breaking their backs to manaaki te ao Māori, I do take my hat off to them. "I fail to have words really to bestow upon them just what they've done not just today, but since the establishment of the Kiingitanga." The Kiingitanga has been a burden on the people of Tainui in many ways, but they continued to carry it with such humility, Mātāmua said. Labour MP Cushla Tangaere Manuel arrived representing her iwi Ngāti Porou and the wider Tairawhiti. "I think what you observe when you come here is that people are born into manaaki here. "Intergenerational jobs, people have their role from generations and they are just a well oiled machine," she said. Another iwi, Rangitāne, travelled up to Waikato from Wairarapa on Monday, and instead of having to return home straight after paying their respects they were hosted at Te Kauri Marae in Rāhui Pōkeka, Huntly. Rangitāne kaumātua Manahi Paewai said being welcomed onto a marae by their hosts beat traveling through the night in a bus by a wide margin. "Miharo, kātahi te miharo nā rātau i tūwhera mai ō rātau kuwaha kia noho mai mātau Rangitāne o te Wairarapa, Rangitāne o Tamaki nui a rua. (The level of hospitality was amazing, they opened their doors to us of Rangitāne o te Wairarapa and Rangitāne o Tamaki nui a rua.)" Related

Whakataukī (Māori proverbs) are a fun and powerful way to help rangatahi develop their own voices and find grounding in the "continuum of whakapapa", Dr Hinemoa Elder says. Although this "older, more colonised" message about the place of young people still prevails in New Zealand culture, it is critical that whānau seek to understand young people's actual lived experience, she says, as they did in generations past. "I'm constantly trying to tune into a tūpuna [ancestral] voice in thinking about their struggles and trying to retain at least some of the older kōrero." Most young people are just trying to please their families, she says, and are "exquisitely attuned" to how their whānau receives them. "I'm often saying to parents 'Hey, our teenagers, our rangatahi get a bit of a bad rap but actually they're very caring because they've been keeping their pain private in order to protect your feelings and they pay a big price for that'." "I'm really quite shocked about the degree of complexity and the amount of difficulty that our whānau are trying to absorb themselves without professional help at all. "We need to make sure that rural communities are better resourced with mental health services and these services are functioning as well as looking at prevention." 43.text:
[Page 1] From Tangata Whenua to Tangata Tiriti, from seasoned attendees to first time visitors, their visions for Aotearoa share a common theme kotahitanga. Waka mana wāhine inspire the next gen Out on the moana, Tanya Rogers stands as the kaihautū (captain) of Tī Eke Waka o Te Arawa, one of the few waka exclusively paddled by wāhine. Representing Ngāti Whakaue and Taranaki, she said the journey to Waitangi was hard work, but ultimately rewarding. "We practiced all through winter, through dry land paddles. For most of us, this was our first time paddling here, and it was absolutely magical," But she said their mission extends beyond the water. "Our job is to bring our rangatahi up. We hope we've been an inspiration to them so they can reach their aspirations of being wāhine toa." What she hopes for the future of Aotearoa she said, is kotahitanga. "I'd like to see more unity, more coming together, to see our Māori people standing together, being strong and taking us into the future. And again, our rangatahi are doing that." 'Paving the way for our mokopuna' Kataraina WiHongi, attending Waitangi with her mokopuna, envisions a future grounded in peace and justice. "If we aim for justice and peace for our tamariki and mokopuna, with their whakapapa and whakaaro, i raro i te humārie the humbleness and the peace then kia tau te rangimārie i roto i ngā mea katoa," While watching the waka celebrations with her mokopuna, she reflected on how much the space has changed. "When I was a little girl, I just swam here, because it was a Pākehā space. But now, it is very Māori. Our tamariki are growing up with te reo in kōhanga, in kura kaupapa and we need to embrace that." A space for all New Zealanders Pat Gray, Agnes Hermans, Ange Jones and Margo Irvine are representatives of Whangārei Network Waitangi, an organisation they said has spent decades educating Pākehā on Treaty issues. Their focus now is on constitutional transformation, guided by Matike Mai, a report envisioning a future where tino rangatiratanga is honoured. "We believe that an Aotearoa that upholds Te Tiriti benefits all New Zealanders," Hermans said. "A constitution based on Matike Mai would create a future for all of us." Jones added, "For us, tino rangatiratanga, honouring te tiriti is good for all New Zealand. Te ao Māori, the values, the values system care for the environment etcetera, this is what makes Aotearoa great." While being at Waitangi, kitted out in their 'Tangata Tiriti' kākahu, Hermans said they have received "lots of aroha and lots of support." "Particularly from tangata whenua, saying 'kia ora thank you for showing up' 'we really appreciate you being here." But they also received a lot of nods and smiles from Pākehā too, she said. "I think we are being a witness to something that is bigger than just the few of us, there is real base support." For Margo Irvine, attending Waitangi is an experience every New Zealander should have at least once. "I wish that all New Zealanders could experience the atmosphere here the passion, the fun, the colour, the kotahitanga. It is a very special thing." A first time visitor's whakaaro For one first time visitor from Tāmaki Makaurau, Waitangi was an unforgettable experience. "Waitangi is absolutely wonderful, it's inclusive, it's welcoming, I understand now why its so popular for Tangata Whenua and Pākehā like myself... Lifes an adventure and this is part of it." Looking ahead, she hoped for "a more cohesive society, one that respects tangata whenua." Such mentor programmes didn't exist when Ihimaera was himself a young writer, but that may have helped him find his voice, he said. 46.text:
[Page 1] Historically, Māori did not have a sole leader over all the people, says historian Vincent O'Malley. O'Malley, who has just released a new book The Invasion of Waikato, Te Riri ki Tainui, spoke to Saturday Morning about the history of the Kiingitanga after its seventh monarch, Kiingi Tuheitia Pootatau Te Wherowhero, died early on Friday. After a number of Māori went to England and met Queen Victoria, they advocated for a Māori monarch, he said. "In Māori culture, there wasn't really this notion of a single leader. You saw that in some other Pacific cultures you know, Tonga, Hawaii and so on but it was something entirely new here." https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/saturday/audio/2018 953559/vincent o malley reflects on kiingi tuuheitia The Māori monarch was not set up to take away power from Queen Victoria, but rather to complement her, said O'Malley. But the wider context was that in the 1850s, settler numbers in Aotearoa were surging. In 1854, the first Parliament convened in Auckland with no Māori members, and very few Māori men were eligible to vote at the time. Members of Parliament had to own property from the Crown, and while Māori owned land, very few had a piece of paper from the Crown declaring they were the land owners, he explained. "Tainui at this time [were] developing a very prosperous economy based on feeding the settlers in Auckland, even exporting wheat to Australia, California and elsewhere," said O'Malley. But that way of life was under threat because of the exclusion of Māori from Parliament. "So that's really the context in which the kiingitanga is established in 1858. Pootatau Te Wherowhero is raised up as the first Māori King and Tuheitia is, of course, a direct descendant and the seventh Māori monarch," he said. In the beginning, the kiingitanga was seen as a "positive development" by some Pākehā. In fact, Tainui were seen as the most loyal iwi in the country and it was "inconceivable" that Tainui would be seen as rebels. "They were regarded as extremely loyal, in terms of their relationship with the Crown and with settlers," said O'Malley. But by 1858, Māori were being outnumbered by the settlers for the first time, setting the scene for the invasion of Waikato in 1863. "You had a huge number of British imperial troops arrive in the country and the context here is that in the 1860s, Britain is the world's sole superpower so Māori are fighting this great power that has the latest weapons and technology," he said. "Māori have none of that ... the British have armoured plated steamers and Māori have wooden canoes and really, this should have been no contest. "So this is what Māori [were] up against during the New Zealand Wars in the 1860s." Related

46.document_title: Monarchy a 'new' idea for Māori, historian says
46.document_summary: Historian Vincent O'Malley discusses the establishment of the Kiingitanga (Māori monarchy) in 1858, explaining that monarchy was a novel concept for Māori who historically lacked a single leader. The institution was created following Māori delegations to England and meetings with Queen Victoria, designed to complement rather than challenge Crown authority. Established during a period of rapid European settlement and Māori political exclusion—the 1854 Parliament had no Māori members—the Kiingitanga represented a response to threats to Māori prosperity and autonomy. Initially viewed positively by some Pākehā, particularly regarding Tainui's loyalty, the institution emerged amid growing settler dominance. By 1858, settlers outnumbered Māori for the first time, setting the stage for the 1863 Waikato invasion, where Māori faced British imperial forces with superior weaponry and technology.

1.fileDescription: Kaitiakitanga is a foundational Māori concept of guardianship and environmental stewardship rooted in the worldview that humans are part of nature. A kaitiaki is a guardian recognized by tangata whenua to care for natural areas such as lakes, forests, and waterways. Traditional conservation practices include temporary rāhui (resource restrictions), use of the lunar calendar (maramataka) for planting and harvesting, sustainable hunting and fishing, and blessing of mauri stones by tohunga (priests). Key spiritual concepts include mana (spiritual power), tapu (spiritual restriction), and mauri (life force). Today, kaitiakitanga is experiencing renewal as iwi (tribes) restore ecosystems and apply traditional knowledge in modern contexts. Practical examples include Ngāi Tahu's guardianship of pounamu resources, Ngāti Toa's fishery restoration at Pukerua Bay, and multi-tribal efforts to stop river pollution and protect endangered species. The document outlines challenges in collaborating with non-Māori stakeholders and details legislative frameworks such as the Resource Management Act 1991 and Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 that incorporate kaitiakitanga principles. Kaitiakitanga offers perspectives on environmental stewardship and kinship with nature, enabling Māori to fulfill ancestral responsibilities while contributing to broader environmental sustainability.

chunkHighlights.text: By Te Ahukaramū Charles Royal

Understanding kaitiakitanga Kaitiakitanga means guardianship and
protection. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the Māori world view. A kaitiaki is a guardian. This can be a person or group that cares for an area such as a lake or forest. They are given that role by the local iwi . Māori world view In the Māori world view, people are closely connected to the land and nature. Kaitiakitanga is based on this idea of humans as part of the natural world. Traditional practices In the past, people followed traditional practices when they were hunting, fishing, growing or finding food. These helped them to care for the environment. They included: temporary bans (rāhui) on taking food from an area using the lunar calendar (maramataka) to decide when to plant and harvest taking only what was needed hunting and fishing only for food, not as sport using bird snares at the right time – for example, not when the birds were breeding. Mana, tapu and mauri Mana means spiritual power. If a forest has mana , it will have plenty of flowers, fruit and birds. Tapu can mean spiritual restriction. Sometimes rāhui (restrictions) are needed to help the mana of the forest. A rāhui might stop people taking birds, fish or fruit from a certain area, or at a certain time. Mauri means life force. This must be protected in forests, rivers, gardens, lakes and the sea. Special mauri stones, which tohunga (priests) said prayers over, were used to preserve this force. Kaitiakitanga today Today there is growing interest in kaitiakitanga. Iwi are restoring their environment and culture, and using traditional ideas in the modern world. Ngāi Tahu are guardians of pounamu (greenstone) in the South Island. Te Āti Awa ki Taranaki made a claim to the government to stop pollution in their fishing areas. Four iwi (Ngāti Kahungunu, Rangitāne, Muaūpoko and Ngāti Raukawa) have come together to stop the Manawatū River being polluted. The Te Rarawa people are working to save the kūkupa (New Zealand pigeon). Kaitiakitanga has also been included in some laws,
such as the Resource Management Act 1991.

chunkHighlights.text: Legislation

Kaitiakitanga has been included in some legislation. The Resource Management Act 1991 aims to enable sustainable management of environmental resources. It states that people managing resources under the act must take kaitiakitanga into account.

The act defines kaitiakitanga as ‘the exercise of guardianship by the tangata whenua of an area in accordance with tikanga Māori in relation to natural and physical resources; and includes the ethic of stewardship’.
Kaitiakitanga was also included in the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004, where it has the same meaning.

6.fileDescription: Kennedy Warne reflects on his deep personal connection to the Hauraki Gulf in New Zealand, tracing memories from childhood through his grandfather's swordfishing boat. He explores the concept of guardianship and stewardship through the Inuit legend of the mother of the sea—a story about how people's disrespect for the ocean causes the sea's bounty to disappear until a shaman restores harmony by combing her hair. Warne connects this ancient wisdom to the Māori concept of kaitiakitanga, arguing it represents a profound stewardship that goes beyond mere resource management. He observes a growing movement of individuals taking environmental responsibility into their own hands, becoming "ministers of the environment" by caring for wetlands, forests, and oceans. The essay emphasizes humanity's forgotten relationship with the sea and calls for a return to reverence and respect for the natural world.

chunkHighlights.text: And that, I think, is what kaitiakitanga is about—a kind of stewardship far deeper than the resource management that politicians and bureaucrats understand. It is about revering the world and holding it dear.
