## Te Tikanga o 'Kaitiakitanga'

Ko 'kaitiakitanga' tētahi kupu Māori whakahirahira, ā, he maha āna tikanga. Ko te tikanga matua — **guardianship, protection, preservation, and sheltering** — arā, te tiaki, te manaaki, me te ārai i te taiao. [[1]](cite://1/1)

### Te Pūtake o te Kupu

Ko *tiaki* te tūāpū o te kupu 'kaitiakitanga'. Ko ōna tikanga: to guard, to preserve, to foster, to protect, and to shelter. Ko te kuputauritenga *kai-* he tohu mō te tangata e mahi ana i tētahi mahi. Nō reira, ko te *kaitiaki* he tangata, he rōpū rānei e tiaki ana, e manaaki ana, e ārai ana i tētahi mea. [[2]](cite://2/1)[[3]](cite://3/1)

### He Aha te Kaitiaki?

Ko te kaitiaki he tangata, he rōpū, he atua rānei e tiaki ana i tētahi taonga — ahakoa he awa, he ngahere, he roto rānei. Ko ngā atua o te taiao ngā kaitiaki tuatahi — hei tauira, ko Tāne te kaitiaki o te ngahere. Ko ngā hapū me ngā whānau e whai ake i tērā tauira. [[3]](cite://3/2)[[4]](cite://4/1)

### Te Hononga ki te Ao Māori

E ai ki te ao Māori, he hono tōtika tā te tangata ki te whenua me te taiao. Nō tēnei whakaaro ka tipu ake te kaitiakitanga. He tikanga tēnei e whakaaro ana ko te tangata he wāhanga o te taiao, kaua ko te rangatira o te taiao. [[5]](cite://5/1)[[1]](cite://1/2)

He maha ngā tikanga kaitiakitanga ō mua:

- Ko te **rāhui** — he aukati mō wāhi, mō wā rānei, kia ora ai te taiao
- Ko te **maramataka** — te mahere o ngā wā tika hei māra, hei hī ika rānei
- Ko te tikanga o te **mauri** — te hau ora o ngā awa, ngā roto, ngā ngahere
- Ko te **tapu** — ōna tikanga tiaki [[1]](cite://1/3)

### Kaitiakitanga mō ngā Taonga

E kore e mutu ana ki te taiao anake — ka taea hoki te kaitiakitanga ki ngā taonga tuku iho, pērā i ngā korowai, ngā mere pounamu, ngā pukapuka whakapapa. Ka noho ēnei taonga hei rawa tūārangi mō ngā uri katoa, ā, ka tiakina e tētahi kaitiaki i runga i te ingoa o te iwi whānui. [[6]](cite://6/1)

### Kaitiakitanga i Roto i ngā Ture

Kua whakaurua te kaitiakitanga ki roto i ngā ture o Aotearoa. Ko te Resource Management Act (RMA) 1991 tētahi — e kī ana me whai wāhi te kaitiakitanga ki ngā tikanga whakahaere taiao, ā, ko tāna whakamāramatanga: *"the exercise of guardianship by the tangata whenua of an area in accordance with tikanga Māori in relation to natural and physical resources; and includes the ethic of stewardship."* [[7]](cite://7/1)

### He Tikanga Whānui

E kī ana tētahi kaituhi: ko te kaitiakitanga he momo tiakitanga e hōhonu ake ana i te mahi whakahaere rawa noa iho — he whakaaro nui ki te ao, he manaaki i te ao, he aroha ki te ao. [[8]](cite://8/1) He tikanga tēnei e taea ana e Māori me Pākehā ngā tohutohu o ō rātou tūpuna ki tēnei ao hurihuri. [[9]](cite://9/1)

---

He pai ake tō māramatanga ki tēnei kaupapa — ka hiahia ana koe ki te mōhio ake ki ētahi tauira o te kaitiakitanga e mahi ana i Aotearoa ināianei?

1.text:
[Page 1] By Te Ahukaramū Charles Royal Understanding kaitiakitanga Kaitiakitanga means guardianship and protection. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the Māori world view. A kaitiaki is a guardian. This can be a person or group that cares for an area such as a lake or forest. They are given that role by the local iwi . Māori world view In the Māori world view, people are closely connected to the land and nature. Kaitiakitanga is based on this idea of humans as part of the natural world. Traditional practices In the past, people followed traditional practices when they were hunting, fishing, growing or finding food. These helped them to care for the environment. They included: temporary bans (rāhui) on taking food from an area using the lunar calendar (maramataka) to decide when to plant and harvest taking only what was needed hunting and fishing only for food, not as sport using bird snares at the right time for example, not when the birds were breeding. Mana, tapu and mauri Mana means spiritual power. If a forest has mana , it will have plenty of flowers, fruit and birds. Tapu can mean spiritual restriction. Sometimes rāhui (restrictions) are needed to help the mana of the forest. A rāhui might stop people taking birds, fish or fruit from a certain area, or at a certain time. Mauri means life force. This must be protected in forests, rivers, gardens, lakes and the sea. Special mauri stones, which tohunga (priests) said prayers over, were used to preserve this force. Kaitiakitanga today Today there is growing interest in kaitiakitanga. Iwi are restoring their environment and culture, and using traditional ideas in the modern world. Ngāi Tahu are guardians of pounamu (greenstone) in the South Island. Te Āti Awa ki Taranaki made a claim to the government to stop pollution in their fishing areas. Four iwi (Ngāti Kahungunu, Rangitāne, Muaūpoko and Ngāti Raukawa) have come together to stop the Manawatū River being polluted. The Te Rarawa people are working to save the kūkupa (New Zealand pigeon). Kaitiakitanga has also been included in some laws, such as the Resource Management Act 1991. Kaitiakitanga means guardianship, protection, preservation or sheltering. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the traditional Māori world view.

1.document_title: Kaitiakitanga: Māori Guardianship, Environmental Stewardship, and Traditional Conservation Practices
1.document_summary: Kaitiakitanga is a foundational Māori concept of guardianship and environmental stewardship rooted in the worldview that humans are part of nature. A kaitiaki is a guardian recognized by tangata whenua to care for natural areas such as lakes, forests, and waterways. Traditional conservation practices include temporary rāhui (resource restrictions), use of the lunar calendar (maramataka) for planting and harvesting, sustainable hunting and fishing, and blessing of mauri stones by tohunga (priests). Key spiritual concepts include mana (spiritual power), tapu (spiritual restriction), and mauri (life force). Today, kaitiakitanga is experiencing renewal as iwi (tribes) restore ecosystems and apply traditional knowledge in modern contexts. Practical examples include Ngāi Tahu's guardianship of pounamu resources, Ngāti Toa's fishery restoration at Pukerua Bay, and multi-tribal efforts to stop river pollution and protect endangered species. The document outlines challenges in collaborating with non-Māori stakeholders and details legislative frameworks such as the Resource Management Act 1991 and Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 that incorporate kaitiakitanga principles. Kaitiakitanga offers perspectives on environmental stewardship and kinship with nature, enabling Māori to fulfill ancestral responsibilities while contributing to broader environmental sustainability.

2.text:
[Page 11] Legislation Kaitiakitanga has been included in some legislation. The Resource Management Act 1991 aims to enable sustainable management of environmental resources. It states that people managing resources under the act must take kaitiakitanga into account. The act defines kaitiakitanga as ‘the exercise of guardianship by the tangata whenua of an area in accordance with tikanga Māori in relation to natural and physical resources; and includes the ethic of stewardship’. Kaitiakitanga was also included in the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004, where it has the same meaning.

[Page 7] The prefix kai means someone who carries out an action. A kaitiaki is a person, group or being that acts as a carer, guardian, protector and conserver. The gods of the natural world were considered to be the original kaitiaki for instance, Tāne, god of the forest, was the kaitiaki of the forest. All other kaitiaki emulate those original ones. Many hapū (sub tribes) and whānau (families) care for a place such as a lake or forest. They work to conserve the natural heritage, address environmental problems and reclaim traditional knowledge.

[Page 3] Kaitiakitanga can also apply to valued items. These include family heirlooms such as korowai (cloaks), mere pounamu (jade clubs) and books about whakapapa (genealogy). An item that belongs to a person later becomes the property of all their descendants. It is cared for by an individual kaitiaki on behalf of the group. The kaitiaki is responsible for bringing the object to important occasions such as funerals, and for holding information about it.

12.document_title: New Zealand Rivers: Comprehensive Guide to Geography, Ecology, Culture, and Conservation
12.document_summary:
This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's extensive river systems across both the North and South Islands, covering over 180,000 kilometres of mapped rivers including the Waikato (425 km) and Clutha (largest by volume). It details river formation through high rainfall, glacial activity, and geological processes, describing distinct river types: deep, fast-flowing rivers in the North Island hills and wide, braided rivers in the South Island's east.

The document emphasizes the profound cultural significance of rivers to Māori people, including their roles in exploration, transportation, food sources, and spiritual traditions involving taniwha (river spirits). It documents European settlement impacts including military conquest, transport use, 19th-century gold rushes, and industrial/agricultural pollution.

13.document_title: Kaitiakitanga: Māori Guardianship, Environmental Stewardship, and Traditional Conservation Practices
13.document_summary: Kaitiakitanga is a foundational Māori concept of guardianship and environmental stewardship rooted in the worldview that humans are part of nature. A kaitiaki is a guardian recognized by tangata whenua to care for natural areas such as lakes, forests, and waterways. Traditional conservation practices include temporary rāhui (resource restrictions), use of the lunar calendar (maramataka) for planting and harvesting, sustainable hunting and fishing, and blessing of mauri stones by tohunga (priests). Key spiritual concepts include mana (spiritual power), tapu (spiritual restriction), and mauri (life force). Today, kaitiakitanga is experiencing renewal as iwi (tribes) restore ecosystems and apply traditional knowledge in modern contexts. Practical examples include Ngāi Tahu's guardianship of pounamu resources, Ngāti Toa's fishery restoration at Pukerua Bay, and multi-tribal efforts to stop river pollution and protect endangered species. The document outlines challenges in collaborating with non-Māori stakeholders and details legislative frameworks such as the Resource Management Act 1991 and Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 that incorporate kaitiakitanga principles. Kaitiakitanga offers perspectives on environmental stewardship and kinship with nature, enabling Māori to fulfill ancestral responsibilities while contributing to broader environmental sustainability.

14.text:
[Page 1] In traditional Māori society, children were seen as belonging to, and being the responsibility of, the wider whānau and hapū . Children quickly learnt to identify with their hapū community. The natural parents were not the sole caregivers child raising involved grandparents, uncles, aunts, great uncles and great aunts. This collective responsibility and these kinship ties ensured the safety and welfare of children, who were seen as representing the future heritage of the tribe. This principle was conveyed in the proverb: ‘He kai poutaka me kinikini atu, he kai poutaka me horehore atu, mā te tamaiti te iho’ (pinch off a bit of the potted bird, peel off a bit of the potted bird, but the inside is for the child save the best for the child).

14.document_title: Ngā Tamariki: Māori Childhood, Education, and Youth Development - Traditional Practices to Contemporary Change
14.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores Māori childhood, education, and youth development across traditional, colonial, and contemporary periods in New Zealand. It examines traditional Māori child-rearing practices where children were raised collectively by extended whānau and hapū, cherished as the tribe's future, and educated through observation, play, and formal instruction at whare wānanga. Traditional practices included birth rituals like the tohi ceremony and the tamaiti whāngai (customary fostering) system, where grandparents and extended family served as primary educators. European influence through mission schools (early 19th century) and native schools (1867) transformed Māori childhood by introducing literacy, English language, new discipline methods, and European values. Mid-20th century urbanization disrupted traditional family structures, leading to health disparities and social challenges. The document addresses contemporary issues including child abuse and describes legislative reforms, particularly the 1989 Children, Young Persons and their Families Act, which incorporated Māori customs into child welfare systems through family group conferences. Modern cultural preservation efforts include kōhanga reo (Māori-language pre-schools) established in 1982, kura kaupapa Māori (Māori-language schools), and iwi and hapū initiatives providing scholarships and cultural immersion for Māori youth.

15.document_title: Māori Housing in New Zealand: Historical Evolution, Challenges, and Contemporary Solutions
15.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of Māori housing from pre-colonial times through the early 21st century in New Zealand. Traditionally, Māori lived in family-based kāinga (villages) with rectangular wharepuni (sleeping houses) constructed from natural materials. European settlers introduced European-style housing from the early 1800s, though most Māori initially maintained traditional dwellings. From the late 1800s, poor sanitary conditions—including inadequate water, sewerage, and overcrowding—led to disease outbreaks, prompting government intervention that resulted in the demolition of 1,256 houses and construction of 2,103 cottages by 1909. The 1918 influenza epidemic devastated Māori communities and prompted new housing initiatives including the Native Housing Act 1935. Post-WWII urbanization saw Māori migrate to cities like Auckland and Wellington, facing discrimination from landlords and living in overcrowded subdivided apartments. State housing policies effectively excluded Māori through discriminatory practices until 1944, while housing designs ignored Māori cultural values (tikanga), contributing to assimilation policies. By the 1980s-90s, Māori home ownership remained significantly lower than the general population (29-49% vs. 50-73%). Persistent problems in the early 21st century included substandard, cold, damp housing; overcrowding (23% of Māori in 2006 vs. 4% for Europeans); and poor health outcomes. Modern solutions emerged through iwi-led initiatives including papakāinga schemes, rural housing programs, and the government's Whānau Ora scheme (2010), which combines housing with health, education, and legal support, representing a shift toward Māori self-determination.

16.text:
[Page 3] And that, I think, is what kaitiakitanga is about—a kind of stewardship far deeper than the resource management that politicians and bureaucrats understand. It is about revering the world and holding it dear.

16.document_title: A Gulf in my Thinking
16.document_summary: Kennedy Warne reflects on his deep personal connection to the Hauraki Gulf in New Zealand, tracing memories from childhood through his grandfather's swordfishing boat. He explores the concept of guardianship and stewardship through the Inuit legend of the mother of the sea—a story about how people's disrespect for the ocean causes the sea's bounty to disappear until a shaman restores harmony by combing her hair. Warne connects this ancient wisdom to the Māori concept of kaitiakitanga, arguing it represents a profound stewardship that goes beyond mere resource management. He observes a growing movement of individuals taking environmental responsibility into their own hands, becoming "ministers of the environment" by caring for wetlands, forests, and oceans. The essay emphasizes humanity's forgotten relationship with the sea and calls for a return to reverence and respect for the natural world.

17.document_title: Kōura: Māori Stewardship, Conservation, and Freshwater Ecosystem Restoration in Aotearoa New Zealand
17.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection explores the ecological, cultural, and conservation significance of kōura (New Zealand freshwater crayfish) through multiple interconnected narratives. It traces the historical role of kōura in Māori diet and culture, documenting how Māori ancestors practiced kaitiakitanga (environmental stewardship) by translocating crayfish across the country for centuries to ensure food security. The document examines kōura's ecological importance as ecosystem engineers that control invasive species and restore waterway health. It details the dramatic decline of kōura populations due to trout predation, forest clearing, invasive species (particularly brown bullhead catfish and marron), and water quality degradation, with some populations experiencing up to 99% decline. The collection highlights contemporary restoration efforts led by iwi and freshwater biologists using adapted traditional harvesting methods like the tau kōura technique. It features innovative approaches including John Hollows' professional kōura farming operations in Southland wetlands, which demonstrate sustainable aquaculture, and Kāti Huirapa rūnanga's initiatives to reconnect whānau with traditional food sources. The document emphasizes that mātauranga (Māori knowledge) remains essential for freshwater conservation and advocates for transferring ecosystem management responsibility back to indigenous communities.

18.text:
[Page 9] Step up one more level on Maslow’s pyramid and you breathe the necessary air of esteem. Recognition from others, knowing one’s worth, a sense of mana—these are as essential to human wholeness as food, security and companionship, the previous three. Kearns gave Maslow’s category a further spin, speaking of the mutual esteem that grows between people and place. He spoke of how repeated engagements lead to pride and care of a space, further creating a sense of belonging. In time, an ethic of kaitiakitanga, or guardianship, develops. Of all nights to hear that message—only an hour earlier I had thrown in my lot with the Friends, paid my membership and offered my services. I could see a direct cause and effect at work. As fondness, indeed almost reliance, on the creek had grown, I had felt keenly a desire to assist its protection. At the time, that was no idle concern. There was still a possibility that the space could be compromised by the Auckland motorway extension. The direct threat of the reserve’s being sacrificed for an above ground road had been averted; the connection between New Windsor and Waterview was to be by way of a tunnel. But the details of how the construction would be managed with ecological sensitivity were still being negotiated. It was a good time to be thinking about kaitiakitanga.

18.document_title: Pilgrim at Oakley Creek: Urban Nature, Memory, and Human Flourishing
18.document_summary: This comprehensive collection of interconnected essays by Kennedy Warne explores the transformative power of Oakley Creek (Te Auaunga) in Auckland, New Zealand, examining it through multiple lenses: personal pilgrimage, human psychology, historical memory, and place attachment. The work chronicles Warne's six-month photographic journey from winter to summer solstice, inspired by contemplative writers and Zen philosophy, demonstrating how mindful observation of urban nature fosters deep ecological connection. The essays apply Maslow's hierarchy of needs to show how urban green spaces fulfill fundamental human requirements—from physiological exercise and emotional security to social belonging and self-actualization—while highlighting the critical importance of preserving these spaces as Auckland's open space availability declines. Through archival research and personal narrative, Warne traces the layered histories converging at Oakley Creek, including indigenous Māori heritage, colonial discoveries, the legacy of Carrington Psychiatric Hospital, and the story of patient Rolfe Hattaway whose artistic vision inspired modernist artists. The collection advocates for kaitiakitanga (guardianship) and "locaphilia"—binding oneself to place through loving attention, storytelling, and ceremonial engagement—demonstrating how individuals can expand a place's narrative and experience meaningful homecoming through relationship-based environmental engagement.

19.document_title: Eyes in the Land: Dune Lakes, Wetlands, and Indigenous Stewardship in Northland
19.document_summary: This comprehensive collection explores New Zealand's dune lakes and wetlands in Northland, examining their ecological significance and cultural importance to iwi communities. The articles document indigenous stewardship and scientific conservation efforts, featuring Lake Ngatu and NIWA scientist Paul Champion's research on unique flora including kuta sedge and tuatara plants. Key threats include invasive species such as hornwort, Egeria densa, Gambusia affinis, and grass carp. The collection emphasizes kaitiakitanga (environmental stewardship) as the foundation for restoration, incorporating ecological and cultural dimensions. Monitoring strategies using the LakeSPI bio-assessment tool are detailed, alongside management approaches including herbicide applications and freshwater mussel restoration. The narrative incorporates the Māori proverb "Te roto tāpokopoko, he wai whakahuihui, he pukenga ora" (a dune lake is an oasis that gathers and grows life) and explores te mana o te repo (the mana of wetlands) as intermediaries between Tāne (forests) and Tangaroa (seas). Community engagement initiatives like "Get to Know Your Dune Lake" days link lake conservation to Māori traditions and reconnect communities with their ancestral lands.

20.text:
[Page 9] If everyone foraged, would we strip the land? Wellington author Johanna Knox (Ngāti Tukorehe, Ngāti Raukawa ki te Tonga, Ngāti Ranginui, Tangata Tiriti), who wrote the book on foraging in New Zealand, thinks that eating the environment is a pretty good way of reconnecting with it. She reckons foraging could resurrect the idea of the commons—not just the tragedy of it. It could bring back the concept of places that are used and maintained by people for each other—and for future generations. That idea has been largely lost from the Pākehā world, but it’s remained intact in te ao Māori. Despite the destruction of traditional food gathering areas, despite the theft of land, the depletion of resources, and the loss of kōrero about how different species are prepared—despite all of that, the philosophy of how to gather food sustainably remains intact. It’s the concept of kaitiakitanga. “A big difference between Western environmentalism and Māori kaitiakitanga is how they see humans in the environment,” says Knox. “So in Pākehā conservation, it’s like, ‘We must keep these areas pristine. Nobody can take anything from here,’ but in te ao Māori it’s like, ‘People are part of the landscape. It’s a reciprocal relationship, so of course we’re taking stuff.’ McKenzie and Mikhail Shatura, head chef at downtown Auckland restaurant Ahi, taste the morning’s foraging. Shatura assembles a dish of quail, chickweed, huruhuru whenua and ureure. Foraged ingredients don’t form the bulk of a dish, says McKenzie, but they bring the flavours of a place onto the plate. “These are supporting characters,” he says. “So I come at foraging from the perspective that if you get right out there and involve yourself in the landscape—which means taking what you can, but respectfully and sustainably and at the same time giving back—that’s just a really good way to do things.” Raglan ecologist and rongoā practitioner Mahuru Wilcox (Ngāti Awa, Ngāti Ranginui) echoes Knox. She forages native plants traditionally used for medicinal purposes for her small business, Hau Botanicals. “How can you teach people to value something if you can’t connect to it?” she asks. “These [plants] are valued because they were important as kai or as rongoā or they were important as ancestors, as tūpuna. If you’re really thinking of our world around us as our tūpuna, as our ancestors, how would you respect your tūpuna? So using those principles for how you connect.” Even in the most densely populated parts of the city, plants move through the cycles of the year. Retreating into their roots to conserve water, springing forth with new shoots. Exploding into colour for a week or two. “It’s such a reminder in your daily life as a human that everything has a season,” says Wilcox. Over time, you start to see it: the living calendar, the shifts in weather and sunlight reflected in the plants changing, day by day, in all the gaps between the fixed and immobile parts of the city.

20.document_title: The Weed Eaters: Urban and Rural Foraging in New Zealand
20.document_summary: This comprehensive article explores the growing practice of foraging in New Zealand, examining both urban and rural contexts. The piece follows multiple narratives: in Auckland, forager Bella Burgess leads a Facebook community group on Maungawhau/Mount Eden, teaching participants to identify and harvest edible wild plants including vetch, wild brassica, pūhā, nasturtium, oxalis, and onion weed while emphasizing ethical foraging practices. In Canterbury, Peter Langlands scouts for elderflower and wild parsnips for restaurants, demonstrating how roadsides and berms provide abundant biodiversity and foraged ingredients. The article features interviews with professional foragers like Nate McKenzie and Rico Birndt who maintain sustainable harvesting practices. It highlights the cultural and philosophical dimensions of foraging, connecting it to Māori philosophy of kaitiakitanga—a reciprocal relationship with the environment—and contrasting this with Western conservation approaches. The piece explores the underlying human desire for self-reliance and independence from modern systems, noting how the surge in foraging interest during COVID-19 lockdowns reflects deeper needs for connection and resilience. The article showcases how edible plants grow abundantly in plain sight throughout New Zealand's towns and cities, challenging cultural hesitation about harvesting from public spaces while advocating for sustainable practices and "feral parks" instead of manicured lawns.

21.document_title: Between a Rock and a Hard Place
21.document_summary: This article examines the contentious Denniston Plateau mining debate, which pits resource extraction against environmental preservation. With 6.1 million tonnes of bituminous coal beneath a 150-hectare site, the proposed open-cast mine would generate 14 million tonnes of CO2 emissions when burned—equivalent to New Zealand's annual dairy herd emissions. The article explores the tension between economic benefits ($46 million in salaries for a struggling West Coast region) and environmental costs, including mercury, selenium, arsenic emissions, and climate change contributions. It presents three perspectives: exploitation versus preservation, and a Māori concept of land as taonga (treasure and resource), emphasizing guardianship (kaitiakitanga) and respect for the land's living essence. The author questions whether this traditional approach might offer a less-destructive path to prosperity.

The author argues that the traditional binary approach of designating areas for total protection or total exploitation is outdated. Drawing on Māori concepts of kaitiakitanga (stewardship), the piece advocates for a balanced approach that allows both protection and sustainable use of natural resources. 24.document_title: Blue Carbon in New Zealand: Fiords, Coastal Wetlands, and Seagrass Restoration
24.document_summary: This comprehensive collection examines New Zealand's blue carbon ecosystems and their role in climate regulation. New Zealand's fiords, particularly Doubtful Sound and Dusky Sound, store approximately 2.24 billion tonnes of carbon—about one percent of the world's seabed carbon. These fiords bury organic carbon faster than similar ecosystems worldwide due to unique geography, steep valleys, heavy rainfall, and anaerobic mud conditions. Scientists at the Cawthron Institute are pioneering seed-based seagrass restoration methods, discovering that Zostera muelleri flowers more frequently than previously believed. Seagrass ecosystems capture carbon 55 times faster than tropical rainforests and store four times more carbon per hectare in soils. Coastal wetland restoration projects like Te Wahapū o Waihī integrate mātauranga Māori with coastal ecology, with five iwi collaborating on restoration efforts. Seaweed research reveals varying decomposition rates in deep-sea environments, though scientists raise concerns about accurately measuring seaweed's carbon removal potential. The research emphasizes protecting natural carbon sinks while addressing legal complexities involving Māori rights and rangatiratanga, highlighting kaitiakitanga (stewardship) and cultural significance of coastal ecosystem restoration.

25.text:
[Page 16] [Chapter Break] On an autumn afternoon in early March, I pull off State Highway 6 just south of Hokitika, into the carpark at Mananui Bush. Powerlines stretch overhead, curving north across fields of fodder beet. Lake Mahinapua lies across the highway to the east, hidden by thick coastal bush. Through the open window, in the quiet after I switch off the engine, I hear the faint boom and hiss of Te Tai o Rehua, the Tasman Sea. A group of Pākehā men and women stand waiting in the small clearing beneath a fierce sun. Between the laughter and the bags of kai lined up in the back of a nearby van, they could be friends on a package tour except for the hefty spiral bound books in their hands and the two huge maps spread on the ground. Clifton is kneeling on the ground, pointing at the map. The others, ranged in a semicircle, are conservation ecologist Bill Lee, veteran conservation leader Jo Breese, archaeologist Katharine Watson and landscape architect Philip Blakely. COVID related work disruptions have kept mātauranga expert Marama Muru Lanning (Waikato, Ngāti Maniapoto, Ngāti Whātua) in Auckland today. On paper their depth of experience is intimidating; in person they’re attentive and intelligent, though a little fatigued. It’s their final day together in the field—they’ve visited around 90 per cent of the stewardship land parcels, and flown over those too big to take in on foot. They’ve travelled from southern Kohaihai in Kahurangi right down to Fiordland. I ask how it’s been. “Intense,” several say at once. “Bill is our resident scientist,” Breeze says, “and he’s been recording our entrances and exits to vehicles. Our record is 54 movements in a day.” “Be careful how you phrase that,” Lee says to me, straight faced. The grazed area in the photograph above is stewardship land, at the mouth of the Karamea River, at Māori Point. It’s blocks like these that are potential candidates for an assessment of low or no conservation values, which could lead to their sale. Climate advocates argue such blocks should be reforested instead. That intensity has largely come from the volume of complex information. “We rely heavily on these,” Neil says, brandishing his Conservation Value Report for the area: a compendium of DOC’s information about each block, grouped into sections such as mātauranga, ecology, landscape, recreation and heritage. Depending on the dominant values in a block, different experts have taken the lead, as the group analyses the values against what they find on the ground, debates the merits of different classifications, talks the issues through with local DOC rangers. I ask how it worked if they needed more information.

25.document_title: Stewardship Land Reclassification in New Zealand: Conservation, Māori Rights, and the Old Ghost Road
25.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection examines New Zealand's stewardship land—nine percent of Aotearoa's total land area—through interconnected narratives spanning conservation policy, indigenous rights, and economic development. The collection begins with the Old Ghost Road project in the Mokihinui Gorge, illustrating how stewardship land's lower protection status both threatened and enabled conservation initiatives, ultimately generating $4 million annually for local communities after Meridian Energy abandoned its proposed dam project. The documents trace the government's 2021 fast-tracked reclassification process, which proposed appointing expert panels to assess stewardship land within eight months. This initiative sparked significant controversy, particularly from Ngāi Tahu iwi, who filed urgent High Court proceedings citing consultation breaches and Treaty of Waitangi violations. The historical context reveals how the Crown's 1859 acquisition of the West Coast from Poutini Ngāi Tahu for £300 left the iwi with only 4,000 hectares despite claiming 151,757 hectares, with 87% of their territory now managed by DOC with minimal iwi input. The collection explores the tension between traditional conservation frameworks and contemporary approaches that integrate mātauranga (Māori knowledge) and recognize Māori cultural values extending beyond preservation to include economic and commercial use on ancestral land. Through case studies such as Lake Mahinapua, the documents examine how mana whenua and national assessment panels are collaboratively developing integrated conservation models that respect rangatiratanga while addressing concerns about mining interests and the Stockton Coal Mine on Denniston Plateau.

[Page 1] Māori AI expert Dr Karaitiana Taiuru shares his favourite whakataukī 2024 03 18 22:44:07+13:00 Dr Karaitiana Taiuru. Tino rangatiratanga: mō tātou, ā, mō kā uri ā muri ake nei. It is the whakataukī (Māori proverb) that means most to Māori data, AI and technology ethicist Dr Karaitiana Taiuru (Ngāi Tahu, Ngāti Kahungunu, Ngāti Toa). Translated to English, it means "the ability to create and control our destiny for generations to come". It links in well with his work and family life, Taiuru told RNZ Nights. For his work, it reminded Taiuru why he still does what he does and that there was a new generation of children who will not know life without AI and it was "our role to create the new normal for them". Taiuru applies a te ao Māori perspective to AI. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/nig new generation of children who will not know life without AI and it was "our role to create the new normal for them". Taiuru applies a te ao Māori perspective to AI. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/nig hts/audio/2018930609/whakatauki of the week with karaitiana taiuru Listen to the full interview on Nights "We already know that internationally, there's bias against minority peoples so what I do, in conjunction with international best practices with artificial intelligence and other technologies, is bring that Māori voice and Te Tiriti o Waitangi considerations to play." There were "a number" of cultural values that needed to be considered in terms of AI, he said. Many Māori have moko (facial tattoos) so understanding how that was considered with facial technologies was a big factor. In his personal life, the whakataukī applied to his whānau. "For me, I consider that I have an opportunity to create wealth and opportunities for my children and also for my grandchildren. "I live by that rule. I make that sure my children have the opportunities that I didn't always have, make sure they have access to education, financial resources, a home, and part of my planning in life is that my grandchildren will also have the same access and all going well in life, I should see my great grandchildren and maybe great great grandchildren whom I will also ensure that they have equal access. "And I know my children also that they consider the same sort of philosophies in life where they want to protect their whānau as well for the future." Taiuru said the whakataukī came out of working groups around the South Island when Ngāi Tahu was trying to identify a new tribal vision that would be carried into the future. It came after settlements with the Crown in 1996. "That whakataukī was the key whakataukī that came out of those hui." Related

37.document_title: Waka Jumper, Mahi and Chilly Bin Added to Oxford English Dictionary
37.document_summary: The Oxford English Dictionary has added several New Zealand words and phrases to its latest update, including "waka jumper" (a member of Parliament who switches parties during a term), "mahi" (work or activity in Māori contexts), "chilly bin" (portable insulated container), and various te reo Māori terms like "tikanga," "kapa haka," and "Aotearoan." The addition reflects the increasing use of te reo Māori in New Zealand society and media. While experts celebrate the inclusion of Māori words as a sign of language normalization, some, including Māori Language Commission chief executive Ngahiwi Apanui, expressed concerns about "Aotearoan," viewing it as inconsistent with Māori orthographic conventions. Linguists note this represents the evolving and distinctive nature of New Zealand English.

The role was eventually offered to a rangatira of great mana, Pootatau Te Wherowhero who after initially declining, accepted the role. Today the home of Te Kiingitanga is Turangawaewae in Ngaaruawaahia and for many generations Waikato whaanau have devoted their entire lives to serving their monarch. [Page 1] 2024 01 29 21:53:12+13:00 Anton Matthews is the director of Hustle Group, a company operating a bunch of restaurants and catering companies in Ōtautahi Christchurch. He's also a big advocate for people learning te reo Māori, also running online course Normalising Te Reo Māori. In the next in a weekly series, he shares a favourite whakataukī, or traditional Māori aphorism, with Emile Donovan. Ko te amorangi ki mua, ko te hāpai ō ki muri The leader at the front and the workers behind the scenes This simple whakataukī, or Māori proverb, is a multi layered favourite of Matthews. While he was fortunate to grow up immersed in te ao Māori, including being educated at kohanga reo and kura kaupapa, Matthews tells Nights anyone exposed to a lot of te reo Māori quickly learns that it’s a language rich in metaphor. “There’s the literal meaning of whatever has been said, but it often takes a couple of years (sometimes it never actually dawns on us), but there is a hidden meaning there as well. “That’s what I love about whakataukī is that yep, there's that kind of surface layer literally, what is the person saying? But what's the hidden meaning? What are they really trying to explain or what sort of message or idea are they trying to convey when they use the whakataukī? That's the beauty of language, not just te reo Māori, but any language has those kinds of beautiful nuances, I think.” Matthews says he loves all sorts of different whakataukī for different reasons and occasions, but his favourite is particularly appropriate to his work in the hospitality sector. Ko te amorangi ki mua, ko te hāpai ō ki muri has two parts to it, Matthews says. Amorangi is a term that refers to recognised iwi leaders, the ones who are front and centre when leading a pōwhiri, or welcome, onto the marae. “These are the familiar faces that everyone kind of knows… these people are highly respected. They have a lot of mana. We look to them when we need guidance.” Te hāpai ō referred to in the second part of the whakataukī is the complete opposite, Matthews says.

40.document_title: Whakataukī of the Week: Ko te amorangi ki mua, ko te hāpai ō ki muri
40.document_summary: Anton Matthews, director of Hustle Group and advocate for te reo Māori, shares his favorite whakataukī (Māori proverb): "Ko te amorangi ki mua, ko te hāpai ō ki muri" (The leader at the front and the workers behind the scenes). This multi-layered aphorism illustrates the duality and balance fundamental to te ao Māori. The amorangi represents recognized iwi leaders at the front, while te hāpai ō (food carriers) work behind the scenes. Matthews emphasizes that both roles are equally important and worthy of mana, requiring constant communication and interdependence. He applies this philosophy to hospitality, arguing that all staff—whether in the kitchen or front-of-house—develop skills valued on the marae and contribute equally to organizational success. The whakataukī demonstrates that everyone has a vital place, and no role is more important than another.

41.document_title: Kotahitanga in Action: Hundreds Gather at Treaty Grounds with Kiingitanga and Rātana
41.document_summary: On February 4, 2024, hundreds of Māori gathered at the Waitangi Treaty Grounds in a powerful display of kotahitanga (unity). Led by Kiingi Tuuheitia and Rātana Tumuaki Manuao, iwi leaders from across the country assembled to voice concerns about the government's proposed Treaty principles bill. The pōwhiri featured speeches emphasizing unity and peaceful resistance, with leaders like Ngāpuhi Rangatira Matua Hone Sadler urging iwi to remain peaceful while standing firm. Bayden Barber referenced the 1990s kotahitanga movement, calling for continued strategic planning. Te Taepa Kameta criticized Minister Shane Jones's absence, while Rāhui Papa emphasized mobilizing under mana motuhake and ensuring He Whakaputanga receives equal standing with Te Tiriti. The gathering concluded with Tainui representatives singing in harmony, marking a historic moment of Māori solidarity.

[Page 1] Dr Hinemoa Elder: How Māori proverbs can support children's wellbeing 2024 10 26 20:03:35+13:00 Over nearly 20 years as a child psychiatrist, Dr Hinemoa Elder has witnessed first hand how connection with culture can help Māori youth navigate and heal from challenges. Whakataukī (Māori proverbs) are a fun and powerful way to help rangatahi develop their own voices and find grounding in the "continuum of whakapapa", Dr Hinemoa Elder says. The child psychiatrist and author weaves observations from her professional life into the new book Dear Moko a child centred reshaping of her beloved 2020 whakataukī collection. https://www.rnz.co.nz/nation professional life into the new book Dear Moko a child centred reshaping of her beloved 2020 whakataukī collection. https://www.rnz.co.nz/nation al/programmes/saturday/audio/2018961498/hinemoa elder dear moko The idea that children should be "seen and not heard" first introduced to Aotearoa by Pākehā settlers is one that Elder challenges in Dear Moko. Although this "older, more colonised" message about the place of young people still prevails in New Zealand culture, it is critical that whānau seek to understand young people's actual lived experience, she says, as they did in generations past. "I'm constantly trying to tune into a tūpuna [ancestral] voice in thinking about their struggles and trying to retain at least some of the older kōrero." Most young people are just trying to please their families, she says, and are "exquisitely attuned" to how their whānau receives them. "I'm often saying to parents 'Hey, our teenagers, our rangatahi get a bit of a bad rap but actually they're very caring because they've been keeping their pain private in order to protect your feelings and they pay a big price for that'." An illustration from Dear Moko. As both a child psychiatrist and whānau advocate, Elder sees Māori around New Zealand facing "very serious challenges" when it comes to mental health, particularly in under served rural areas. "I'm really quite shocked about the degree of complexity and the amount of difficulty that our whānau are trying to absorb themselves without professional help at all. "We need to make sure that rural communities are better resourced with mental health services and these services are functioning as well as looking at prevention." 43.document_summary: Dr Hinemoa Elder, a child psychiatrist with nearly 20 years of experience, discusses how Māori proverbs (whakataukī) support youth wellbeing and cultural connection. [Page 1] As well as being an award winning and critically acclaimed novelist and short story writer, Witi Ihimaera is also chair of Te Kaituhi Māori, the Māori writers' organisation within the New Zealand Society of Authors. Te Kaituhi Māori have just opened applications for its 2025 Kupu Kaitiaki and Kaituhi Māori programmes, fostering emerging and developing Māori writers. It's a "mighty mentor programme," Ihimaera told RNZ's Nights. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/nights/audio/201897 7273/whakatauki of the week with witi ihimaera "In the past people like Paula Morris, people like Emma Hislop, Steph Matuku and Tanya Roxborogh have been the mentors. "And so, whoever goes in for this Māori mentor programme, they get the best teaching, and we hope will become the best in the next 20 years." Such mentor programmes didn't exist when Ihimaera was himself a young writer, but that may have helped him find his voice, he said. "I had to begin my career from a Māori perspective, and a Māori point of view. "Had I possibly had help from Pākehā institutions, then I possibly could have started to write in Pākehā ways and according to Pākehā frameworks." The Kaituhi Māori mentorship programme happened for the first time in 2024. When Ihimaera read through the work produced it brought him great joy, he said. 45.text:
[Page 1] Historically, Māori did not have a sole leader over all the people, says historian Vincent O'Malley. O'Malley, who has just released a new book The Invasion of Waikato, Te Riri ki Tainui, spoke to Saturday Morning about the history of the Kiingitanga after its seventh monarch, Kiingi Tuheitia Pootatau Te Wherowhero, died early on Friday. After a number of Māori went to England and met Queen Victoria, they advocated for a Māori monarch, he said. "In Māori culture, there wasn't really this notion of a single leader. You saw that in some other Pacific cultures you know, Tonga, Hawaii and so on but it was something entirely new here." https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/saturday/audio/2018 953559/vincent o malley reflects on kiingi tuuheitia The Māori monarch was not set up to take away power from Queen Victoria, but rather to complement her, said O'Malley. But the wider context was that in the 1850s, settler numbers in Aotearoa were surging. In 1854, the first Parliament convened in Auckland with no Māori members, and very few Māori men were eligible to vote at the time. Members of Parliament had to own property from the Crown, and while Māori owned land, very few had a piece of paper from the Crown declaring they were the land owners, he explained. "Tainui at this time [were] developing a very prosperous economy based on feeding the settlers in Auckland, even exporting wheat to Australia, California and elsewhere," said O'Malley. But that way of life was under threat because of the exclusion of Māori from Parliament. "So that's really the context in which the kiingitanga is established in 1858. Pootatau Te Wherowhero is raised up as the first Māori King and Tuheitia is, of course, a direct descendant and the seventh Māori monarch," he said. In the beginning, the kiingitanga was seen as a "positive development" by some Pākehā. In fact, Tainui were seen as the most loyal iwi in the country and it was "inconceivable" that Tainui would be seen as rebels. "They were regarded as extremely loyal, in terms of their relationship with the Crown and with settlers," said O'Malley. But by 1858, Māori were being outnumbered by the settlers for the first time, setting the scene for the invasion of Waikato in 1863. "You had a huge number of British imperial troops arrive in the country and the context here is that in the 1860s, Britain is the world's sole superpower so Māori are fighting this great power that has the latest weapons and technology," he said. "Māori have none of that ... the British have armoured plated steamers and Māori have wooden canoes and really, this should have been no contest. "So this is what Māori [were] up against during the New Zealand Wars in the 1860s." Related

45.document_title: Monarchy a 'new' idea for Māori, historian says
45.document_summary: Historian Vincent O'Malley discusses the establishment of the Kiingitanga (Māori monarchy) in 1858, explaining that monarchy was a novel concept for Māori who historically lacked a single leader. The institution was created following Māori delegations to England and meetings with Queen Victoria, designed to complement rather than challenge Crown authority. Established during a period of rapid European settlement and Māori political exclusion—the 1854 Parliament had no Māori members—the Kiingitanga represented a response to threats to Māori prosperity and autonomy. Initially viewed positively by some Pākehā, particularly regarding Tainui's loyalty, the institution emerged amid growing settler dominance. By 1858, settlers outnumbered Māori for the first time, setting the stage for the 1863 Waikato invasion, where Māori faced British imperial forces with superior weaponry and technology.

1.fileDescription: Kaitiakitanga is a foundational Māori concept of guardianship and environmental stewardship rooted in the worldview that humans are part of nature. A kaitiaki is a guardian recognized by tangata whenua to care for natural areas such as lakes, forests, and waterways. Traditional conservation practices include temporary rāhui (resource restrictions), use of the lunar calendar (maramataka) for planting and harvesting, sustainable hunting and fishing, and blessing of mauri stones by tohunga (priests). Key spiritual concepts include mana (spiritual power), tapu (spiritual restriction), and mauri (life force). Today, kaitiakitanga is experiencing renewal as iwi (tribes) restore ecosystems and apply traditional knowledge in modern contexts. Practical examples include Ngāi Tahu's guardianship of pounamu resources, Ngāti Toa's fishery restoration at Pukerua Bay, and multi-tribal efforts to stop river pollution and protect endangered species. The document outlines challenges in collaborating with non-Māori stakeholders and details legislative frameworks such as the Resource Management Act 1991 and Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 that incorporate kaitiakitanga principles. Kaitiakitanga offers perspectives on environmental stewardship and kinship with nature, enabling Māori to fulfill ancestral responsibilities while contributing to broader environmental sustainability.

chunkHighlights.text: By Te Ahukaramū Charles Royal

Understanding kaitiakitanga Kaitiakitanga means guardianship and
protection. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the Māori world view. A kaitiaki is a guardian. This can be a person or group that cares for an area such as a lake or forest. They are given that role by the local iwi . Māori world view In the Māori world view, people are closely connected to the land and nature. Kaitiakitanga is based on this idea of humans as part of the natural world. Traditional practices In the past, people followed traditional practices when they were hunting, fishing, growing or finding food. These helped them to care for the environment. They included: temporary bans (rāhui) on taking food from an area using the lunar calendar (maramataka) to decide when to plant and harvest taking only what was needed hunting and fishing only for food, not as sport using bird snares at the right time – for example, not when the birds were breeding. Mana, tapu and mauri Mana means spiritual power. If a forest has mana , it will have plenty of flowers, fruit and birds. Tapu can mean spiritual restriction. Sometimes rāhui (restrictions) are needed to help the mana of the forest. A rāhui might stop people taking birds, fish or fruit from a certain area, or at a certain time. Mauri means life force. This must be protected in forests, rivers, gardens, lakes and the sea. Special mauri stones, which tohunga (priests) said prayers over, were used to preserve this force. Kaitiakitanga today Today there is growing interest in kaitiakitanga. Iwi are restoring their environment and culture, and using traditional ideas in the modern world. Ngāi Tahu are guardians of pounamu (greenstone) in the South Island. Te Āti Awa ki Taranaki made a claim to the government to stop pollution in their fishing areas. Four iwi (Ngāti Kahungunu, Rangitāne, Muaūpoko and Ngāti Raukawa) have come together to stop the Manawatū River being polluted. The Te Rarawa people are working to save the kūkupa (New Zealand pigeon). Kaitiakitanga has also been included in some laws,
such as the Resource Management Act 1991.

chunkHighlights.text: Legislation

Kaitiakitanga has been included in some legislation. The Resource Management Act 1991 aims to enable sustainable management of environmental resources. It states that people managing resources under the act must take kaitiakitanga into account.

The act defines kaitiakitanga as ‘the exercise of guardianship by the tangata whenua of an area in accordance with tikanga Māori in relation to natural and physical resources; and includes the ethic of stewardship’.
Kaitiakitanga was also included in the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004, where it has the same meaning.

8.fileDescription: Kennedy Warne reflects on his deep personal connection to the Hauraki Gulf in New Zealand, tracing memories from childhood through his grandfather's swordfishing boat. He explores the concept of guardianship and stewardship through the Inuit legend of the mother of the sea—a story about how people's disrespect for the ocean causes the sea's bounty to disappear until a shaman restores harmony by combing her hair. Warne connects this ancient wisdom to the Māori concept of kaitiakitanga, arguing it represents a profound stewardship that goes beyond mere resource management. He observes a growing movement of individuals taking environmental responsibility into their own hands, becoming "ministers of the environment" by caring for wetlands, forests, and oceans. The essay emphasizes humanity's forgotten relationship with the sea and calls for a return to reverence and respect for the natural world.

chunkHighlights.text: And that, I think, is what kaitiakitanga is about—a kind of stewardship far deeper than the resource management that politicians and bureaucrats understand. It is about revering the world and holding it dear.

[Page 1] In traditional Māori society, children were seen as belonging to, and being the responsibility of, the wider whānau and hapū . Children quickly learnt to identify with their hapū community. Members of Parliament had to own property from the Crown, and while Māori owned land, very few had a piece of paper from the Crown declaring they were the land owners, he explained. "Tainui at this time [were] developing a very prosperous economy based on feeding the settlers in Auckland, even exporting wheat to Australia, California and elsewhere," said O'Malley. But that way of life was under threat because of the exclusion of Māori from Parliament. "So that's really the context in which the kiingitanga is established in 1858. response.response_text:
## Te Tikanga o 'Kaitiakitanga'

Ko **kaitiakitanga** he kupu whakamārama i te mahi tiaki, i te mahi ārai, i te mahi tohu hoki mō te taiao. I roto i te reo Ingarihi, ko tōna tikanga ko *guardianship*, *protection*, *preservation* me *stewardship* — arā, te tiaki i te ao tūroa. [[1]](cite://1/1)

He kupu ahu mai i te kupu **tiaki**, ā, ko tōna tikanga ko te tiaki, ko te tohu, ko te ārai, ko te haumaru hoki. Nō reira, ko ngā whakaaro o te tiakitanga me te ārainga kei te pūtake o kaitiakitanga. [[2]](cite://2/1) Ko te **kai-** he tāruarua e tohu ana i tētahi e mahi ana i tētahi mahi — ā, ko te **kaitiaki** he tangata, he rōpū, he atua rānei e mahi ana hei tiaki, hei kaihaumaru i tētahi wāhi. [[3]](cite://3/1)

## Te Ao Māori me Kaitiakitanga

I roto i te ao Māori, he piri tōpū tō te tangata ki te whenua me te taiao whānui. Ko kaitiakitanga tētahi whakaaro e tipu ake ana i tēnei hononga, ā, e whakahua ana i tērā hononga i roto i ngā horopaki hou. [[4]](cite://4/1) He ara whakahaere taiao tēnei i runga i te tirohanga ao Māori — arā, ko te tangata he wāhanga o te taiao, ehara ia i te rangatira nōna anō. [[1]](cite://1/2)

Ko ngā atua o te ao tūroa i kiia ko rātou ngā kaitiaki tuatahi. Hei tauira, ko **Tāne**, ko ia te kaitiaki o te ngahere. Ko ngā kaitiaki katoa o muri iho e aro atu ana ki ērā tūāhuatanga tapu. [[3]](cite://3/2)

## Ko Wai te Kaitiaki?

Ka taea e tētahi tangata, e tētahi hapū, e tētahi iwi rānei te tū hei kaitiaki — heoi, me whakaaetia rātou e ngā tangata whenua o taua rohe. [[5]](cite://5/1) Ka haere tēnei kawenga tiaki i tētahi whakatupuranga ki tētahi atu — he āhua "ancestral mantle" e whakatakotoria ana ki ngā pakihiwi o ia reanga, ia reanga. [[6]](cite://6/1)

E kore e mutu ana ngā āhuatanga o kaitiakitanga ki te taiao anake. Ka taea anō te tono atu ki ngā **taonga tuku iho** — pērā i ngā korowai (cloaks), ngā mere pounamu, ngā pukapuka whakapapa hoki. Ko ēnei taonga, ahakoa nō tētahi tangata i mua, ka tūāhurihia hei taonga nō ngā uri katoa, ā, ka tiakina e tētahi kaitiaki mō te katoa. [[7]](cite://7/1)

## Kaitiakitanga i Ēnei Rā

Kei roto hoki a kaitiakitanga i ētahi ture o Aotearoa — pērā i te Resource Management Act (RMA) 1991, e tino whakamāramatia ana i tērā ture ko kaitiakitanga ko "the exercise of guardianship by the tangata whenua of an area in accordance with tikanga Māori in relation to natural and physical resources; and includes the ethic of stewardship." [[8]](cite://8/1)

He mea nui hoki tēnei kaupeka mō ngā Māori o ēnei rā — ko ia te ara e tūhono ai rātou ki ngā tūmanako o ō rātou tūpuna. Mō ngā tāngata ehara i te Māori, ka tukua e kaitiakitanga tētahi whakaaro e pā ana ki te whanaungatanga ki te taiao, ā, he nui te hua o tērā i roto i tēnei ao e tūkino ana i te taiao. [[9]](cite://9/1)

E ai ki tētahi kōrero, ko kaitiakitanga "a kind of stewardship far deeper than the resource management that politicians and bureaucrats understand. It is about revering the world and holding it dear." [[10]](cite://10/1)

He pātai āu: Ka hiahia koe ki te mōhio ake mō ēhea iwi e mahi ana i ngā kaupeka o kaitiakitanga i ēnei rā?

1.text:
[Page 1] By Te Ahukaramū Charles Royal Understanding kaitiakitanga Kaitiakitanga means guardianship and protection. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the Māori world view. A kaitiaki is a guardian. This can be a person or group that cares for an area such as a lake or forest. They are given that role by the local iwi . Māori world view In the Māori world view, people are closely connected to the land and nature. Kaitiakitanga is based on this idea of humans as part of the natural world. Traditional practices In the past, people followed traditional practices when they were hunting, fishing, growing or finding food. These helped them to care for the environment. They included: temporary bans (rāhui) on taking food from an area using the lunar calendar (maramataka) to decide when to plant and harvest taking only what was needed hunting and fishing only for food, not as sport using bird snares at the right time for example, not when the birds were breeding. Mana, tapu and mauri Mana means spiritual power. If a forest has mana , it will have plenty of flowers, fruit and birds. Tapu can mean spiritual restriction. Sometimes rāhui (restrictions) are needed to help the mana of the forest. A rāhui might stop people taking birds, fish or fruit from a certain area, or at a certain time. Mauri means life force. This must be protected in forests, rivers, gardens, lakes and the sea. Special mauri stones, which tohunga (priests) said prayers over, were used to preserve this force. Kaitiakitanga today Today there is growing interest in kaitiakitanga. Iwi are restoring their environment and culture, and using traditional ideas in the modern world. Ngāi Tahu are guardians of pounamu (greenstone) in the South Island. Te Āti Awa ki Taranaki made a claim to the government to stop pollution in their fishing areas. Four iwi (Ngāti Kahungunu, Rangitāne, Muaūpoko and Ngāti Raukawa) have come together to stop the Manawatū River being polluted. The Te Rarawa people are working to save the kūkupa (New Zealand pigeon). Kaitiakitanga has also been included in some laws, such as the Resource Management Act 1991. Kaitiakitanga means guardianship, protection, preservation or sheltering. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the traditional Māori world view.

1.document_title: Kaitiakitanga: Māori Guardianship, Environmental Stewardship, and Traditional Conservation Practices
1.document_summary: Kaitiakitanga is a foundational Māori concept of guardianship and environmental stewardship rooted in the worldview that humans are part of nature. A kaitiaki is a guardian recognized by tangata whenua to care for natural areas such as lakes, forests, and waterways. Traditional conservation practices include temporary rāhui (resource restrictions), use of the lunar calendar (maramataka) for planting and harvesting, sustainable hunting and fishing, and blessing of mauri stones by tohunga (priests). Key spiritual concepts include mana (spiritual power), tapu (spiritual restriction), and mauri (life force). Today, kaitiakitanga is experiencing renewal as iwi (tribes) restore ecosystems and apply traditional knowledge in modern contexts. Practical examples include Ngāi Tahu's guardianship of pounamu resources, Ngāti Toa's fishery restoration at Pukerua Bay, and multi-tribal efforts to stop river pollution and protect endangered species. The document outlines challenges in collaborating with non-Māori stakeholders and details legislative frameworks such as the Resource Management Act 1991 and Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 that incorporate kaitiakitanga principles. Kaitiakitanga offers perspectives on environmental stewardship and kinship with nature, enabling Māori to fulfill ancestral responsibilities while contributing to broader environmental sustainability.

2.text:
[Page 11] Legislation Kaitiakitanga has been included in some legislation. The Resource Management Act 1991 aims to enable sustainable management of environmental resources. It states that people managing resources under the act must take kaitiakitanga into account. The act defines kaitiakitanga as ‘the exercise of guardianship by the tangata whenua of an area in accordance with tikanga Māori in relation to natural and physical resources; and includes the ethic of stewardship’. Kaitiakitanga was also included in the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004, where it has the same meaning.

4.text:
[Page 7] The prefix kai means someone who carries out an action. A kaitiaki is a person, group or being that acts as a carer, guardian, protector and conserver. The gods of the natural world were considered to be the original kaitiaki for instance, Tāne, god of the forest, was the kaitiaki of the forest. All other kaitiaki emulate those original ones. Many hapū (sub tribes) and whānau (families) care for a place such as a lake or forest. They work to conserve the natural heritage, address environmental problems and reclaim traditional knowledge.

[Page 3] Kaitiakitanga can also apply to valued items. These include family heirlooms such as korowai (cloaks), mere pounamu (jade clubs) and books about whakapapa (genealogy). An item that belongs to a person later becomes the property of all their descendants. It is cared for by an individual kaitiaki on behalf of the group. The kaitiaki is responsible for bringing the object to important occasions such as funerals, and for holding information about it.

[Page 11] Challenges There are some challenges in applying kaitiakitanga today. Practitioners need to understand traditional concepts such as mana (status), tapu (spiritual restriction) and mauri (the life principle), and relate them to the modern setting. Forest or waterway management involves parties such as land owners and regional authorities, who may have different world views and values.

14.document_title: Hawke's Bay Region: Comprehensive Geography, History, Society, and Development
14.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an extensive overview of Hawke's Bay, a diverse region in New Zealand's North Island. Geographically, it features varied landscapes including mountains, hills, coastlines, and plains, positioned at the intersection of the Australian and Pacific tectonic plates, making it earthquake-prone. The region's geology includes mudstone hills, limestone ranges, and sedimentary plains, with notable dinosaur fossil discoveries. Historically, Māori settlement began around 1250-1300 CE, with Ngāti Kahungunu becoming the dominant iwi by the 1500s. European contact commenced with Captain Cook's 1769 visit, followed by whalers, traders, and missionaries. From 1849 onwards, pastoral farming expanded dramatically, with refrigeration in 1884 enabling meat production. The region's economy evolved to become New Zealand's largest apple, peach, and squash-growing area, and the second-largest wine region. The 1931 earthquake led to extensive art deco reconstruction that defines Napier today. Infrastructure includes railways (1891-1943), hydroelectric power stations (1926-1948), and Napier Airport (1932). Demographically, the 2013 population was 78.1% European and 24.2% Māori, with significant regional inequality between prosperous Napier-Hastings urban centers and the declining Wairoa district. Social challenges include areas of extreme deprivation and limited employment diversity, with agriculture representing 17.6% of employment versus 5.8% nationally.

17.document_title: Kōura: Māori Stewardship, Conservation, and Freshwater Ecosystem Restoration in Aotearoa New Zealand

19.document_title: Eyes in the Land: Dune Lakes, Wetlands, and Indigenous Stewardship in Northland
19.document_summary: This comprehensive collection explores New Zealand's dune lakes and wetlands in Northland, examining their ecological significance and cultural importance to iwi communities. The articles document indigenous stewardship and scientific conservation efforts, featuring Lake Ngatu and NIWA scientist Paul Champion's research on unique flora including kuta sedge and tuatara plants. Key threats include invasive species such as hornwort, Egeria densa, Gambusia affinis, and grass carp. Monitoring strategies using the LakeSPI bio-assessment tool are detailed, alongside management approaches including herbicide applications and freshwater mussel restoration. The narrative incorporates the Māori proverb "Te roto tāpokopoko, he wai whakahuihui, he pukenga ora" (a dune lake is an oasis that gathers and grows life) and explores te mana o te repo (the mana of wetlands) as intermediaries between Tāne (forests) and Tangaroa (seas). 20.text:
[Page 9] If everyone foraged, would we strip the land? Wellington author Johanna Knox (Ngāti Tukorehe, Ngāti Raukawa ki te Tonga, Ngāti Ranginui, Tangata Tiriti), who wrote the book on foraging in New Zealand, thinks that eating the environment is a pretty good way of reconnecting with it. She reckons foraging could resurrect the idea of the commons—not just the tragedy of it. It could bring back the concept of places that are used and maintained by people for each other—and for future generations. That idea has been largely lost from the Pākehā world, but it’s remained intact in te ao Māori. Despite the destruction of traditional food gathering areas, despite the theft of land, the depletion of resources, and the loss of kōrero about how different species are prepared—despite all of that, the philosophy of how to gather food sustainably remains intact. It’s the concept of kaitiakitanga. “A big difference between Western environmentalism and Māori kaitiakitanga is how they see humans in the environment,” says Knox. “So in Pākehā conservation, it’s like, ‘We must keep these areas pristine. Nobody can take anything from here,’ but in te ao Māori it’s like, ‘People are part of the landscape. It’s a reciprocal relationship, so of course we’re taking stuff.’ McKenzie and Mikhail Shatura, head chef at downtown Auckland restaurant Ahi, taste the morning’s foraging. Shatura assembles a dish of quail, chickweed, huruhuru whenua and ureure. Foraged ingredients don’t form the bulk of a dish, says McKenzie, but they bring the flavours of a place onto the plate. “These are supporting characters,” he says. “So I come at foraging from the perspective that if you get right out there and involve yourself in the landscape—which means taking what you can, but respectfully and sustainably and at the same time giving back—that’s just a really good way to do things.” Raglan ecologist and rongoā practitioner Mahuru Wilcox (Ngāti Awa, Ngāti Ranginui) echoes Knox. She forages native plants traditionally used for medicinal purposes for her small business, Hau Botanicals. “How can you teach people to value something if you can’t connect to it?” she asks. “These [plants] are valued because they were important as kai or as rongoā or they were important as ancestors, as tūpuna. If you’re really thinking of our world around us as our tūpuna, as our ancestors, how would you respect your tūpuna? So using those principles for how you connect.” Even in the most densely populated parts of the city, plants move through the cycles of the year. Retreating into their roots to conserve water, springing forth with new shoots. Exploding into colour for a week or two. “It’s such a reminder in your daily life as a human that everything has a season,” says Wilcox. Over time, you start to see it: the living calendar, the shifts in weather and sunlight reflected in the plants changing, day by day, in all the gaps between the fixed and immobile parts of the city.

The article explores the tension between economic benefits ($46 million in salaries for a struggling West Coast region) and environmental costs, including mercury, selenium, arsenic emissions, and climate change contributions. It presents three perspectives: exploitation versus preservation, and a Māori concept of land as taonga (treasure and resource), emphasizing guardianship (kaitiakitanga) and respect for the land's living essence. 24.document_title: Blue Carbon in New Zealand: Fiords, Coastal Wetlands, and Seagrass Restoration
24.document_summary: This comprehensive collection examines New Zealand's blue carbon ecosystems and their role in climate regulation. New Zealand's fiords, particularly Doubtful Sound and Dusky Sound, store approximately 2.24 billion tonnes of carbon—about one percent of the world's seabed carbon. These fiords bury organic carbon faster than similar ecosystems worldwide due to unique geography, steep valleys, heavy rainfall, and anaerobic mud conditions. Scientists at the Cawthron Institute are pioneering seed-based seagrass restoration methods, discovering that Zostera muelleri flowers more frequently than previously believed. Seagrass ecosystems capture carbon 55 times faster than tropical rainforests and store four times more carbon per hectare in soils. Coastal wetland restoration projects like Te Wahapū o Waihī integrate mātauranga Māori with coastal ecology, with five iwi collaborating on restoration efforts. Seaweed research reveals varying decomposition rates in deep-sea environments, though scientists raise concerns about accurately measuring seaweed's carbon removal potential. The research emphasizes protecting natural carbon sinks while addressing legal complexities involving Māori rights and rangatiratanga, highlighting kaitiakitanga (stewardship) and cultural significance of coastal ecosystem restoration.

25.text:
[Page 16] [Chapter Break] On an autumn afternoon in early March, I pull off State Highway 6 just south of Hokitika, into the carpark at Mananui Bush. Powerlines stretch overhead, curving north across fields of fodder beet. Lake Mahinapua lies across the highway to the east, hidden by thick coastal bush. Through the open window, in the quiet after I switch off the engine, I hear the faint boom and hiss of Te Tai o Rehua, the Tasman Sea. A group of Pākehā men and women stand waiting in the small clearing beneath a fierce sun. Between the laughter and the bags of kai lined up in the back of a nearby van, they could be friends on a package tour except for the hefty spiral bound books in their hands and the two huge maps spread on the ground. Clifton is kneeling on the ground, pointing at the map. The others, ranged in a semicircle, are conservation ecologist Bill Lee, veteran conservation leader Jo Breese, archaeologist Katharine Watson and landscape architect Philip Blakely. COVID related work disruptions have kept mātauranga expert Marama Muru Lanning (Waikato, Ngāti Maniapoto, Ngāti Whātua) in Auckland today. On paper their depth of experience is intimidating; in person they’re attentive and intelligent, though a little fatigued. It’s their final day together in the field—they’ve visited around 90 per cent of the stewardship land parcels, and flown over those too big to take in on foot. They’ve travelled from southern Kohaihai in Kahurangi right down to Fiordland. I ask how it’s been. “Intense,” several say at once. “Bill is our resident scientist,” Breeze says, “and he’s been recording our entrances and exits to vehicles. Our record is 54 movements in a day.” “Be careful how you phrase that,” Lee says to me, straight faced. The grazed area in the photograph above is stewardship land, at the mouth of the Karamea River, at Māori Point. It’s blocks like these that are potential candidates for an assessment of low or no conservation values, which could lead to their sale. Climate advocates argue such blocks should be reforested instead. That intensity has largely come from the volume of complex information. “We rely heavily on these,” Neil says, brandishing his Conservation Value Report for the area: a compendium of DOC’s information about each block, grouped into sections such as mātauranga, ecology, landscape, recreation and heritage. Depending on the dominant values in a block, different experts have taken the lead, as the group analyses the values against what they find on the ground, debates the merits of different classifications, talks the issues through with local DOC rangers. I ask how it worked if they needed more information.

25.document_title: Stewardship Land Reclassification in New Zealand: Conservation, Māori Rights, and the Old Ghost Road
25.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection examines New Zealand's stewardship land—nine percent of Aotearoa's total land area—through interconnected narratives spanning conservation policy, indigenous rights, and economic development. The collection begins with the Old Ghost Road project in the Mokihinui Gorge, illustrating how stewardship land's lower protection status both threatened and enabled conservation initiatives, ultimately generating $4 million annually for local communities after Meridian Energy abandoned its proposed dam project. The documents trace the government's 2021 fast-tracked reclassification process, which proposed appointing expert panels to assess stewardship land within eight months. This initiative sparked significant controversy, particularly from Ngāi Tahu iwi, who filed urgent High Court proceedings citing consultation breaches and Treaty of Waitangi violations. The historical context reveals how the Crown's 1859 acquisition of the West Coast from Poutini Ngāi Tahu for £300 left the iwi with only 4,000 hectares despite claiming 151,757 hectares, with 87% of their territory now managed by DOC with minimal iwi input. The collection explores the tension between traditional conservation frameworks and contemporary approaches that integrate mātauranga (Māori knowledge) and recognize Māori cultural values extending beyond preservation to include economic and commercial use on ancestral land. Through case studies such as Lake Mahinapua, the documents examine how mana whenua and national assessment panels are collaboratively developing integrated conservation models that respect rangatiratanga while addressing concerns about mining interests and the Stockton Coal Mine on Denniston Plateau.

[Page 1] Māori AI expert Dr Karaitiana Taiuru shares his favourite whakataukī 2024 03 18 22:44:07+13:00 Dr Karaitiana Taiuru. Tino rangatiratanga: mō tātou, ā, mō kā uri ā muri ake nei. It is the whakataukī (Māori proverb) that means most to Māori data, AI and technology ethicist Dr Karaitiana Taiuru (Ngāi Tahu, Ngāti Kahungunu, Ngāti Toa). Translated to English, it means "the ability to create and control our destiny for generations to come". It links in well with his work and family life, Taiuru told RNZ Nights. For his work, it reminded Taiuru why he still does what he does and that there was a new generation of children who will not know life without AI and it was "our role to create the new normal for them". Taiuru applies a te ao Māori perspective to AI. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/nig new generation of children who will not know life without AI and it was "our role to create the new normal for them". Taiuru applies a te ao Māori perspective to AI. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/nig hts/audio/2018930609/whakatauki of the week with karaitiana taiuru Listen to the full interview on Nights "We already know that internationally, there's bias against minority peoples so what I do, in conjunction with international best practices with artificial intelligence and other technologies, is bring that Māori voice and Te Tiriti o Waitangi considerations to play." There were "a number" of cultural values that needed to be considered in terms of AI, he said. Many Māori have moko (facial tattoos) so understanding how that was considered with facial technologies was a big factor. In his personal life, the whakataukī applied to his whānau. "For me, I consider that I have an opportunity to create wealth and opportunities for my children and also for my grandchildren. "I live by that rule. I make that sure my children have the opportunities that I didn't always have, make sure they have access to education, financial resources, a home, and part of my planning in life is that my grandchildren will also have the same access and all going well in life, I should see my great grandchildren and maybe great great grandchildren whom I will also ensure that they have equal access. "And I know my children also that they consider the same sort of philosophies in life where they want to protect their whānau as well for the future." Taiuru said the whakataukī came out of working groups around the South Island when Ngāi Tahu was trying to identify a new tribal vision that would be carried into the future. It came after settlements with the Crown in 1996. "That whakataukī was the key whakataukī that came out of those hui." Related
